AI Visibility Assessment: 实解智能 (SolveReal Systems)

Website reviewed: https://me.itheheda.online/
Assessment date: September 30, 2026
Language of this report: English

Executive Summary

SolveReal Systems presents a clear, honest, and technically competent picture of its core business: designing and delivering custom AI automation systems for small and medium-sized businesses in China. The website explains what the company does, how it works, and — unusually — what it will not do. This clarity is a genuine strength for AI visibility.

However, the site currently leaves several important questions unanswered that AI systems and prospective buyers alike would need to resolve before choosing this provider. The most significant gaps are the absence of verifiable company identity details, the lack of concrete project evidence that can be independently checked, and the absence of dedicated service pages that AI systems can easily retrieve and cite. The domain name itself (me.itheheda.online) does not match the brand, which adds avoidable friction to trust-building.

The good news: the site already has a strong technical foundation (score 90/100), publishes robots.txt, sitemap.xml, and llms.txt, and maintains an active, well-written content program. The improvements needed are about filling information gaps and restructuring existing content — not fixing broken fundamentals.

What the Website Communicates Today

Business Identity and Positioning

The homepage immediately identifies the company as 实解智能 (SolveReal Systems), a China-based provider of enterprise AI system design and delivery. The target audience is clearly stated: small and medium-sized business owners and operations leaders who have repetitive manual workflows that could benefit from AI automation.

The core value proposition is distinctive and well-articulated: the company does not sell fixed industry templates. Every engagement starts from the client's actual workflow — the real steps, frequency, responsible persons, inputs, outputs, and exceptions. This "start from your real process" positioning is repeated consistently across the homepage, services page, about page, and all four project pages.

Service Description

The site describes four capability areas:

  1. Multi-source intake — consolidating documents, spreadsheets, and business web pages into one traceable operating record
  2. Repeated decisions and entry — giving stable rules to the system while humans retain exceptions and high-risk decisions
  3. Handoffs between systems — carrying state across files and business systems with fewer manual transfers
  4. Recovery and human review — recording exceptions and recovery points so operations can continue after interruptions

These four areas are presented as numbered lists with clear semantic hierarchy. An AI system reading this page can extract the service scope without ambiguity.

The delivery method is described as a four-stage process: diagnose the current workflow, design the human boundary, validate with real samples, and deliver with traceable evidence. This is repeated consistently across all pages, which helps AI systems associate the company with a specific, repeatable methodology.

What the Site Explicitly Does Not Claim

One of the site's most distinctive features is its explicit boundary-setting. The company states it will not:

  • Sell fixed industry templates
  • Promise fully unattended operation
  • Use fabricated metrics or unapproved client identities as sales proof
  • Treat an initial submission as an automatic quote
  • Present technical implementation as legal compliance or security certification

This honesty is rare and valuable. For AI systems that assess credibility, this transparency signals a provider that understands the limits of what it can promise. It also helps the site stand out from competitors who make inflated claims.

Project Evidence

The site lists four projects, each described with a consistent three-part structure: the customer's current workflow, which steps the system takes over, and what the customer gains. The projects are:

  1. Open GEO Console — a public product that diagnoses a website's visibility in AI search (marked as currently available)
  2. Hermes Notebook — a deployable enterprise knowledge engine
  3. Freight Lead Agent — a deployable system for finding and contacting target companies (featured in detail)
  4. Codex Feishu Bridge — a deployable system connecting OpenAI's Codex to Feishu workspaces

Each project page includes explicit limitations. For example, Freight Lead Agent processes public business information only and requires human review of all outreach content. Hermes Notebook only provides the knowledge organization kernel — upper-layer applications must be built separately.

The projects are framed as reference examples, not prescriptive products. Every project page concludes with: "Your business does not need to copy this project; diagnosis starts from the actual workflow."

Content Library

The site maintains an active content program with 22 Chinese articles and 14 English articles (as of the assessment date), covering GEO methodology, AI search visibility, and enterprise AI workflows. The articles are dated August–September 2026, indicating recent publishing activity.

The content is practical and evidence-oriented, repeatedly emphasizing real sample testing, clear human/AI responsibility boundaries, and traceable records. Several articles are technically accurate and appropriately hedged — for example, the article on how language models read web pages correctly notes that Google has no fixed ideal length requirement and that llms.txt is not a required condition for Google AI search.

How AI Systems Currently See This Site

What AI Systems Can Readily Extract

Based on the page content and structure, an AI system asked "Which companies in China can design and deliver custom AI automation systems?" would find the following directly answerable:

  • Company name: 实解智能 / SolveReal Systems
  • Service: Enterprise AI system design and delivery
  • Location: China
  • Target audience: Small and medium-sized businesses
  • Delivery approach: Four-stage method starting from real workflow diagnosis
  • Human oversight: Explicitly retained for key decisions and high-risk actions

The site's structured presentation — numbered lists, clear headings, consistent terminology — makes this information relatively easy for AI systems to parse and cite.

What AI Systems Cannot Currently Determine

An AI system would struggle to answer several questions that a prospective buyer would reasonably ask:

  1. Who exactly is behind this company? The site identifies the responsible person only as "fengc" — no full name, position, background, or credentials. The Facebook profile references "Chao Feng," but this connection is not made on the website itself.

  2. Is this a registered business? No company registration information, office address, team size, or founding date is provided anywhere on the site.

  3. Can the projects be independently verified? No demo links, code repositories, deployment documentation, or customer acceptance records are provided. The site states this is intentional — only reviewed facts are published — but this limits what AI systems can confirm.

  4. What does this cost? No pricing information or indicative ranges are provided.

  5. What technology is used? No specific AI models or platforms are disclosed.

  6. Is the contact information valid? The email address appears as a redacted or placeholder value in the page source. The WeChat ID "404" may indicate a placeholder or error. The English contact form was observed in a loading state.

How AI Systems Currently Describe This Company

Based on the retained observations, an AI system would likely describe SolveReal Systems as:

A China-based provider of enterprise AI automation systems that starts from real workflow diagnosis, retains human oversight for key decisions, and delivers runnable systems with traceable evidence. The company explicitly avoids fixed templates and inflated promises.

This is an accurate but incomplete picture. The missing elements — verifiable identity, independent project evidence, pricing signals, and technical specifics — would likely cause an AI system to present this company as one option among several, without the confidence that would come from verifiable credentials.

What the Site's Own GEO Analysis Says About Itself

The site's own Open GEO Console product has already analyzed this website. The sample report (dated September 4, 2026) identifies three gaps:

  1. Lack of clear service listings — the four capability areas are described but not presented as distinct, individually retrievable service pages
  2. Missing specific examples of results — no concrete outcomes with verifiable metrics
  3. No structured sections AI can easily pull from — the information is present but not organized into the kind of discrete, self-contained passages that AI systems prefer to cite

The first-priority recommendation in the sample report is to create dedicated service pages for each of the four system directions. The Chinese version of the report adds a recommendation to create a technical information page explaining the site's robots.txt, sitemap.xml, and llms.txt files.

These findings are consistent with the independent assessment in this report. The site's own diagnostic tool has identified the same structural gaps.

What Should Be Verified Before Acting

Before making changes, the following should be confirmed:

  1. Contact information accuracy — The email address and WeChat ID should be verified as real, working contact methods. If they are placeholders, this is a critical fix.

  2. English contact form functionality — The form was observed in a loading state; its actual submission capability should be tested.

  3. Domain strategy — Whether the me.itheheda.online subdomain is the intended permanent home, or whether a brand-matching domain is planned. This affects whether content restructuring should happen on the current domain or a new one.

  4. Company registration details — Whether the company has registration information that can be published, and whether the responsible person is willing to be identified by full name and role.

  5. Project evidence availability — Whether any of the four projects can be documented with verifiable evidence (deployment packages, acceptance records, or other artifacts) without violating client confidentiality.

Recommended Improvements, in Priority Order

Priority 1: Create Dedicated Service Pages

The four capability areas (multi-source intake, repeated decisions and entry, handoffs between systems, recovery and human review) should each have their own page. Each page should:

  • State the business problem the capability addresses
  • Describe what the system does and what humans retain
  • Explain the delivery approach for that capability
  • Include the relevant limitations and boundaries

This directly addresses the gap identified by the site's own Open GEO Console analysis. It also gives AI systems discrete, self-contained passages to retrieve and cite when answering questions about specific automation needs.

Priority 2: Publish Verifiable Company Identity Information

The site should add, in a clearly visible location:

  • Company registration name and number (if available)
  • Office location (city-level at minimum)
  • The full name and role of the responsible person
  • Team size or structure (even approximate)

This does not require revealing sensitive information. A city-level location, a full name with role, and a registration number would substantially increase the verifiable facts an AI system can cite.

Priority 3: Add Concrete, Verifiable Project Evidence

The project pages should include at least one of the following for each project:

  • A link to a public deployment package or repository
  • A documented acceptance record (with client approval)
  • A reproducible demo that can be independently tested
  • A technical specification document

The site's own articles describe how to create traceable acceptance records. Applying this methodology to the company's own projects would demonstrate the practice in action.

Priority 4: Address the Domain and Contact Issues

Two issues should be resolved:

  • Domain: If possible, move to a brand-matching domain (e.g., solvereal.com or similar). If the current domain must remain, add a clear explanation of the relationship between the domain and the brand.
  • Contact details: Verify that the email address and WeChat ID are real and working. Replace any placeholder values.
Priority 5: Add Pricing Signals

The site does not need to publish full pricing, but it should provide some indication of:

  • Whether pricing is project-based or time-based
  • An indicative range or starting point
  • What factors affect the final price

This helps AI systems answer the practical question "what does this cost?" and helps prospective buyers self-qualify before contacting the company.

Priority 6: Create a Technical Information Page

A single page explaining the site's technical setup — robots.txt, sitemap.xml, llms.txt, structured data, canonical URLs, and language versions — would serve two purposes:

  • It demonstrates the company's technical competence in AI visibility
  • It gives AI systems a clear, self-contained reference for the site's technical accessibility

This was also recommended in the site's own Open GEO Console report.

What Should Not Change

Several aspects of the site are working well and should be preserved:

  • The honest limitation disclosures — These are a differentiator and should remain prominent
  • The "start from real workflow" positioning — This is clear, consistent, and distinctive
  • The four-stage delivery method — Repeated consistently across pages, this helps AI systems associate the company with a specific methodology
  • The active content program — The articles are well-written, technically accurate, and appropriately hedged
  • The bilingual presence — Both Chinese and English versions of key pages exist, which is essential for a China-based company serving international clients
  • The explicit human oversight boundaries — This addresses a common buyer concern and is stated clearly

What This Report Does Not Claim

This report does not:

  • Promise any specific ranking, citation, or traffic outcomes
  • Assign responsibility for implementing changes
  • Provide a timeline for completion
  • Suggest duplicating existing content
  • Recommend turning the homepage into an evidence checklist

The improvements suggested here are about making existing information more retrievable and verifiable — not about adding new claims or inflating the company's profile.

Conclusion

SolveReal Systems has built a website that is honest, technically competent, and clearly positioned. The core business — custom AI automation for SMBs in China, starting from real workflow diagnosis, with explicit human oversight — is well-articulated and would be readily understood by AI systems.

The gaps are in verifiability and structure. The site tells prospective buyers what the company does, but not who exactly is behind it, what it has actually delivered, or how to verify those deliveries. The four capability areas are described but not presented as distinct, retrievable service pages.

These are fixable issues. The site's own diagnostic tool has already identified the same priorities. The technical foundation is solid, the content program is active, and the positioning is distinctive. What remains is to fill the information gaps and restructure existing content into more retrievable forms — without changing the honest, evidence-oriented character that makes this site stand out.

Custom AI Automation for SMBs: A Buyer's Guide to the Workflow-First Delivery Path

Small and medium businesses considering AI automation are often caught between template-based vendors promising "full automation" and the reality of their own messy, cross-system workflows. This guide explains what a custom, workflow-first AI automation engagement actually looks like from the buyer's perspective—how the diagnosis works, what the human/AI boundary means in practice, what deliverables to expect, and how to verify a provider's claims before committing.

The Problem with "AI Automation" as a Sales Pitch

If you run a small or medium business in China, you have probably heard some version of this pitch: "Our AI solution will fully automate your workflow, save you 80% of your team's time, and integrate with everything you use."

The pitch sounds compelling. The reality is usually different.

A vendor who promises "full automation" before asking a single question about your actual process is not selling you a system. They are selling you a template—a generic solution looking for a problem to attach itself to. When the template meets your real workflow—the one with exception cases, missing inputs, system handoffs, and human judgment calls—it often fails. The "80% time savings" turns out to be a marketing number, not a measured outcome.

This article is a buyer's guide to a different path: custom AI automation that starts from your actual workflow, retains human oversight for key decisions, and delivers traceable evidence rather than promises.

We will walk through what a legitimate custom engagement looks like from the buyer's perspective, what to expect at each stage, and how to verify a provider's claims before you commit.

What "Custom AI Automation" Actually Means for an SMB

Custom AI automation is not about building something from scratch for the sake of it. It is about designing a system around the workflow you actually have—not the workflow a vendor assumes you have.

For an SMB, this distinction matters more than it does for a large enterprise. You do not have a dedicated IT team to adapt a generic product to your needs. You do not have the budget to absorb a failed implementation. When a system does not fit your process, you feel it immediately: work stops, errors multiply, and your team loses trust in automation altogether.

A workflow-first approach starts with a simple premise: before designing a solution, understand the problem. This means mapping the real steps, frequency, responsible people, inputs, outputs, and exceptions of the process you want to improve. It means asking questions like:

  • Where does the input actually come from—email, spreadsheets, chat, a business system?
  • Who handles each step, and how do they know the work is complete?
  • What goes wrong most often—missing information, format changes, system failures?
  • Which decisions require human judgment, and which follow stable rules?

The answer to these questions determines whether automation is even appropriate, and if so, what kind. Sometimes the diagnosis concludes that the workflow is not ready for automation yet—the rules are too unstable, the data is too messy, or the responsibilities are not clearly defined. That is a useful outcome. It saves you from investing in a system that would fail.

This is the core difference between a workflow-first provider and a template-based vendor. The template vendor starts with a solution and looks for a problem to fit it. The workflow-first provider starts with your problem and designs a solution around it.

The Human/AI Boundary: What the System Handles, What People Retain

One of the most important concepts in custom AI automation is the human/AI boundary. This is the explicit line between what the system is allowed to do on its own and what requires human confirmation.

A responsible provider will not promise that every step will be unattended. Instead, they will work with you to define the boundary based on risk and judgment.

What the system can handle

AI systems are well-suited for tasks that are:

  • Stable and repeatable — the rules do not change frequently
  • Verifiable — the output can be checked against the input
  • Low-risk — an error does not cause significant harm

Examples include:

  • Multi-source intake — consolidating documents, spreadsheets, and business web pages into one traceable operating record
  • Repeated decisions and entry — applying stable rules to classify, check, and enter information into other systems
  • Handoffs between systems — carrying state across files and business systems with fewer manual transfers
What humans retain

The boundary is not about removing people from the process. It is about moving people to where their judgment matters most. Humans should retain:

  • Key decisions — choices that affect customers, finances, or strategy
  • High-risk actions — external sending, payments, publishing, or any action with irreversible consequences
  • Exceptions — cases that do not fit the stable rules and require situational judgment

For example, a system might draft a personalized outreach email based on a prospect's website content. But a human must review the target company, the website context, the public contacts, and the message itself before it is sent. The system handles the research and drafting; the human handles the judgment and the final decision.

This boundary is not a limitation. It is a design feature. It ensures that the system reduces manual work where it is safe to do so, while keeping human oversight where it matters most.

What a Legitimate Custom Engagement Looks Like: The Four-Stage Delivery Method

When you commission a custom AI automation system, you should expect a structured process. At SolveReal Systems, we use a four-stage method. This is not the only valid approach, but it is a useful framework for what a buyer should expect from any serious provider.

Stage 1: Diagnose the Current Workflow

The engagement begins with understanding your current process in detail. This is not a high-level overview. It is a working session to map:

  • The real inputs and where they come from
  • The processing steps and who performs them
  • The responsible people at each stage
  • The exceptions that occur and how they are handled
  • The deliverable outcomes and how completion is verified

The goal is to identify which parts of the workflow are candidates for automation, which parts require human judgment, and which parts are too unstable to automate reliably.

What to expect: The provider should ask detailed questions about your process. They should be able to explain your workflow back to you in their own words, including the exceptions and edge cases. If they cannot do this, they do not understand your problem.

Stage 2: Design the Human Boundary

Based on the diagnosis, the provider designs the human/AI boundary. This is a written specification of:

  • What the system will handle autonomously
  • What decisions require human review
  • Which actions require explicit human authorization
  • How exceptions and uncertain outputs are routed to people

This boundary is agreed before any development begins. It is not an afterthought.

What to expect: The provider should present a clear written description of the boundary. You should be able to review it and confirm that it matches your risk tolerance and operational requirements.

Stage 3: Validate with Real Samples

This is where the provider's claims are tested. Instead of a polished demo showing an ideal path, the provider uses your real samples—actual inputs, outputs, and exception cases from your workflow—to validate the system.

The validation covers:

  • Normal inputs and expected outputs
  • Missing information and how the system handles it
  • Repeated submissions and potential duplicates
  • Common exceptions and recovery paths
  • Human review points and authorization steps

What to expect: The provider should ask for a small set of approved, de-identified samples before development begins. They should use these samples to demonstrate that the system works with your real data, not just a hypothetical ideal case. The results should be recorded in a traceable format that you can review.

Stage 4: Deliver and Improve

The final stage is delivery. A legitimate delivery includes:

  • A runnable system — not just a demo or a presentation, but a working system you can operate
  • Operating instructions — documentation of routine operation, required access, and human review entry points
  • Exception and recovery paths — records of what happens when something goes wrong and how to resume
  • Acceptance samples — the real samples used for validation, with expected and actual results recorded
  • Handover scope — clear definition of system ownership, maintenance, and follow-up support

After delivery, the system should continue to improve based on real use. The provider should be open to adjusting the system as you discover new edge cases or changing requirements.

What to expect: The deliverable is a system you can use, not a document describing a system. You should be able to operate it, understand its boundaries, and know what to do when something fails.

How to Verify a Provider Before You Commit

The four-stage method gives you a framework for what to expect. But how do you verify that a provider will actually deliver on their promises?

Here are the practical checks that matter:

1. Can they reproduce your real workflow?

Ask the provider to explain your workflow back to you—the inputs, the steps, the exceptions, the responsible people. If they can only repeat the name of your requirement without understanding the details, they are not ready to design a solution.

2. Is the deliverable a system or a demonstration?

A screen recording, a slide deck, or a prototype of an ideal path is not a deliverable. Ask what you will receive at the end: a runnable system, a deployment package, operating instructions, and acceptance records. If the answer is vague, that is a warning sign.

3. Are exceptions and recovery designed?

Ask what happens when an input is missing, an external interface fails, an account expires, or a process times out. The system should have an exception record, a recovery point, and a way to retry or hand the work back to a person. If the provider has not thought about failure, they have not designed a system for real operations.

4. How are data and permissions handled?

Confirm which real samples are needed, where data is processed, which accounts and tokens are used, how long information is retained, and how it is backed up or deleted. The system should use only the permissions needed for the agreed process. High-risk actions—external sending, payments, publishing—should retain human authorization.

5. How will the project be accepted?

Acceptance should use real samples agreed by both parties, covering normal input, edge cases, and common exceptions. The results should be recorded with expected and actual outcomes, human review points, and recovery results. A single successful demo or a provider-reported metric is not enough.

6. What does ongoing support include?

Clarify system ownership, routine operation, defect fixes, changes to business rules, changes to third-party interfaces, and new requests. "Long-term support" without a defined scope is not a commitment.

What a Provider Should Not Promise

A responsible provider will be honest about limitations. Here are the promises you should be suspicious of:

  • "Full automation" — no legitimate provider can promise that every step will be unattended. Key decisions and high-risk actions require human oversight.
  • Specific improvement percentages — no one can promise "you will save 30% of your team's time" without understanding your workflow, data, and usage patterns. Actual results depend on these factors.
  • Fixed industry templates — if a provider sells the same solution to every client in your industry, they are not designing around your workflow. They are fitting your problem to their product.
  • Unverifiable metrics — customer identities, accuracy rates, and improvement percentages that cannot be verified are not evidence. They are marketing.

The site's published delivery principles are worth quoting here: no fixed industry templates are sold, no commitment that all steps are unattended, no fabricated metrics or unapproved project results are used as sales proof, and an initial submission is a screening step—not an automatic quote or guaranteed meeting.

Data and Permission Handling: What to Agree Before Starting

Data and permissions are not an appendix to the project. They are part of the solution design and acceptance criteria. Before implementation begins, you should agree on:

  • Necessary data and real samples — only the samples needed to validate the real workflow, with sensitivity, purpose, and permitted use confirmed before work starts
  • Deployment and processing location — local, private environment, or cloud, determined jointly based on your systems, data requirements, and operating conditions
  • Least privilege and account control — the system uses only the access needed for the agreed workflow; where practical, you retain control of accounts, tokens, and final authorization
  • Retention, backups, and deletion — retention periods, copies, backups, and deletion methods defined per engagement
  • Human authorization for high-risk actions — external sending, payment, publication, and other high-risk actions retain human authorization or an explicit approval point

A provider who avoids questions about data location, account permissions, logs, retention, or deletion is not ready to handle your business data responsibly.

Illustrative Examples: What Custom Systems Can Address

To make this concrete, here are three examples of deployable systems that illustrate the workflow-first approach. These are reference examples, not prescriptive products. Your business does not need to copy any of them; diagnosis starts from your actual workflow.

Hermes Notebook: Enterprise Knowledge Engine

Many companies have valuable information scattered across PDFs, Word documents, Excel spreadsheets, PowerPoint files, images, local folders, and business web pages. Employees struggle to find it, and every new AI application requires the same data to be cleaned and imported again.

Hermes Notebook addresses this by importing multiple formats, restoring document structure, building traceable knowledge nodes and retrieval indexes, and providing evidence to downstream applications through permission-scoped APIs. The system handles the organization and retrieval; administrators decide which folders and sources enter each knowledge base, and business owners confirm whether retrieved evidence supports the answer.

Freight Lead Agent: Prospecting and Personalized Outreach

Sales teams often need to find target companies on Google Maps, verify each official website, understand the business, locate public contacts, and prepare a personalized message for every company. This is difficult to scale manually.

Freight Lead Agent collects companies by keyword and region, extracts business context and public contacts from each website, and generates a personalized message for human review. The system handles the research and drafting; the sales team reviews the target company, website context, public contacts, and message for accuracy before sending.

Codex Feishu Bridge: Enterprise AI Collaboration

Employees often move requests, files, and results between chat tools and separate AI tools. Complex work is delegated to a few people who know how to operate the AI tool, and tasks become difficult to continue once people leave their desks.

Codex Feishu Bridge connects an AI tool to an enterprise Feishu workspace. Members can submit questions, files, and long-running tasks from a computer or phone, then add context, check status, and receive deliverables after leaving their desks. The system handles task orchestration and state tracking; members check whether the final response and attachments are complete and usable, and new reusable workflows require team confirmation before they are adopted.

The Next Step: Describe Your Workflow, Not Your Requirements

If you are considering custom AI automation, the next step is not to write a detailed requirements document. It is to describe the workflow that is consuming your team's time.

A good initial submission includes:

  • The current workflow steps, in order
  • The frequency of the workflow (daily, weekly, monthly, event-driven)
  • The responsible people at each step
  • The tools and systems involved
  • The problems you encounter most often (errors, delays, bottlenecks, traceability issues)

This information is enough for a provider to assess whether the workflow is a good candidate for automation and, if so, where AI could help.

At SolveReal Systems, the contact form is not an automatic quote generator. Submissions are reviewed by a person who then determines where AI could help. The initial submission is a screening step to assess fit—not a commitment to a project or a guaranteed meeting.

If you have a repetitive, fragile workflow that is consuming staff time, start by describing it. The diagnosis will tell you whether automation is the right path—and if it is, what kind of system would actually work for your business.

Supplementary judgment and retained decision

AI Visibility Assessment: 实解智能 (SolveReal Systems)

Website reviewed: https://me.itheheda.online/ Assessment date: September 30, 2026 Language of this report: English

Executive Summary

SolveReal Systems presents a clear, honest, and technically competent picture of its core business: designing and delivering custom AI automation systems for small and medium-sized businesses in China. The website explains what the company does, how it works, and — unusually — what it will not do. This clarity is a genuine strength for AI visibility.

However, the site currently leaves several important questions unanswered that AI systems and prospective buyers alike would need to resolve before choosing this provider. The most significant gaps are the absence of verifiable company identity details, the lack of concrete project evidence that can be independently checked, and the absence of dedicated service pages that AI systems can easily retrieve and cite. The domain name itself (me.itheheda.online) does not match the brand, which adds avoidable friction to trust-building.

The good news: the site already has a strong technical foundation, publishes robots.txt, sitemap.xml, and llms.txt, and maintains an active, well-written content program. The improvements needed are about filling information gaps and restructuring existing content — not fixing broken fundamentals.

What the Website Communicates Today

Business Identity and Positioning

The homepage immediately identifies the company as 实解智能 (SolveReal Systems), a China-based provider of enterprise AI system design and delivery. The target audience is clearly stated: small and medium-sized business owners and operations leaders who have repetitive manual workflows that could benefit from AI automation.

The core value proposition is distinctive and well-articulated: the company does not sell fixed industry templates. Every engagement starts from the client's actual workflow — the real steps, frequency, responsible persons, inputs, outputs, and exceptions. This "start from your real process" positioning is repeated consistently across the homepage, services page, about page, and all four project pages.

Service Description

The site describes four capability areas:

  1. Multi-source intake — consolidating documents, spreadsheets, and business web pages into one traceable operating record
  2. Repeated decisions and entry — giving stable rules to the system while humans retain exceptions and high-risk decisions
  3. Handoffs between systems — carrying state across files and business systems with fewer manual transfers
  4. Recovery and human review — recording exceptions and recovery points so operations can continue after interruptions

These four areas are presented as numbered lists with clear semantic hierarchy. An AI system reading this page can extract the service scope without ambiguity.

The delivery method is described as a four-stage process: diagnose the current workflow, design the human boundary, validate with real samples, and deliver with traceable evidence. This is repeated consistently across all pages, which helps AI systems associate the company with a specific, repeatable methodology.

What the Site Explicitly Does Not Claim

One of the site's most distinctive features is its explicit boundary-setting. The company states it will not:

  • Sell fixed industry templates
  • Promise fully unattended operation
  • Use fabricated metrics or unapproved client identities as sales proof
  • Treat an initial submission as an automatic quote
  • Present technical implementation as legal compliance or security certification

This honesty is rare and valuable. For AI systems that assess credibility, this transparency signals a provider that understands the limits of what it can promise. It also helps the site stand out from competitors who make inflated claims.

Project Evidence

The site lists four projects, each described with a consistent three-part structure: the customer's current workflow, which steps the system takes over, and what the customer gains. The projects are:

  1. Open GEO Console — a public product that diagnoses a website's visibility in AI search (marked as currently available)
  2. Hermes Notebook — a deployable enterprise knowledge engine
  3. Freight Lead Agent — a deployable system for finding and contacting target companies (featured in detail)
  4. Codex Feishu Bridge — a deployable system connecting OpenAI's Codex to Feishu workspaces

Each project page includes explicit limitations. For example, Freight Lead Agent processes public business information only and requires human review of all outreach content. Hermes Notebook only provides the knowledge organization kernel — upper-layer applications must be built separately.

The projects are framed as reference examples, not prescriptive products. Every project page concludes with: "Your business does not need to copy this project; diagnosis starts from the actual workflow."

Content Library

The site maintains an active content program with 22 Chinese articles and 14 English articles (as of the assessment date), covering GEO methodology, AI search visibility, and enterprise AI workflows. The articles are dated August–September 2026, indicating recent publishing activity.

The content is practical and evidence-oriented, repeatedly emphasizing real sample testing, clear human/AI responsibility boundaries, and traceable records. Several articles are technically accurate and appropriately hedged — for example, the article on how language models read web pages correctly notes that Google has no fixed ideal length requirement and that llms.txt is not a required condition for Google AI search.

How AI Systems Currently See This Site

What AI Systems Can Readily Extract

Based on the page content and structure, an AI system asked "Which companies in China can design and deliver custom AI automation systems?" would find the following directly answerable:

  • Company name: 实解智能 / SolveReal Systems
  • Service: Enterprise AI system design and delivery
  • Location: China
  • Target audience: Small and medium-sized businesses
  • Delivery approach: Four-stage method starting from real workflow diagnosis
  • Human oversight: Explicitly retained for key decisions and high-risk actions

The site's structured presentation — numbered lists, clear headings, consistent terminology — makes this information relatively easy for AI systems to parse and cite.

What AI Systems Cannot Currently Determine

An AI system would struggle to answer several questions that a prospective buyer would reasonably ask:

  1. Who exactly is behind this company? The site identifies the responsible person only as "fengc" — no full name, position, background, or credentials. The Facebook profile references "Chao Feng," but this connection is not made on the website itself.

  2. Is this a registered business? No company registration information, office address, team size, or founding date is provided anywhere on the site.

  3. Can the projects be independently verified? No demo links, code repositories, deployment documentation, or customer acceptance records are provided. The site states this is intentional — only reviewed facts are published — but this limits what AI systems can confirm.

  4. What does this cost? No pricing information or indicative ranges are provided.

  5. What technology is used? No specific AI models or platforms are disclosed.

  6. Is the contact information valid? The email address appears as a redacted or placeholder value in the page source. The WeChat ID "404" may indicate a placeholder or error. The English contact form was observed in a loading state.

How AI Systems Currently Describe This Company

Based on the retained observations, an AI system would likely describe SolveReal Systems as:

A China-based provider of enterprise AI automation systems that starts from real workflow diagnosis, retains human oversight for key decisions, and delivers runnable systems with traceable evidence. The company explicitly avoids fixed templates and inflated promises.

This is an accurate but incomplete picture. The missing elements — verifiable identity, independent project evidence, pricing signals, and technical specifics — would likely cause an AI system to present this company as one option among several, without the confidence that would come from verifiable credentials.

What the Site's Own GEO Analysis Says About Itself

The site's own Open GEO Console product has already analyzed this website. The sample report (dated September 4, 2026) identifies three gaps:

  1. Lack of clear service listings — the four capability areas are described but not presented as distinct, individually retrievable service pages
  2. Missing specific examples of results — no concrete outcomes with verifiable metrics
  3. No structured sections AI can easily pull from — the information is present but not organized into the kind of discrete, self-contained passages that AI systems prefer to cite

The first-priority recommendation in the sample report is to create dedicated service pages for each of the four system directions. The Chinese version of the report adds a recommendation to create a technical information page explaining the site's robots.txt, sitemap.xml, and llms.txt files.

These findings are consistent with the independent assessment in this report. The site's own diagnostic tool has identified the same structural gaps.

What Should Be Verified Before Acting

Before making changes, the following should be confirmed:

  1. Contact information accuracy — The email address and WeChat ID should be verified as real, working contact methods. If they are placeholders, this is a critical fix.

  2. English contact form functionality — The form was observed in a loading state; its actual submission capability should be tested.

  3. Domain strategy — Whether the me.itheheda.online subdomain is the intended permanent home, or whether a brand-matching domain is planned. This affects whether content restructuring should happen on the current domain or a new one.

  4. Company registration details — Whether the company has registration information that can be published, and whether the responsible person is willing to be identified by full name and role.

  5. Project evidence availability — Whether any of the four projects can be documented with verifiable evidence (deployment packages, acceptance records, or other artifacts) without violating client confidentiality.

Recommended Improvements, in Priority Order

Priority 1: Create Dedicated Service Pages

The four capability areas (multi-source intake, repeated decisions and entry, handoffs between systems, recovery and human review) should each have their own page. Each page should:

  • State the business problem the capability addresses
  • Describe what the system does and what humans retain
  • Explain the delivery approach for that capability
  • Include the relevant limitations and boundaries

This directly addresses the gap identified by the site's own Open GEO Console analysis. It also gives AI systems discrete, self-contained passages to retrieve and cite when answering questions about specific automation needs.

Priority 2: Publish Verifiable Company Identity Information

The site should add, in a clearly visible location:

  • Company registration name and number (if available)
  • Office location (city-level at minimum)
  • The full name and role of the responsible person
  • Team size or structure (even approximate)

This does not require revealing sensitive information. A city-level location, a full name with role, and a registration number would substantially increase the verifiable facts an AI system can cite.

Priority 3: Add Concrete, Verifiable Project Evidence

The project pages should include at least one of the following for each project:

  • A link to a public deployment package or repository
  • A documented acceptance record (with client approval)
  • A reproducible demo that can be independently tested
  • A technical specification document

The site's own articles describe how to create traceable acceptance records. Applying this methodology to the company's own projects would demonstrate the practice in action.

Priority 4: Address the Domain and Contact Issues

Two issues should be resolved:

  • Domain: If possible, move to a brand-matching domain (e.g., solvereal.com or similar). If the current domain must remain, add a clear explanation of the relationship between the domain and the brand.
  • Contact details: Verify that the email address and WeChat ID are real and working. Replace any placeholder values.
Priority 5: Add Pricing Signals

The site does not need to publish full pricing, but it should provide some indication of:

  • Whether pricing is project-based or time-based
  • An indicative range or starting point
  • What factors affect the final price

This helps AI systems answer the practical question "what does this cost?" and helps prospective buyers self-qualify before contacting the company.

Priority 6: Create a Technical Information Page

A single page explaining the site's technical setup — robots.txt, sitemap.xml, llms.txt, structured data, canonical URLs, and language versions — would serve two purposes:

  • It demonstrates the company's technical competence in AI visibility
  • It gives AI systems a clear, self-contained reference for the site's technical accessibility

This was also recommended in the site's own Open GEO Console report.

What Should Not Change

Several aspects of the site are working well and should be preserved:

  • The honest limitation disclosures — These are a differentiator and should remain prominent
  • The "start from real workflow" positioning — This is clear, consistent, and distinctive
  • The four-stage delivery method — Repeated consistently across pages, this helps AI systems associate the company with a specific methodology
  • The active content program — The articles are well-written, technically accurate, and appropriately hedged
  • The bilingual presence — Both Chinese and English versions of key pages exist, which is essential for a China-based company serving international clients
  • The explicit human oversight boundaries — This addresses a common buyer concern and is stated clearly

What This Report Does Not Claim

This report does not:

  • Promise any specific ranking, citation, or traffic outcomes
  • Assign responsibility for implementing changes
  • Provide a timeline for completion
  • Suggest duplicating existing content
  • Recommend turning the homepage into an evidence checklist

The improvements suggested here are about making existing information more retrievable and verifiable — not about adding new claims or inflating the company's profile.

Conclusion

SolveReal Systems has built a website that is honest, technically competent, and clearly positioned. The core business — custom AI automation for SMBs in China, starting from real workflow diagnosis, with explicit human oversight — is well-articulated and would be readily understood by AI systems.

The gaps are in verifiability and structure. The site tells prospective buyers what the company does, but not who exactly is behind it, what it has actually delivered, or how to verify those deliveries. The four capability areas are described but not presented as distinct, retrievable service pages.

These are fixable issues. The site's own diagnostic tool has already identified the same priorities. The technical foundation is solid, the content program is active, and the positioning is distinctive. What remains is to fill the information gaps and restructure existing content into more retrievable forms — without changing the honest, evidence-oriented character that makes this site stand out.

Which companies in China can design and deliver custom AI automation systems for my business?

Model response

Full answer

Based on the available search results, I can provide a starting point for identifying Chinese companies that design and deliver custom AI automation systems, though the information is somewhat limited and requires further verification.

Directly Identified Company:

  • Limen AI Lab is explicitly mentioned as an AI automation agency in China. Their website claims they help businesses implement AI and automation that delivers results, focusing on turning repetitive tasks into efficient systems. This appears to be a direct match for your needs, but I recommend visiting their site and reviewing their portfolio and client testimonials to assess their fit for your specific business.

Broader Resource for Finding Companies:

  • A more comprehensive resource is RevenueBase.ai, which lists the 10 largest of 286 custom automation solution providers based in China, ranked by team size. This directory is a valuable tool for you to explore a wide range of companies, compare their sizes, and read descriptions of their services. I suggest using this list as a primary starting point to shortlist potential partners.

Context on the Chinese AI Landscape:

  • One search result notes that major Chinese tech companies integrate AI into their enterprise platforms. For example, Alibaba's Tongyi Qianwen AI is natively embedded into DingTalk, their collaboration and communication platform. This is relevant if you are looking for AI automation that integrates with existing Chinese business software ecosystems, similar to how Claude Enterprise integrates with Slack.

Important Caveats:

  • Several of the search results (e.g., from EffectiveSoft, DesignRush, Master of Code) focus on AI automation companies in the USA or globally, not specifically in China. These lists may include companies with global operations, but they are not a reliable source for finding firms based in China.
  • The results do not provide detailed information on the specific industries, technical stacks, or pricing models of the Chinese companies mentioned. You will need to conduct further research on the shortlisted companies to determine if they have experience in your industry and can meet your specific requirements.

Recommendation for Next Steps:

  1. Explore the RevenueBase.ai directory to build a list of Chinese custom automation providers.
  2. Visit the websites of the top companies on that list, as well as Limen AI Lab, to review their case studies, technical expertise, and client reviews.
  3. Contact several companies directly to discuss your project requirements, ask about their experience with similar businesses, and request proposals.

In summary, while Limen AI Lab is a directly identified candidate, the RevenueBase.ai directory is your best resource for a comprehensive search. Given the limited detail in the search results, I strongly advise you to conduct your own due diligence on any company you consider.

Diagnosis

The website for 实解智能 (SolveReal Systems) presents a clear and technically competent picture of a company that designs and delivers custom AI automation systems for small and medium-sized businesses in China. The site's core positioning is distinctive: it explicitly starts from the client's actual workflow rather than selling fixed industry templates, and it retains human oversight for key decisions and high-risk actions. This honest, evidence-oriented approach is a genuine strength and is communicated consistently across the homepage, services page, about page, and project pages.

The site describes four capability areas—multi-source intake, repeated decisions and entry, handoffs between systems, and recovery with human review—and a four-stage delivery method: diagnose the current workflow, design the human boundary, validate with real samples, and deliver with traceable evidence. It also publishes four project references, including Hermes Notebook, Freight Lead Agent, and Codex Feishu Bridge, each framed as an illustrative example rather than a prescriptive product. The site maintains an active bilingual content program and has a solid technical foundation, including robots.txt, sitemap.xml, and llms.txt.

However, several gaps would prevent an AI system from recommending this company with full confidence. 02Question 2

What kind of AI automation solution fits a small or medium business in China that wants to reduce manual, repetitive work without replacing human oversight?

Model response

Full answer

For a small or medium-sized business (SMB) in China, the best AI automation solution is one that uses "human-in-the-loop" (HITL) automation—software that handles the repetitive, high-volume grunt work but automatically routes anything unusual, sensitive, or judgment-based to a human for approval. This approach reduces manual labor while keeping your team firmly in control of decisions.

Based on the search results, here are the most practical fits for your needs:

1. Workflow Automation Platforms (e.g., Zapier, Make, or local equivalents like Jianda or Yida) These tools connect your existing apps (WeChat Work, DingTalk, ERP, CRM) to automate data entry, invoice matching, and approval routing. They are ideal for reducing manual errors in payroll, scheduling, and order processing. You set the rules, and the AI only executes within those boundaries—anything outside them is flagged for a human to review.

2. AI-Powered Document Processing (e.g., OCR + NLP tools) For Chinese SMBs dealing with contracts, invoices, or customs paperwork, AI can extract key fields (dates, amounts, supplier names) from scanned documents and populate your systems. The AI flags discrepancies or missing data for human verification, so you never lose oversight on financial or legal documents.

3. Customer Service Copilots (e.g., WeChat/CRM-integrated chatbots) Instead of replacing your support staff, deploy an AI assistant that drafts responses, categorizes tickets, and handles FAQs. Complex or angry customers are automatically escalated to human agents. This reduces repetitive typing while keeping a human on the final reply for quality control.

4. Marketing and Content Assistants (e.g., Notion AI, Microsoft Copilot) These tools draft social media posts, translate content between Chinese and English, and summarize reports. They don't publish anything without your approval—they simply cut the time spent on first drafts and research.

Key considerations for China specifically:

  • Data compliance: Ensure any cloud-based AI tool stores data on servers compliant with China's PIPL (Personal Information Protection Law). Many global tools (like Zapier) may have data residency issues; consider domestic alternatives like Alibaba Cloud's Quick BI or Tencent's AI solutions.
  • Human oversight is built-in: Look for tools with "approval workflows" and "exception handling" features. The goal is a 60–70% reduction in manual work for repetitive tasks (as cited in the search results), not 100% automation.
  • Start small: Pick one high-friction process (e.g., invoice entry or customer ticket triage) and pilot it for 30 days. Measure time saved and error rates before expanding.

Bottom line: The right solution is not a single "AI robot" but a layered system of workflow automation, document intelligence, and copilot tools—all configured with human checkpoints. This gives you the efficiency gains of AI without sacrificing the judgment and accountability that your business needs.

Diagnosis

The website for 实解智能 (SolveReal Systems) directly addresses your question about AI automation for a small or medium business in China. The company positions itself specifically around the approach you are looking for: custom AI automation that reduces manual, repetitive work while keeping human oversight in place.

The site clearly states that it designs and delivers custom AI automation systems for SMBs in China, and it emphasizes a "workflow-first" method. This means every project starts by diagnosing your actual business process—the real steps, frequency, responsible people, inputs, outputs, and exceptions—rather than selling a fixed industry template. This is a strong match for your stated need.

The website describes four capability areas that such a system might address: consolidating documents and spreadsheets into one traceable record, applying stable rules to repeated decisions and data entry while humans handle exceptions, carrying state across different systems to reduce manual transfers, and recording exceptions and recovery points so operations can continue after interruptions.

A core part of the company's stated philosophy is the "human/AI boundary." The site explicitly says it will not promise fully unattended operation. Instead, the design keeps humans in control of key decisions, high-risk actions, and exception situations. The delivery method is described as a four-stage process: diagnose the current workflow, design the human boundary, validate with real samples, and deliver with traceable evidence.

The site also publishes several reference projects, such as a knowledge engine, a lead generation agent, and a bridge connecting an AI tool to Feishu workspaces. These are framed as examples of the delivery approach, not as prescriptive products, and each project page notes its limitations and the human review points involved.

One thing to be aware of is that the website currently provides limited verifiable company identity details. It does not publish company registration information, an office location, the full name of the responsible person, or concrete project evidence like deployment packages or acceptance records. The contact information also appears to have some issues, with an email address that looks like a placeholder and a WeChat ID that may be an error. If you are evaluating this provider, you would likely want to verify these details directly before proceeding.

The site's own diagnostic tool has identified similar gaps, recommending dedicated service pages for each capability area and more structured, retrievable content. The technical foundation of the site is solid, and the content is honest and well-written, but the missing identity and evidence details are worth confirming with the company if you choose to contact them.

03Question 3

What should I compare or verify before choosing a provider for an enterprise AI system, such as project evidence, contact details, or delivery approach?

Model response

Full answer

Before choosing a provider for an enterprise AI system, you should conduct a structured due-diligence process that goes beyond marketing claims and demo videos. Based on the available guidance, here are the key areas to compare and verify:

1. Project Evidence and Proven Track Record Do not rely solely on vendor promises. Ask for concrete, verifiable proof of past success. This includes:

  • Case studies and references: Request detailed case studies from your specific industry or use case (e.g., customer service, document processing, analytics). Ask for direct contact with existing clients who have deployed similar systems, not just the vendor's preferred references.
  • Pilot projects: Strongly consider starting with a small, well-defined pilot project before committing to a full enterprise rollout. This validates the technology in your environment and tests the vendor's delivery capabilities.
  • Independent validation: Look for third-party audits, security certifications, or benchmark results that prove the system's performance and reliability, rather than just internal vendor claims.

2. Contact Details and Vendor Legitimacy Verify that the provider is a legitimate, stable organization you can hold accountable. Check:

  • Physical address and legal entity: Confirm their registered business address, legal name, and jurisdiction. Be wary of providers with only a website and no verifiable physical presence.
  • Direct contacts: Ensure you have direct access to technical leads, project managers, and support staff—not just a sales representative. Test their responsiveness before signing a contract.
  • Financial stability: For long-term enterprise systems, assess the vendor's financial health and longevity. A provider that may go out of business in a year poses a significant risk to your AI system's lifecycle.

3. Delivery Approach and Methodology Understand exactly how the provider will implement and support the system. Compare:

  • Build vs. buy vs. hybrid: Evaluate whether the vendor offers a turnkey product, a custom-built solution, or a hybrid approach. Assess your internal capability and total cost of ownership for each option.
  • Implementation timeline and process: Ask for a detailed delivery roadmap, including milestones, dependencies, and what resources you must provide. Clarify whether they use agile sprints, waterfall phases, or a different methodology.
  • Integration capabilities: Verify how the AI system will integrate with your existing enterprise software (e.g., CRM, ERP, databases). Ask for specifics on APIs, data connectors, and system architecture.
  • Post-deployment support: Clarify the service-level agreements (SLAs), maintenance plans, and how updates or model retraining are handled. Determine whether support is in-house or outsourced.

4. Security, Governance, and Compliance For enterprise AI, security and governance are non-negotiable. Verify:

  • Data privacy and security: Confirm how your data is stored, encrypted, and protected. Ask about compliance with relevant regulations (e.g., GDPR, local data laws in your region) and whether the provider can prove its security posture.
  • Governance and control: Ensure the provider offers strong governance features, such as audit trails, access controls, and the ability to explain AI decisions. This is critical for accountability and regulatory compliance.

5. Technology and Model Transparency Finally, compare the underlying technology:

  • Model selection: Ask which AI models they use (e.g., proprietary vs. open-source) and why. Verify that the models are suitable for your data types and performance requirements.
  • Customization and flexibility: Determine whether the system can be tailored to your specific workflows and whether you retain ownership of any custom models or data.

In summary, your verification checklist should include: proof of past performance (case studies and pilots), verifiable contact and legal details, a clear and realistic delivery methodology, robust security and governance measures, and transparency about the underlying technology. Treat any provider that cannot provide concrete evidence in these areas as a higher-risk choice.

Diagnosis

Based on the review of the website at https://me.itheheda.online/, here is an assessment of how the site addresses your question about what to compare or verify before choosing an enterprise AI provider.

The website, which presents the company 实解智能 (SolveReal Systems), directly engages with your question. It provides a detailed, practical framework for evaluating a provider, and it is notably honest about its own limitations. The site's guidance aligns well with the core areas you asked about: project evidence, contact details, and delivery approach.

What the Website Communicates Well

The site's strongest contribution is its clear articulation of a delivery approach. It describes a four-stage method: diagnosing the current workflow, designing the human/AI boundary, validating with real samples, and delivering with traceable evidence. This is a concrete, verifiable methodology that a buyer can use to structure their own evaluation. The site also explains what a legitimate deliverable looks like—a runnable system with operating instructions and acceptance records, not just a demo—and emphasizes that human oversight is retained for key decisions and high-risk actions.

The site is also explicit about what it will not do, which is a valuable signal. It states it does not sell fixed industry templates, does not promise fully unattended operation, and does not use fabricated metrics or unapproved client identities as sales proof. This transparency is a differentiator and helps set realistic expectations.

Gaps in the Website's Evidence

While the site provides a strong framework for evaluation, it does not fully demonstrate its own credentials in the areas you mentioned.

  • Project Evidence: The site describes four projects (e.g., Hermes Notebook, Freight Lead Agent) but provides no independently verifiable evidence for them. There are no demo links, code repositories, deployment documentation, or customer acceptance records. The site states this is intentional—only reviewed facts are published—but this limits what a prospective buyer can confirm.
  • Contact Details and Company Identity: The site identifies the responsible person only as "fengc" and provides no company registration details, office address, or founding date. The contact email appears as a placeholder value in the page source, and the WeChat ID "404" may be an error. This makes it difficult to verify the legitimacy and stability of the organization.
  • Pricing and Technology: No pricing information or indicative ranges are provided, and no specific AI models or platforms are disclosed.

Overall Assessment

The website offers a thoughtful and honest guide to evaluating an AI provider, particularly regarding delivery methodology and the importance of human oversight. However, it does not currently provide the verifiable project evidence, clear company identity, or working contact details that its own guidance suggests a buyer should seek. The site's own diagnostic tool has identified similar gaps, including the lack of dedicated service pages and structured sections for AI systems to easily retrieve.

In summary, the site is strong on philosophy and process but weak on verifiable proof. A prospective buyer would find its framework useful but would need to request the missing evidence directly from the company before making a decision.

Service Facts · 可引用服务事实 — Page Analysis

1. Page Overview

This is the services page of a provider offering enterprise AI automation services and workflow system delivery (企业 AI 自动化服务与工作流系统交付). The page is written in Chinese and targets small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) that face problems with repetitive manual work, cross-system data flow, or processing of unstructured documents.

The core positioning is stated clearly: the provider first diagnoses the real process, then designs the human-machine boundary, exception recovery, and acceptance methods, and finally delivers a custom AI automation system that fits the enterprise's actual operations.

2. Target Audience and Eligibility Criteria

The page defines who should consider a diagnostic engagement:

Situations suitable for initial diagnosis:

  • Business processes that are high-frequency, relatively stable in rules, and require cross-file or cross-system flow
  • Processes where AI handles unstructured information but key results still require human review
  • Automation projects that need to preserve state, exceptions, recovery records, and auditable output

What the client must provide before starting:

  • Real steps, frequency, and responsible persons of the current process
  • Input, output, and exception samples that can be used for verification
  • Key decisions or high-risk actions that must retain human confirmation

3. Operating Model (01)

The page defines a clear division between system and human responsibilities:

  • System handles: Relatively stable, repeatable verification tasks — sorting, judgment, and cross-system flow
  • Human review: Key decisions, high-risk actions, and exception situations retain explicit human confirmation and takeover entry points
  • Delivery evidence: A runnable system, operational boundaries, and traceable records of status, exceptions, recovery, and output

4. Delivery Method (02)

The delivery process consists of four stages:

  1. Diagnose current state — reconstruct real inputs, processing steps, responsible persons, exceptions, and delivery results
  2. Design human-machine boundary — clarify what AI can handle, who reviews key decisions, and which actions require manual confirmation
  3. Validate with real processes — use real samples to verify inputs, exceptions, recovery, review, and output, rather than only demonstrating the ideal path
  4. Deliver and continuously optimize — deliver a runnable system, operational boundaries, and tracking evidence, then adjust based on actual usage

Important caveat: Specific functions, timelines, and deliverables are determined by process diagnosis and real-sample validation; an initial submission is not an automatic quote.

5. Standard Deliverables and Acceptance Criteria (03)

Six standard deliverables are listed, with the note that specific scope adjusts per project:

  1. Current process and system boundary — steps, responsible persons, inputs/outputs, exceptions; what the system takes over and what humans retain
  2. Runnable system and deployment results — a runnable system, or reproducible deployment package, configuration, and run entry point — not just a demo document
  3. Operating instructions and human review entry — daily operations, required permissions, manual confirmation, exception takeover, and responsibility assignment
  4. Exception and recovery paths — exception records, recovery points, retry or manual takeover methods, to avoid restarting from scratch after interruption
  5. Acceptance samples and result records — mutually agreed real samples recording expected vs. actual results, exceptions, and traceable output
  6. Handover and follow-up support scope — system ownership, maintenance, change scope, and follow-up support defined in the project agreement; no fixed service duration is implicitly promised

6. Operating Boundary: Data, Permissions, and Runtime (04)

The page emphasizes that data and permissions are part of solution design and acceptance, not post-delivery add-ons. The following must be confirmed in the real environment before implementation:

  • Necessary data and real samples: Only samples necessary to verify the real process are requested; data sensitivity, purpose, and scope of use are confirmed before starting

Core offering: A custom AI automation system designed for day-to-day operation, delivered through a four-stage method: workflow diagnosis, human boundary design, real-sample validation, and delivery with ongoing improvement.

Human oversight model: The system handles organization, decisions, and cross-system handoffs where rules are stable and testable. Key decisions, high-risk actions, and exceptions retain explicit human confirmation and takeover points. High-risk actions such as external sending, payment, and publication require human authorization.

Data and access are treated as part of solution design, not post-delivery appendices. Key constraints include:

This page functions as a qualification and expectation-setting document rather than a traditional sales page. Page Analysis: SolveReal Systems — About Page

1. What this page is

This is the About / How We Work page for SolveReal Systems, a consultancy describing itself as focused on "Enterprise AI Systems Design & Delivery." The page's core promise is stated plainly: "Make AI truly run inside the enterprise."

The page is not a technical specification, a portfolio, or a pricing sheet. It is a positioning and process-description page aimed at prospective clients who have operational workflows they suspect could be automated or improved with AI, but who may not yet have a formal requirements document.

2. Core claims and service description

The page describes a service model built around workflow diagnosis first, system building second. The stated starting point is:

"Start with workflow diagnosis, identify automation opportunities, human-review boundaries, failure recovery, and deliverable outcomes, then build a working custom system."

The problems the firm claims to be suited for are:

  • High-frequency workflows with relatively stable rules that move across files or systems
  • Workflows where AI handles unstructured information but critical results still require human review
  • Automation that must preserve state, exceptions, recovery records, and auditable outputs

These are specific, non-trivial constraints. They rule out one-off creative tasks, fully autonomous high-risk decision-making, and workflows that cannot tolerate audit trails.

3. Explicit boundaries and limitations

The page is unusually explicit about what the firm will not do. This is a notable feature of the copy and worth preserving in any report:

  • No fixed industry templates are sold — every engagement starts from the actual workflow.
  • Not every step is promised to be unattended — critical decisions and high-risk actions retain human review.
  • No invented metrics, customer identities, or unapproved project outcomes are used as sales proof.
  • An initial submission is not an automatic quote or a guaranteed meeting.

The last point is a meaningful limitation: submitting a business problem does not commit the firm to a proposal, nor does it guarantee a follow-up conversation. The page frames the initial submission as a screening step, not a sales funnel commitment.

4. Who leads the project

The page states:

"SolveReal Systems is currently led by fengc. The same owner coordinates early discussions, workflow mapping, system design, and delivery."

This is a single-operator model — the same person handles early discussions, workflow mapping, system design, and delivery. The page explicitly says you do not need a complete requirements document first; you only need to explain:

  • The workflow consuming staff time
  • The tools already in use
  • The problems you are encountering

This is a low-friction entry point, but it also implies capacity constraints — a single leader may not be able to scale to many concurrent engagements. The page does not disclose current availability or backlog.

5. The four-step process

The page outlines a four-stage engagement model:

  1. Diagnose the current workflow — map real inputs, processing steps, owners, exceptions, and deliverable outcomes.
  2. Design the human boundary — define what AI may handle, who reviews critical decisions, and which actions require confirmation.
  3. Validate the real workflow — validate inputs, exceptions, recovery, review, and outputs with real samples rather than an idealized demo path.
  4. Deliver and improve — deliver a working system, operating boundaries, and traceable evidence, then improve it from real use.

The emphasis on "real samples rather than an idealized demo path" is a deliberate anti-hype stance. The page is positioning against vendors who demo well but fail in production.

6. How collaboration starts

The page describes a three-part pre-engagement assessment:

  1. Confirm whether the problem is worth solving — reviewing frequency, manual effort, and the impact of errors.
  2. Divide responsibilities between system and people — AI takes stable steps; key decisions retain human confirmation.
  3. Validate with real data — then deploy and improve through actual use.

This is a funnel with explicit gates. The firm reserves the right to decline work it deems not worth solving.

7. Call to action

The primary CTA is "Submit a business problem." The page asks for:

  • The current workflow
  • Frequency
  • Manual effort

And states the firm will "first assess whether it is suitable for improvement, then decide whether to begin an initial diagnosis."

8. Notable omissions and uncertainties

  • No pricing information is provided anywhere on the page.
  • No timeline estimates for diagnosis, validation, or delivery.
  • No client names, case studies, or metrics — consistent with the stated policy against using unapproved outcomes as sales proof.
  • No details on technology stack (e.g., which AI models, platforms, or infrastructure are used).
  • No information on data handling, security, or compliance — relevant given the emphasis on auditable outputs and enterprise contexts.
  • No contact details beyond the submission form — no email, phone, or physical address is visible in the retained text.
  • The name "fengc" appears to be a username or handle rather than a full name; no credentials, background, or prior work history is disclosed on this page.

9. Overall assessment

This is a deliberately restrained, anti-hype positioning page. It makes specific, defensible claims about what the firm will and will not do, and it explicitly refuses to promise unattended automation for critical decisions. The single-operator model and the screening-first approach suggest a boutique, high-touch consultancy rather than a productized service.

For a prospective client, the page is useful in setting expectations but leaves open questions about cost, timeline, technical approach, and the operator's track record. The absence of any verifiable proof points — by design — means the reader must rely on the initial screening conversation to assess credibility.

Key takeaway for a paid GEO report: This page is best characterized as a process-and-boundaries statement for a niche enterprise AI workflow automation service, led by a single operator, with a strong emphasis on human review boundaries and real-data validation. It is not a typical agency landing page; it is closer to a consulting engagement brief with explicit refusal points.
