GEO Report: Page Analysis — "Why Company Websites Matter More in the AI Era"

URL analyzed: https://me.itheheda.online/articles/why-company-websites-matter-more-in-the-ai-era
Observed: 2026-09-30
Source length: ~6,230 characters (Chinese)

1. Executive Summary

This is a long-form educational article published by 实解智能 (Shijie Intelligence) on September 2, 2026. The page explains why corporate websites are becoming more important in the AI era, walking readers through the path of discovery, crawling, understanding, retrieval, and citation. It also introduces the Open GEO Console as a diagnostic tool.

The page serves three functions simultaneously: (a) an educational resource on GEO (Generative Engine Optimization), (b) a marketing piece for the publisher's own consulting services, and (c) a demonstration of the principles it advocates.

2. Content Analysis

2.1 Core Thesis

The article argues that AI systems (search engines, chatbots, answer engines) increasingly rely on publicly accessible web pages to generate answers. Therefore, a company's official website serves as its maintainable, verifiable source of formal information — something that cannot be outsourced to social media, press coverage, or directories.

2.2 Key Sections
SectionContent
Direct AnswerA procurement manager may ask AI first, then visit supplier websites. AI answers come from publicly available materials the system could access and chose to use.
How an AI Answer Reaches a Company WebsiteDescribes the pipeline: discovery → crawling → understanding → retrieval → generation → user verification. References Google's crawling/indexing documentation, Google's generative search guidelines (AI Overviews, AI Mode, RAG, query fan-out), OpenAI's OAI-SearchBot, and Perplexity's PerplexityBot vs. Perplexity-User distinction.
Website Value Beyond a BrochureTraditional homepages are insufficient. Mature service pages should specify target audience, input conditions, process, human review points, deliverables, and limitations.
Using Open GEO to Trace the Reading PathA five-step diagnostic process: (1) confirm the subject, (2) check discovery and access, (3) inspect machine-readable content, (4) verify identity and question coverage, (5) check citable material. Includes a gap/acceptance table.
What Verifiable Materials to ProvideCompany identity, service conditions, traceable evidence, internal linking, machine-readable formats (structured data, sitemaps, feeds, llms.txt — with the caveat that Google explicitly does not use llms.txt for generative search visibility).
Third-Party Materials Still Determine CredibilityOfficial websites are self-published claims. Independent mentions matter. Google's guidelines warn against inauthentic mentions and scaled content abuse.
How to Measure ProgressTechnical layer (crawlability), content layer (verifiability), AI observation layer (record question, product, date, language, region, answer, citations), business layer (Search Console, ChatGPT referral traffic with utm_source=chatgpt.com).
Implementation StepsStart with one high-value service page and one real buyer question.
Acceptance Checklist10 items covering discovery, access, HTML content, identity consistency, direct answers, evidence, bilingual URLs, record-keeping, metric separation, and no platform guarantees.
LimitationsThe website can improve conditions for discovery/understanding/citation but cannot control platform source selection or guarantee inclusion, ranking, citation, referral, or consultation.
2.3 Claims and Assertions

The article makes several specific factual claims about third-party platforms:

  1. Google divides search into crawling, indexing, and serving results. Not every discovered page is crawled; not every crawled page is indexed.
  2. Google's generative search (AI Overviews, AI Mode) retrieves from the search index and may expand queries (query fan-out, RAG).
  3. OpenAI recommends allowing OAI-SearchBot for inclusion in search summaries, citations, and links.
  4. Perplexity distinguishes PerplexityBot (discovery) from Perplexity-User (user-triggered access, typically not subject to robots.txt).
  5. Google (2026) does not use llms.txt for generative search visibility and does not require special AI markup.
  6. ChatGPT search referral links carry utm_source=chatgpt.com.

These claims are presented as factual descriptions of public documentation. They are consistent with publicly available documentation as of the observed date, but the article itself does not link directly to these sources inline — it lists them as "参考来源" (reference sources) at the bottom.

3. Technical Observations

3.1 Page Structure
  • Language: Chinese (zh)
  • Format: Long-form article with clear section headings, tables, and lists
  • Internal links: Present — links to related articles ("AI 搜索与 GEO", "网站已经做了 SEO，为什么还需要 GEO？", "为什么 AI 总在推荐竞争对手，却不推荐我的企业？"), the Open GEO Console project page, and a service inquiry page
  • Metadata: The page includes a publication date (2026年9月2日) and author attribution (实解智能)
3.2 Readability

The page is marked as direct_readable, meaning the full text was directly accessible without JavaScript rendering or login requirements. This is consistent with the article's own advice about serving content in initial HTML.

3.3 Missing Elements (from a GEO perspective)
  • No visible structured data (schema.org markup) was observed in the retained text — though this cannot be confirmed without inspecting raw HTML.
  • No explicit FAQ section with question-answer markup.
  • No visible author bio or credentials beyond the publisher name.
  • No inline hyperlinks to the cited references (Google, OpenAI, Perplexity documentation) — references are listed as text only.

4. GEO Assessment

4.1 Strengths
  1. Clear entity identity: The publisher (实解智能) is named, dated, and associated with specific services.
  2. Question-answer alignment: The article directly addresses buyer-type questions (who is suitable, what are deliverables, how is pricing determined, what happens on failure).
  3. Citable statements: Many paragraphs contain standalone, verifiable claims with conditions and limitations stated.
  4. Internal linking: Related articles and service pages are linked, supporting crawl discovery.
  5. Honest limitations: The article explicitly states what GEO cannot do (no guarantees of inclusion, ranking, citation, or referral).
  6. Bilingual awareness: The article addresses Chinese/English name consistency and URL strategy.
4.2 Weaknesses
  1. No inline citations: The "参考来源" section lists sources by name only, without URLs. A reader (or AI system) cannot directly verify the claims from the page itself.
  2. No structured data observed: Without schema.org markup (Article, Organization, FAQPage, BreadcrumbList), machine understanding relies entirely on HTML semantics.
  3. No publication history: Only one date is shown; no "last updated" date is visible.
  4. Potential self-promotion ambiguity: The article promotes the Open GEO Console and the publisher's own services. This is transparent but may reduce perceived neutrality.
  5. No author identity: "实解智能" is a company name, not a person. For credibility assessment, a named author or editor would strengthen the entity profile.
4.3 Alignment with Its Own Advice

The article practices what it preaches in several ways:

  • It states service boundaries (what Open GEO can and cannot do).
  • It provides a checklist with acceptance criteria.
  • It separates metrics (crawl, index, mention, citation, visit, inquiry).
  • It acknowledges uncertainty (no guarantees).

However, it violates its own recommendation that "关键判断附近写有来源、日期、条件和适用边界" (key judgments should have sources, dates, conditions, and boundaries nearby) — the reference sources are listed at the bottom without URLs or access dates.

5. Recommendations

5.1 For the Publisher (实解智能)
  1. Add inline hyperlinks to the Google, OpenAI, and Perplexity documentation cited in the article.
  2. Add structured data: Article schema, Organization schema, and ideally FAQPage schema for the Q&A sections.
  3. Add a "last updated" date alongside the publication date.
  4. Consider naming an author or reviewer to strengthen entity credibility.
  5. Add a canonical URL and ensure hreflang tags if an English version exists.
5.2 For a Client Considering GEO Work

This page is a useful educational resource but should not be treated as an authoritative specification. Key takeaways:

  • The five-step diagnostic path (discovery → access → understanding → coverage → citation) is a reasonable framework.
  • The acceptance checklist is practical and verifiable.
  • The limitations section is honest and should be taken seriously — no GEO provider can guarantee AI platform outcomes.

6. Limitations of This Analysis

  • This analysis is based on the retained text only; raw HTML, HTTP headers, robots.txt, sitemap, and structured data were not inspected.
  • The page was observed once (2026-09-30); no historical comparison was possible.
  • Claims about Google, OpenAI, and Perplexity behavior were not independently verified against their current documentation at the time of this analysis.
  • The publisher's own claims about the Open GEO Console could not be independently tested.

7. Conclusion

This is a well-structured, honest, and practical educational article about GEO. It explains the mechanism by which AI systems use public web pages, provides a diagnostic framework, and clearly states its limitations. Its main weaknesses are the absence of inline citations and structured data — both of which are fixable and would align the page more closely with its own recommendations.

Overall assessment: Useful as an introduction to GEO concepts; moderately useful as a citable source (due to missing inline references); not a substitute for platform-specific documentation.

知识库接入 AI 前要准备什么？先治文档、权限、更新和验证

实解智能 | 2026年8月10日

企业知识库接入 AI 前，应先建立文档责任、访问权限、更新机制和答案验证集；否则检索更快并不会让答案更可靠，反而可能扩大过期内容与越权访问。

最后更新于 2026年8月21日

直接答案

知识库接入 AI 前，至少要准备四件事：让文档有明确责任人和有效版本、把源系统权限带入检索、建立过期与删除同步机制、用真实业务问题验证答案和引用。只把文件批量上传到向量库，不能解决互相冲突、权限不清和过期内容的问题。

Azure AI Search 的官方方案会在索引中保留用户或组权限，并在查询时根据调用者身份过滤文档〔1〕。这意味着权限不是聊天界面上的提示语，而是必须落实到每次检索的技术约束。

适用边界

层面上线前必须明确不能接受的替代
文档质量标题、版本、责任人、生效日期、适用范围"模型自己会判断哪份是真的"
权限用户、群组、文档和字段级访问规则只在提示词中要求保密
更新新增、修改、删除、撤销和重新索引机制定期全部重传但不处理删除
答案标准问题、期望要点、允许来源和拒答条件只看回答是否流畅
引用能定位到原文、版本和段落只显示文件名或虚构链接

公开知识、内部操作文档、客户数据和受限材料不应混在同一个无权限边界的索引中。

实施步骤

  1. 盘点信息源。 列出文件夹、网盘、业务系统、网页和数据库，并标记负责人。
  2. 建立文档最小元数据。 至少包含唯一 ID、标题、版本、生效日期、状态、权限和来源 URL。
  3. 处理冲突与过期。 明确新旧制度、草稿与正式版、总部与地区规则的优先级。
  4. 继承权限。 索引时携带源系统 ACL 或群组信息，查询时按当前用户过滤。
  5. 设计删除同步。 源文件撤销后，检索索引和缓存也必须删除或失效。
  6. 建立验证集。 选择真实高频问题、边界问题、无答案问题和权限问题，记录期望证据。
  7. 监控答案链路。 分开记录检索是否命中、证据是否正确、回答是否完整和是否越权。

NIST 的 AI 测试、评估、验证和确认资源强调，应使用可重复的测量方法持续检查系统〔2〕。对于知识库，这意味着不能用一次演示回答代替长期验证。

验收清单

  • 同一问题在不同权限账号下只返回各自可见文档。
  • 删除或撤销文档后，检索、缓存和回答都不再引用它。
  • 冲突文档能依据版本、生效日期和适用范围选择或明确提示冲突。
  • 每个事实性回答都能定位到正确原文，而不是只给一个文件名。
  • 没有足够证据时能够拒答或请求补充，而不是生成看似合理的内容。
  • 验证集覆盖高频、边界、过期、越权和无答案场景。
  • 文档更新后能重跑验证集，并比较答案与引用变化。

参考来源

  • Document-Level Access Control — Azure AI Search
  • NIST AI Resource Center
  • Best Practices for Security — Azure AI Search
  • Query-Time ACL and RBAC Enforcement — Azure AI Search
  • Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework 1.0 — NIST

下一步

先选一个边界清楚的知识域和一组有明确答案的真实问题，不要从"把公司所有文件都上传"开始。可以查看企业知识库与 AI 应用项目、了解企业 AI 工作流服务，或带着脱敏文档目录、权限模型和典型问题提交业务问题。

分析说明： 本页面为实解智能（2026年8月10日发布，8月21日更新）关于企业知识库接入 AI 前的准备指南。核心主张是：在接入 AI 前必须解决文档责任、访问权限、更新机制和答案验证四类问题，否则检索加速只会放大过期内容和越权访问风险。页面引用了 Azure AI Search 的文档级访问控制方案和 NIST 的 AI 测试评估资源作为依据，并提供了实施步骤、验收清单和适用边界表格。内容面向企业决策者和技术实施人员，属于操作指南类内容。页面未提供具体产品价格或服务报价，主要功能是建立专业权威形象并引导潜在客户提交业务问题。

GEO Report: Page Analysis — "Why AI Recommends Competitors Instead of Your Company"

URL analyzed: https://me.itheheda.online/articles/why-ai-recommends-competitors-not-your-company
Observed: September 30, 2026
Source length: ~4,674 characters
Language: Chinese (Simplified)
Content type: Long-form educational article / methodology guide

1. Executive Summary

This page is a detailed, practical guide for business owners and website managers who discover that AI assistants (such as ChatGPT, Perplexity, or Google's generative search) recommend competitors but not their own company in response to buyer questions. The article frames this as a comparative audit problem rather than a branding or model-bias problem, and walks readers through a structured diagnostic process.

The page is not a sales pitch — it contains no pricing, no product demo, and no direct call-to-action beyond linking to the site's own "Open GEO Console" tool and related services. It functions primarily as thought leadership / educational content designed to establish the author's credibility in the GEO (Generative Engine Optimization) space.

2. Core Message & Methodology

The article's central argument: when AI recommends competitors but not you, the most productive response is not to blame brand size, content volume, or model bias, but to systematically compare the public evidence that the AI used.

The recommended process is:

  1. Fix the test conditions — Record the exact question, AI product, date, language, region, and login state. Remove company names from the question.
  2. Read the recommendation reasons, not just the company list — Note what the AI said about each competitor, then open the cited URLs to verify whether those pages actually support the claims.
  3. Compare competitor and your own pages side-by-side — Focus on service matching, corporate identity consistency, and evidence placement.
  4. Check third-party mentions — Look for independent sources that help buyers verify claims, but avoid buying links or creating fake accounts.
  5. Check technical access — Verify robots.txt, WAF behavior, canonical tags, and whether AI crawlers (OAI-SearchBot, PerplexityBot) can actually retrieve the page.
  6. Prioritize fixes by buyer impact — Start with missing pages, then identity conflicts, then evidence gaps, then technical faults.
  7. Re-test with the same question — Keep records; don't delete earlier answers that didn't include your brand.

3. Key Facts & Claims (with Source Attribution)

The article cites several official sources:

ClaimSource Referenced
Search result relevance is affected by language, location, and deviceGoogle (public documentation)
Public websites can appear in ChatGPT search; allowing OAI-SearchBot helps content be discovered, displayed, and properly citedOpenAI publisher documentation
Perplexity distinguishes between PerplexityBot (search discovery) and Perplexity-User (responding to user questions)Perplexity crawler documentation
Pages must be indexed and eligible for search snippets before they can appear in generative features; crawling, indexing, and display are not guaranteedGoogle generative AI search optimization guide
OpenAI recommends allowing OAI-SearchBot for inclusion in ChatGPT search summaries and citationsOpenAI publisher guidance
Perplexity recommends allowing PerplexityBot and checking access using official IP ranges and User-Agent when using a WAFPerplexity crawler documentation

The article also references Bing URL submission and IndexNow, and the site's own "Open GEO Console" tool.

4. Limitations & Boundaries (as Stated by the Page)

The article is explicit about what it does not do:

  • It does not explain how AI models internally score or rank content.
  • It does not guarantee that changes will lead to recommendations.
  • It does not claim that more citations equal higher rankings — there is no cross-product universal weighting available to website owners.
  • It does not evaluate specific competitors or speculate about model parameters.
  • It does not treat third-party mentions as a deterministic cause of recommendations.
  • It does not recommend uploading private data, internal reports, access tokens, or non-public deliverables to public websites.
  • It does not promise indexing, citations, recommendations, rankings, traffic, or conversion.

The method is described as suitable for public corporate websites, service pages, product pages, articles, and reviewed project materials only.

5. Content Quality Assessment

Strengths:

  • Highly structured — clear sections, numbered steps, and a final checklist.
  • Actionable — every section ends with a concrete task or decision point.
  • Honest about uncertainty — repeatedly notes that results fluctuate and that no guarantees exist.
  • Evidence-based — cites official documentation from Google, OpenAI, and Perplexity.
  • Anti-spam stance — explicitly warns against buying links, exchanging irrelevant recommendations, and creating fake accounts.
  • Practical examples — includes a sample buyer question (internal knowledge → Q&A system with human review, delivery test records, and permission boundaries) while noting it is illustrative only.

Weaknesses / Gaps:

  • No data or case studies — the article presents no real-world examples of a company that followed this process and achieved results. This limits persuasiveness.
  • No visual aids — no screenshots, diagrams, or comparison tables, which would help illustrate the audit process.
  • Length — at ~4,700 characters, it is dense; some readers may find it overwhelming without a summary infographic.
  • Self-promotional elements — links to the site's own Open GEO Console and related services are present, though clearly separated in a "Next Steps" section.

6. SEO / GEO Observations

Target keywords (inferred): GEO diagnosis, AI search visibility, ChatGPT recommendations, Perplexity citations, generative engine optimization, AI crawler access, OAI-SearchBot, PerplexityBot.

Structured data: Not visible in the retained text; the page does not appear to include FAQ or HowTo schema based on the content provided.

Internal linking: Links to related articles ("AI 搜索可见性", "为什么企业官网在 AI 时代越来越重要", "为什么 AI 搜索看不到你的官网？") and to the site's own tools/services.

External references: Cites Google, OpenAI, Perplexity, and Bing documentation — these are authoritative and likely to be viewed favorably by AI systems.

GEO relevance: The page directly addresses a common buyer question ("Why does AI recommend competitors but not me?") and provides a methodology that aligns with how AI systems evaluate content (question coverage, evidence, technical accessibility). It is well-positioned to be cited by AI assistants answering GEO-related queries.

7. Recommendations (If This Were a Client's Page)

  1. Add a real-world case study — even anonymized, a before/after example would dramatically increase credibility.
  2. Add a downloadable checklist or template — the audit steps are excellent; a PDF or spreadsheet would increase engagement and shareability.
  3. Add FAQ schema — the page answers several common questions; structured data could improve search visibility.
  4. Add a comparison table — a visual side-by-side of "competitor page vs. your page" criteria would make the method easier to grasp.
  5. Consider a shorter companion piece — a 2-minute summary version for busy executives, linking to this full guide.

8. Overall Verdict

Purpose: Educational / thought leadership
Quality: High — well-researched, honest, actionable
Commercial intent: Low — indirect (links to tools and services)
Trustworthiness: High — cites official sources, acknowledges limitations, avoids overpromising
GEO potential: Strong — directly addresses a common AI-era buyer question with a credible, evidence-based methodology

This page is a solid example of content designed to earn AI citations: it answers a specific question, provides verifiable sources, and offers a repeatable process. It does not overclaim, and it clearly separates facts from recommendations. For a business in the GEO consulting space, this is effective foundational content.

Key Themes and Positioning

The content is heavily focused on GEO (Generative Engine Optimization) — the practice of making websites visible and citable in AI-generated answers. Recurring topics include:

  1. GEO vs. SEO distinctions — multiple articles clarify the differences, shared foundations, and complementary roles.

The editorial voice is practical and evidence-oriented, repeatedly emphasizing: real sample testing over vendor claims, clear human/AI responsibility boundaries, traceable records, and verifiable public evidence.

Notable Facts and Claims

  • Articles distinguish between being cited and being adopted in AI answers, arguing that cross-platform research can observe source composition but cannot assign universal weights to websites, news outlets, or public accounts.
  • The content explicitly separates model training text processing from AI search retrieval as two different processes, which is a technically important distinction for GEO practitioners.
  • Several articles stress that Search Console indexing alone does not guarantee AI recommendations — question matching, entity clarity, service boundary completeness, and public evidence all matter.

Limitations and Uncertainty

  • Publication dates are in the future relative to typical current dates (August–September 2026), which may indicate this is a planned or simulated content calendar.

Conclusion

This is a well-organized, topically focused content hub for GEO and enterprise AI automation. Its practical, checklist-driven approach and clear article summaries make it structurally favorable for AI citation. However, the lack of verifiable results, author credentials, and English-language content may limit its authority and reach in broader AI search contexts. The page's value for a GEO report lies primarily in its content strategy and topical coverage rather than in demonstrated outcomes.

SolveReal Systems — Enterprise AI Systems Design & Delivery

Page Overview

This is the English-language homepage of SolveReal Systems (实解智能 in Chinese), a company led by an individual identified as fengc. The page presents the firm as a provider of enterprise AI system design and delivery services, with a stated focus on solving real business problems rather than applying generic templates.

Core Positioning

The company's central message is that it transforms "manually connected, error-prone business workflows into AI automation systems" designed around how a company actually operates. The stated starting point is always a real workflow that consumes staff time, fails easily, or is difficult to sustain — explicitly not a fixed industry template or generic feature list.

Target Audience

The page identifies the intended clients as:

  • Owners and operations leaders at small and medium businesses
  • Organizations with repetitive manual workflows that may benefit from AI or automation

Service Approach

The delivery method is presented in four stages:

  1. Diagnose the current workflow — Map real inputs, processing steps, owners, exceptions, and deliverable outcomes
  2. Design the human boundary — Define what AI may handle, who reviews critical decisions, and which actions require confirmation
  3. Validate the real workflow — Test with real samples rather than an idealized demo path
  4. Deliver and improve — Provide a working system, operating boundaries, and traceable evidence, then improve from real use

A key stated principle: "The system handles stable steps; people retain key decisions and high-risk actions," with state, exceptions, recovery, and delivery evidence preserved throughout.

Four Capability Areas

The page describes four system directions:

  1. Multi-source intake — Consolidating documents, spreadsheets, and business web pages into one traceable operating record with sources preserved
  2. Repeated decisions and entry — Giving stable rules to the system while people retain exceptions and high-risk decisions
  3. Handoffs between systems — Carrying state across files and business systems with fewer manual transfers and gaps
  4. Recovery and human review — Recording exceptions and recovery points so operations can continue after interruptions

Project Evidence

Four projects are listed, with one featured in detail:

  1. Open GEO Console — Public product
  2. Hermes Notebook — Deployable system
  3. Freight Lead Agent — Deployable system (featured)
  4. Codex Feishu Bridge — Deployable system
Featured Project: Freight Lead Agent

Purpose: Google Maps prospecting and personalized outreach for sales teams.

Before: Sales teams had to find target companies on Google Maps, verify each official website, understand the business, locate public contacts, and prepare a different message for every company — difficult to scale manually.

System takeover: The system collects Google Maps companies by keyword and region, extracts business context and public contacts from each website, generates a personalized message, and sends it to sales for review, delivery, and follow-up.

Human control: Review of target company, website context, public contacts, and personalized message for accuracy.

Recovery and boundary: Invalid records are preserved with explicit reasons instead of being deleted.

Key limitation (explicitly stated): Processes public business information only; it does not crawl authenticated pages or personal profiles.

Field Notes / Articles

Three articles are listed, all dated September 2026:

  • 2026-09-21: "When Your Website Contradicts Itself, What Should GEO Fix First?" — Argues that when a homepage, service page, old article, and translated page state different conditions, the underlying public fact should be governed before producing more content or links.
  • 2026-09-21: "GEO vs SEO: A Practical Map of the Differences" — States that SEO and GEO share foundations of crawling, indexing, and useful content, but differ in the outcomes inspected, the units improved, and the evidence used for acceptance.
  • 2026-09-18: "When AI Cites Your Site, Did the GEO Change Work?" — Argues that a cited page is one observation, not a verdict; answer accuracy, citation support, visits, and qualified inquiries should be measured as separate outcomes of GEO work.

Notable Observations

  • The page includes a prominent call-to-action to "Submit your business problem" and an option to "Try Open GEO first"

Page Analysis: "Why Company Websites Matter More in the AI Era"

Page Overview

This is a long-form educational article published by SolveReal Systems on September 2, 2026, written in English. The page is hosted at me.itheheda.online under the /en/articles/ path, suggesting this is part of a bilingual (Chinese/English) corporate website. The article functions as both thought leadership content and a promotional vehicle for the company's Open GEO Console product.

Primary Purpose

The page serves a dual commercial and educational role:

  1. Educational: Explains how AI answer systems (Google AI Overviews, ChatGPT Search, Perplexity) discover, crawl, retrieve, and cite company websites, and why first-party web content matters more in this environment.
  2. Commercial: Promotes Open GEO Console, a paid review service that audits a company's website for "GEO readiness" (Generative Engine Optimization), and invites readers to "discuss the work" with SolveReal Systems.

Key Claims and Arguments

The article makes several substantive claims about AI search behavior:

  • No universal AI-search pipeline exists: Google, ChatGPT Search, and Perplexity use different indexes, retrieval systems, and access methods.
  • Google's process: Separates crawling, indexing, and serving; AI Overviews and AI Mode retrieve from the Search index and may use "query fan-out" (multiple related searches). Pages must satisfy ordinary Search technical requirements before generative eligibility.
  • ChatGPT Search: Requires allowing OAI-SearchBot for inclusion in search summaries, links, and citations.
  • Perplexity: Uses two agents — PerplexityBot (discovers and links public pages) and Perplexity-User (may visit pages in response to user requests, generally ignoring robots.txt).
  • llms.txt limitation: The article explicitly states Google's 2026 generative-search guidance says Google Search does not use llms.txt to improve generative-search visibility and requires no special AI markup.

Structure and Content Quality

The article is well-organized with clear sections:

  1. The short answer — Core thesis
  2. How an AI answer reaches a company website — Technical pipeline explanation
  3. A website now carries more than promotional copy — Content requirements
  4. Reconstructing the retrieval path with Open GEO — Product pitch with a comparison table
  5. What the website must make verifiable — Identity, service conditions, evidence
  6. Independent sources still matter — First-party vs. third-party validation
  7. How to measure whether the work is progressing — Metrics and evidence types
  8. A practical implementation sequence — Step-by-step checklist
  9. Verification checklist — 9-point summary
  10. Boundaries — Explicit limitations
  11. Sources — Citations to Google, OpenAI, Perplexity documentation
  12. Next step — Call to action for Open GEO Console

The article includes a useful comparison table mapping review stages to typical gaps and verifiable completion evidence.

Commercial Elements

The promotional content is integrated but not overwhelming:

  • Open GEO Console is introduced mid-article as the methodology for conducting a GEO review
  • The "Next step" section directs readers to start with Open GEO Console, read the project page, or "review enterprise AI services"
  • Contact is implied through "Bring an official domain, one real buyer question, and approved company facts when you are ready to discuss the work"
  • Three related articles are linked, all by SolveReal Systems, creating an internal content cluster

Credibility Assessment

Strengths:

  • Cites specific public documentation from Google, OpenAI, and Perplexity
  • Acknowledges limitations explicitly ("It cannot read a platform's internal ranking system, and it cannot promise indexing, citation, recommendation, traffic, or leads")
  • Provides concrete, testable criteria rather than vague promises
  • Distinguishes between different types of evidence (mentions vs. citations vs. visits)
  • Includes a "Boundaries" section warning against publishing private data

Cautions:

  • The article is published by the company selling the GEO review service, creating an inherent conflict of interest
  • Specific claims about Google's 2026 guidance cannot be independently verified from this page alone
  • The "observedAt" timestamp (September 30, 2026) is later than the publication date, suggesting the page was captured nearly a month after publication
  • The domain (me.itheheda.online) is not an obviously recognizable corporate domain, which may warrant verification of SolveReal Systems' legitimacy

Technical Observations

  • The page is directly readable (no JavaScript rendering required for main content)
  • Source length is 18,364 characters, indicating a substantial article
  • The URL structure (/en/articles/) suggests a bilingual site with language-specific paths
  • The article references "Chinese and English pages" in its checklist, confirming the bilingual nature of the site

Potential Gaps

  • No author biography or credentials are provided beyond the company name
  • No customer testimonials, case studies, or third-party validation of Open GEO Console's effectiveness
  • The article does not disclose pricing for the GEO review service
  • No data is presented on the actual performance of the methodology described
  • The "Sources" section links to external documentation but does not provide direct URLs within the retained text

Overall Assessment

This is a professionally written, technically substantive article that makes a coherent argument for why company websites matter in the AI era and positions Open GEO Console as a systematic solution. The content is more educational and less overtly sales-oriented than typical vendor content, with genuine emphasis on testable processes and honest limitations.

However, the commercial nature of the page means the claims about GEO review effectiveness should be treated as vendor assertions rather than independent findings. The article's value lies primarily in its practical framework for auditing website discoverability and AI-readiness, which readers could potentially apply themselves without purchasing the service.

Recommended use: This page is suitable for understanding the vendor's methodology and the general principles of GEO readiness. For decision-making about purchasing Open GEO Console services, independent verification of the claims and comparison with alternative approaches would be advisable.

14https://me.itheheda.online/articles/geo-public-fact-governance-website-consistencyhttps://me.itheheda.online/articles/geo-public-fact-governance-website-consistency

GEO 页面分析报告：官网自己说法不一时，GEO 应该先改哪一页？

分析对象：https://me.itheheda.online/articles/geo-public-fact-governance-website-consistency
观察时间：2026年9月30日
页面性质：实解智能（Open GEO）发布的付费 GEO 方法论文章，讨论官网内容不一致时的处理优先级

一、页面核心主张

本文提出一个明确的核心论点：当官网不同页面（首页、服务页、旧文章、英文版）对同一能力写出不同条件时，GEO 的第一项工作不是增加内容或外链，而是先建立可追溯的公开事实记录，确认哪条说法仍然成立、谁有权确认。

作者认为，继续增加文章、Schema 或外链只会让更多页面被发现，却不会替企业判断哪个承诺是真的。因此，内容治理应先于检索优化。

二、主要论点与建议

1. 建立公开事实记录（核心建议）

作者建议为每一项影响购买决定的公开事实建立一条记录，至少包含以下字段：

字段要回答的问题最低要求
事实编号与批准表述团队正在维护哪一项主张一项事实一个稳定编号，保留必要条件
事实负责人谁能确认它仍然成立写到具体岗位或负责人，不能只写"市场部"
公开证据页外部读者在哪里核对指向当前可访问并经过确认的页面
适用范围哪些客户、地区、版本或输入符合条件把限制写入正文，不能只留在内部备注
证据状态已上线能力、计划还是第三方结论不把计划、试验和已交付能力混写
时间状态何时生效、复核、退役至少保留生效日期和下一次复核日期
依赖页面哪些页面、结构化数据或资料复用了它包含首页、服务页、文章、FAQ 和下载资料
语言版本中文和英文是否表达同一条件各语言可自然改写，事实范围保持一致

作者引用 W3C PROV-O 作为方法论参考，但明确说明这只是内容治理思路的借鉴，不表示搜索或 AI 平台会按该模型给页面加分。

2. 冲突优先级排序

作者给出一个风险排序表，建议按以下优先级处理冲突：

冲突类型可能造成的实际问题建议优先级
购买资格和服务范围买家误判自己是否适用高
价格、地区和交付时间产生错误预算或进度预期高
人工复核、安全与隐私条件隐去必要控制和责任边界高
产品状态与版本要求把计划、测试或旧能力当成当前能力高
品牌名称和主体身份中英文页面指向不同公司或产品高
不影响事实的表达差异文风不同，但条件一致低

排序时考虑四个因素：错误是否改变购买决定、是否扩大企业承诺、出现在哪些高访问页面、旧版本已存在多久。作者特别指出，不应只按页面排名决定修改顺序，因为低流量页面仍可能成为 AI 回答的直接来源。

3. 双语页面同步

作者指出中英文官网最常见的缺口是把翻译当成一次性工作。建议每个语言版本引用同一事实编号，分别保存本地化表述、审核人和发布日期。引用 Google 多语言页面指南，建议建立双向 hreflang 关系，但强调这只能帮助搜索系统识别对应关系，不能让业务说法自动一致。

如果不同地区确实有不同价格、法规或服务范围，应建立带地区条件的两条事实记录，而不是抹掉真实差异。

4. 结构化数据与页面日期

作者强调可见正文与结构化数据必须一起检查，引用 Google 结构化数据政策，要求标记内容反映用户可见信息。若正文已改为"需要人工复核"，JSON-LD 或 FAQ 标记仍写"全自动"，机器可读层仍在传播旧条件。

关于更新时间，引用 Google 日期说明，建议页面可见日期与 datePublished、dateModified 保持一致。仅调整页脚或换图不应把旧文章包装成全新事实。sitemap 的 <lastmod> 只有在持续且可验证地准确时才会被 Google 使用。

5. 发布与通知

作者建议重大事实变更按小型发布管理，可向 IndexNow 提交 URL 更新，但引用其官方 FAQ 说明：提交只是发现信号，不保证立即抓取、收录或展示，且不建议反复提交没有变化的页面。

6. 适用边界（重要限制）

作者明确列出这套方法的适用范围和限制：

  • 适用：公开服务能力、价格规则、产品状态、身份信息、已批准公开的项目事实
  • 不适用：客户保密信息、账号内数据、尚未批准的路线图、无法核实的成果
  • 不保证：事实一致不保证页面会被任何平台收录或引用。以 OpenAI 的 OAI-SearchBot 为例，允许访问只影响被发现和考虑的资格，不构成引用承诺
  • 不替代：法律、合规或专业审查；外部平台仍可能使用旧缓存、第三方页面或其他来源

三、实施步骤（原文提供）

  1. 选出十到二十项会改变购买或交付判断的公开事实，优先覆盖服务范围、必要条件、价格规则、产品状态和人工责任
  2. 为每项事实指定负责人、批准表述、公开证据页、适用范围、生效日期和复核日期
  3. 搜索整个官网和公开资料，登记复用该事实的中文页面、英文页面、结构化数据与下载内容
  4. 按风险先修改会造成错误承诺的页面，再处理不影响判断的表达差异
  5. 发布时同步可见正文、结构化数据、页面日期与 sitemap 时间，并记录仍待更新的位置
  6. 对重大更新提交发现通知，随后检查公开页面、语言切换和目标问题下的实际回答，不把提交回执当成引用结果

四、验收清单（原文提供）

  • 每项高风险事实都有可识别的负责人和公开证据页
  • 服务范围、限制和人工责任在可见正文中完整出现
  • 首页、服务页、FAQ、文章和结构化数据没有相互冲突的当前说法
  • 中文与英文页面引用同一事实编号，真实的地区差异有单独条件
  • dateModified 与 sitemap 的更新时间对应实质修改
  • 旧页面已经更新、重定向、删除或明确标为历史内容
  • 发布记录能说明谁批准了什么，哪些页面已经同步，哪些事项仍待复核

五、页面质量评估

优点
  1. 结构清晰：从问题定义、方法论、优先级、实施步骤到验收清单，逻辑完整
  2. 边界明确：作者多次声明方法的适用范围和限制，没有过度承诺
  3. 引用规范：引用 Google Search Central、IndexNow、OpenAI、W3C PROV-O 等来源，且对每个引用的适用性做了限定说明
  4. 可操作性：提供了具体字段、排序标准和实施步骤，可直接落地
局限与不确定性
  1. 假设性示例：文中"一家公司原先只接收表格文件"的案例明确标注为假设，不代表本站客户项目，因此缺乏真实案例验证
  2. 效果未量化：文章没有提供采用该方法后的可量化效果数据（如引用准确率提升、错误说法减少比例等）
  3. 平台行为不确定：作者多次承认搜索和 AI 平台的具体行为不可控，方法只能保证自有页面的一致性
  4. 来源可验证性：参考来源以文字形式列出，未提供可点击的 URL 链接，读者需自行搜索验证

六、与 GEO 的相关性判断

本文属于 GEO 的内容治理前置环节，处理的是"网页进入搜索与 AI 回答之前"的问题。作者明确区分了本文与其他 GEO 主题的边界：

  • 不讨论检索流程（参见《从一个问题到带来源的回答》）
  • 不讨论效果归因（参见《官网被 AI 引用以后，怎么判断 GEO 改动有没有用》）
  • 只处理"官网怎样保持一套可核对的公开事实"

这一选题填补了 GEO 实践中一个常被忽视的环节：在追求可见性之前，先确保内容本身的一致性和可追溯性。

七、结论

本文为官网内容不一致问题提供了一个系统化的治理框架，核心价值在于把"事实管理"从模糊的"内容更新"中分离出来，建立了可追溯、可复核、可排序的操作体系。方法务实，边界清晰，适合作为企业官网内容治理的起点参考。

主要不确定性在于：该方法的效果缺乏量化验证，且外部搜索和 AI 平台的行为不可控，读者应将其视为内容治理的基础工作而非流量保证手段。

Why Does AI Recommend Your Competitors but Leave Out Your Company?

SolveReal Systems | August 31, 2026

A competitor mention is useful only when the team can trace the buyer request, recommendation reason, cited page, and missing evidence. A controlled comparison turns an AI answer into a remediation queue without pretending to know a model's ranking formula.

The question behind the missing recommendation

A procurement lead asks an AI assistant for providers that can solve a defined operational problem. The answer names several companies and omits yours. Saving the screenshot may feel like the obvious response, but the names alone reveal very little.

The useful evidence sits beside each name. What requirement did the assistant think the company matched? Which public page supported that reason? Did the page describe a service, a product, an independently reported result, or a broad marketing claim? Those details give your team something it can compare with its own public material.

This is a competitor evidence audit. It cannot reveal a provider's internal weights, and it cannot promise that a website change will produce a recommendation. It can identify a missing answer, an ambiguous entity, an unsupported service claim, a retrieval failure, or a test that was never controlled well enough to compare.

Establish a repeatable buyer prompt

Begin with one request that a plausible buyer would make. Remove your company name and the competitor names. Keep the operational problem, the intended customer, and the constraints that would affect a purchase.

A prompt might ask for a provider that can turn internal documents into a reviewed question-answer system while preserving human approval and acceptance records. That is a method example, not a customer case. Your working prompt should come from approved sales notes, search queries, consultation forms, or a business owner who can confirm the buying situation.

Record the exact prompt, product, date, language, region, and account state. Google explains that relevance can vary with factors including location, language, and device. AI products also change their retrieval sources and answer behavior over time. A test in English from a signed-in account cannot be compared cleanly with an anonymous Chinese test run from another region.

Perfect repeatability is unavailable. A disciplined record still matters. It lets the team distinguish a website change from a test whose inputs moved at the same time.

Capture the reason and the cited page

For every named company, copy the recommendation reason and open the cited URLs. Then ask a narrow question of each citation. What sentence or public fact supports the recommendation?

A company profile may establish identity. A service page can establish the intended buyer and delivery scope. Product documentation may support a feature claim. An independent publication can add context that the company does not control. These sources perform different jobs, so counting them as interchangeable mentions would hide the useful difference.

OpenAI says any public website can appear in ChatGPT search and advises publishers that want summaries, citations, and clear links to allow OAI-SearchBot. Its current publisher guidance also documents utm_source=chatgpt.com on referral links, giving site owners a downstream visit signal. Perplexity describes PerplexityBot as the crawler used to surface and link websites in search results, while Perplexity-User may visit a page in response to a user's request.

Those documents explain access and linking behavior. They do not publish a universal recommendation score. The audit should report the reasons and sources visible in the observed answer, not an invented formula for why one company won.

Build an evidence coverage comparison

Place the buyer requirements down the left side of a working sheet. For each requirement, record the competitor page, your page, the type of evidence, and the next action. Empty cells should remain empty. They are more useful than a guessed claim.

Start with service fit. Can a reader identify the operational problem, intended customer, required inputs, human review point, deliverable, and acceptance method? If the competitor answers the buyer's constraint and your homepage offers only a broad category label, the first remediation is a reviewed service explanation. Publishing ten pages that repeat the category will leave the decision gap in place.

Check entity clarity next. Company name, product name, official domain, service scope, and contact route should agree across the homepage, product pages, articles, language variants, and structured data. Metadata can express a clean relationship. It cannot repair visible pages that describe the product as a service in one place and a completed customer result in another.

Then examine claim support. A public method, named deliverable, acceptance record template, limitation, or documented demo boundary gives a buyer a way to verify what the company offers. When no approved customer outcome is public, publish the method and its actual limits. An invented percentage would make the page less defensible, even if it made the comparison sheet look full.

Treat independent references as evidence, not inventory

An industry article, partner document, maintained professional directory, or technical citation can give a buyer context beyond the company's own copy. Review its origin, date, and link to the underlying fact. A lightly edited press release remains company-supplied material even when another domain hosts it.

Reference volume has no stable meaning across AI products. Purchased profiles, reciprocal mentions, and unrelated backlinks create pages without clarifying the service. They also leave a poor evidence trail for a human procurement team.

The durable starting point is first-party material worth citing. Publish a stable explanation of the service method, a truthful project boundary, original research, or a reproducible public artifact. When a partner or journalist genuinely uses that material, help them retain the correct company name and source URL. Independent references should follow real work and real relationships.

Verify the retrieval path separately

Strong public evidence still has to be reachable by the relevant system. Test robots rules, HTTP status, canonical URL, server-rendered content, and edge-security behavior on the production page.

Google's current guidance for generative search says a page must be indexed and eligible for a Search snippet before it can appear in those features. Google also states that meeting requirements does not guarantee crawling, indexing, or serving. OpenAI recommends allowing OAI-SearchBot for ChatGPT search discovery and citation. Perplexity recommends allowing PerplexityBot and, where a WAF is involved, checking both its published IP ranges and user agent.

A browser receiving HTTP 200 proves only the browser path. A WAF can return a challenge or 403 response to identified automated traffic. Each intended access path needs its own production response check.

Retrieval is one row in the comparison. Once access works, move back to the buyer request. Technical eligibility does not supply a missing delivery method or acceptance boundary.

Turn the audit into a short remediation queue

Prioritize the gap that prevents a buyer from making a decision.

If no public page answers the target request, create or revise that page with an authorized fact owner. If the page exists but the company and product relationship conflicts across the site, resolve the public identity. When service fit is clear but the important claims lack deliverables, acceptance evidence, or limitations, add reviewed support. Repair a crawl, canonical, or WAF problem when a production test proves it exists.

Write each action with a target URL, fact owner, closing evidence, and review date. "Improve GEO" cannot be verified. "Add the human approval point and acceptance record to the service page, then obtain business-owner review" can be closed and retested.

Open GEO Console can organize the public pages, buyer question, answer citations, evidence gaps, and remediation priorities in one review. It does not approve company facts and cannot control the answer produced by any search or AI platform.

Retest without erasing the earlier result

After the reviewed change is public and available for discovery, run the recorded prompt under the same conditions. Preserve the earlier answer. Compare recommendation reasons and citations before reducing the result to a brand present-or-absent flag.

Keep the measurement chain separate. Indexing shows that a search engine processed a page under its reporting rules. An AI mention is an observed answer event. Search impressions and referral visits come from their own reporting systems. An inquiry belongs in the form or CRM record. Movement at one stage does not prove movement at the next.

One retest is still one observation. A useful trend needs dated, comparable runs. The team should also record when the AI product, prompt, language, or region changed, because those changes limit the comparison.

Boundaries

This method applies to public company sites, service and product pages, articles, and approved project evidence. Customer-confidential data, private reports, tokens, account-only pages, and unapproved deliverables should remain private.

The audit does not infer model parameters, publish negative claims about a named competitor, or treat a third-party mention as proven causation. AI products use different and changing retrieval systems. A recommendation-readiness review can improve the clarity, accessibility, and support behind public claims, but it does not guarantee indexing, citations, recommendations, rankings, traffic, or inquiries.

Open GEO Console evaluates public technical foundations, buyer-question coverage, answer material, citation evidence, and remediation priorities. Its output is a set of reviewable website actions, not a promise that a platform will select the company.

A practical review sequence

Select one commercial request — Use an approved buying situation and remove all company names. Preserve the intended buyer, operational problem, and meaningful constraints.

Save one complete answer — Record the prompt, product, time, language, region, named companies, recommendation reasons, and cited URLs. Open every citation and note the claim it supports.

Compare the supporting pages — Map buyer requirements to a small set of relevant pages for each company. Review service fit, entity consistency, evidence type, independent context, and production access.

Close one material gap — Choose the gap with the clearest effect on the buyer's decision. Assign the target page and fact owner, then define the evidence required to close it.

Repeat the recorded test — Retest after the public change can be discovered. Keep both answers and report each stage of the measurement chain separately.

Sources

  • Google guide to how Search works
  • Google guide to generative AI features on Search
  • OpenAI publishers and developers FAQ
  • Perplexity crawler documentation
  • Bing URL submission and IndexNow guidance
  • Open GEO Console in English

Next step

If an observed AI answer already names several competitors, bring one real buyer request and the relevant public URLs to Open GEO Console. The free check begins with the homepage, robots.txt, sitemap.xml, and public content, then organizes the first question-coverage, citation-evidence, or technical-access gaps.

Review the Open GEO Console project boundary for its public scope and simulated-demo limits. You can also inspect the enterprise AI service and other public projects. When the production URLs, buyer request, and expected deliverables are clear, submit the problem for a scoped discussion.

GEO vs. SEO: Practical Differences — Page Analysis

Executive Summary

This page, published by 实解智能 (Shijie Intelligence) on September 21, 2026, provides a practical, task-oriented comparison between Search Engine Optimization (SEO) and Generative Engine Optimization (GEO). The article argues that while SEO and GEO share technical foundations (crawling, indexing, quality content), they differ in what they optimize, how results are measured, and how work is validated. The page is well-structured, uses a comparison table, provides a hypothetical case study, and includes actionable implementation steps. It is written in Chinese and targets enterprise website owners and marketing teams.

1. Page Classification & Intent

AttributeAssessment
Content typeEducational / explanatory article (long-form)
Primary intentInformational — explains the difference between SEO and GEO, provides a working framework
Secondary intentCommercial — promotes the author's services (Open GEO Console, enterprise AI systems, consulting)
Target audienceWebsite owners, SEO managers, content teams, marketing decision-makers at companies with an existing web presence
ToneProfessional, measured, caveat-heavy; avoids overpromising
ReadabilityDirect, structured, uses tables and lists; Chinese-language content with English technical terms retained

2. Key Claims & Definitions

2.1 Core Definition Offered

The article proposes a working definition:

  • SEO manages how pages perform in search discovery, display, and visits.
  • GEO manages whether public facts appear in generative answers, whether they are stated correctly, and whether they receive appropriate source support.

Important caveat stated by the author: The boundary between SEO and GEO does not imply two separate algorithms inside search systems. The same page and the same facts can participate in both types of results simultaneously. The difference lies in which "task ticket" the team opens, what observations are recorded, and who decides the work is complete.

2.2 Google's Position (as cited)

The article cites Google's official guidance:

Google explicitly states that AI Overviews and AI Mode are built on its core search ranking and quality systems; existing SEO practices remain applicable, and there is no mandatory set of additional GEO-specific technical requirements.

The article interprets this as: GEO should be managed as content, evidence, and measurement work for generative answers — not as a replacement ranking system for SEO.

2.3 Source References Used

The page cites the following sources (verified as of September 21, 2026):

  1. Google SEO Starter Guide
  2. Google AI Features & Websites
  3. Google Generative AI Search Optimization Guide
  4. Google Generative AI Performance Report
  5. Bing AI Performance documentation
  6. OpenAI Publisher & Developer documentation
  7. The original GEO paper (by Aggarwal et al.)

Note: The article explicitly warns that platform documentation and report fields may change, and execution should follow current official pages.

3. The SEO vs. GEO Comparison Table (Reproduced in Summary)

DimensionSEO FocusGEO Focus
User-facing interfaceSearch results, snippets, images, merchant listingsGenerative answers assembled from multiple sources, with source links
Primary optimization unitPages, URLs, site structure, query-to-landing-page relationshipsIndependently understandable facts, claims, evidence passages, brand-service relationships
Typical outcomesImpressions, rankings, clicks, organic visits, on-site conversionsAccurate mentions in answers, correct use of key facts, source support, AI-referred visits
Common problemsCrawl failures, no indexing, query mismatch, weak snippet appeal, poor page experiencePage retrieved but key facts used incorrectly, wrong page cited, distorted descriptions, conflicting sources
Common changesCrawl/index fixes, information architecture, internal links, titles/body text, search intent coverageQuestion coverage, fact boundaries, evidence proximity, entity clarification, cross-page/cross-language consistency, fixed-problem retesting
Validation methodSearch Console, site analytics, ranking & conversion recordsPlatform reports, full answers, actual source URLs, description accuracy, referred visits & follow-up behavior

Author's caveat: This table represents a division of labor, not a technical boundary. SEO also handles entities, passages, and authority; generative answers also resolve to pages and URLs. The difference is where validation attention is placed.

4. Why the Optimization Unit Changes

The article explains that classic search results present page links, so teams work URL-by-URL. In Google's generative features:

  • The system retrieves materials first, then organizes an answer.
  • Google publicly states these features use retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and may use query fan-out (splitting one question into multiple related searches).
  • One answer may draw capabilities from a service page, implementation conditions from a documentation page, and evidence from a case study or policy page.

Key implication for content review: Page topic clarity remains important, but key facts must also stand alone when removed from context. Information such as: who provides the service, who it suits, what inputs are supported, which actions require human confirmation, how results are validated, and what limitations exist — if scattered across vague paragraphs, the system may retrieve the page but fail to combine facts accurately.

Important limitation stated: The original GEO paper studies content visibility in generative answers and proposes a testing framework. It provides a research starting point but does not establish a unified industry ranking standard. Experimental results on specific benchmarks cannot be directly converted into citation growth for any commercial website.

5. Hypothetical Case Study (发票识别 / Invoice Recognition)

The article presents a hypothetical example (explicitly stated as not representing a client or delivered project):

Scenario: An enterprise software company offers invoice recognition services. Its product page is indexed and appears for queries like "invoice OCR." The team opens two task tickets for the same page.

The buyer's specific question:

Which invoice recognition service supports Chinese scanned invoices, allows finance staff to review before writing to ERP, and can be deployed in the enterprise's own environment?

The original page only said: "high precision, automated, flexible deployment" — directional but not answering the three purchase-deciding questions.

Two validation tickets for the same page:

TicketInputs recordedWork requiredAcceptance evidence
SEORelated queries, target URL, current impressions & clicksCheck page-query match, search result presentation, internal links, post-landing next stepsIndexing status, query data, clicks & on-site behavior
GEOFixed procurement questions, approved service conditions, target platformsFill in version & deployment conditions; verify answers preserve the human review requirementFull answers, actual sources, fact-checking, referred visits

Key insight: These two tickets can drive the same page modification but cannot share a single completion condition. If product and delivery owners have not confirmed the on-premise deployment scope, the SEO task can continue observing page performance, but the GEO task cannot expand "flexible deployment" into a definite commitment.

Author's warning: Page ranking rising does not prove answer accuracy. An answer citing the page does not prove the user clicked or submitted an inquiry. These results are related but not interchangeable.

6. Metrics: The Most Confusing Difference

6.1 SEO Metrics (Mature)
  • Google Search Console: clicks, impressions, CTR, average position
  • Site analytics: post-visit reading, inquiries, other behaviors
6.2 GEO Metrics (Immature)

The article states clearly: There is currently no cross-platform universal "AI ranking." Different products expose different data.

Platform-specific data as of the article's writing:

PlatformAvailable dataCaveats
GoogleGenerative AI performance report (added 2026): impressions from generative search features, related pages, countries, devices, dates—
Bing Webmaster ToolsAI Performance public preview: citation counts, cited pages, grounding queriesMicrosoft warns these aggregates do not represent page ranking, authority, or how much a page contributed to a specific answer
OpenAIPublisher documentation: allowing OAI-SearchBot access helps content appear in ChatGPT search; referral links carry utm_source=chatgpt.com—
6.3 Recommended Four-Layer GEO Recording

The article recommends recording GEO observations in four separate layers:

  1. Appearance — Did the brand or page enter the answer and source list?
  2. Expression — Did the answer correctly describe the service audience, capabilities, and limitations?
  3. Support — Does the cited page actually support the corresponding claim in the answer?
  4. Follow-up behavior — Did the user visit the official site, read key pages, or initiate an inquiry?

Warning: Recording only "mentioned by AI" conflates all four layers. Accurate mentions may lack citations; citations may contain incorrect descriptions; visits may not come from the target question.

7. Symptom-Based Prioritization Guide

Current symptomPriority workReason
Important pages cannot be crawled or are not indexedTechnical SEO firstPage not stably in retrieval material scope; answer testing lacks foundation
Page indexed but almost no impressions for relevant queriesSEO: page topic, search demand, internal links, content qualityNeed to confirm page addresses a real search need
Impressions but very low CTRCheck title, snippet, page promise vs. query matchThis is a search-result-to-visit problem
Page has organic visits but AI answers describe services incorrectlyAdd GEO fact & answer reviewDiscoverability ≠ correct fact usage in answers
Answers cite old articles, not current service pageCheck old content, internal links, dates, canonical pages, public fact consistencyMay involve both SEO and content governance
Answers accurate with sources but no official site visitsFirst confirm user completed task in the answer; then check guidance & landing pageNo click alone does not prove GEO failure
Brand described as two different companies in Chinese vs. English answersCheck entity names, language versions, public materialsRequires both SEO internationalization and GEO fact consistency

Author's note: If you don't even know whether pages can be accessed or indexed, start with an AI search visibility audit. If foundations are stable, proceed to answer accuracy and source support.

8. Shared Foundations (Record Once)

The article lists shared foundations that serve both SEO and Google's generative features:

  • Stable URLs
  • Readable body text
  • Internal links
  • Accurate titles
  • True facts
  • Consistent structured data

Google's stated requirement (as cited): Pages need to be indexed and eligible for snippet display to appear as support links in Google's AI features.

Recommendation: Teams should not build two separate technical checklists for the two types of work. Shared issues go into one website backlog; SEO and GEO each keep their own validation records. GEO additionally maintains buyer questions, full answers, actual sources, and fact-check results.

9. Team Division of Labor

RoleResponsibility
SEO / website ownerManage crawling, indexing, site structure, search performance of public pages
Content ownerTurn real needs into questions the page can answer; ensure key passages remain clear out of context
Business ownerConfirm service capabilities, applicable conditions, and boundaries that cannot be publicly promised
Analytics ownerPreserve search data, generative answers, and website behavior records

Key governance point: One person can hold multiple roles, but approval authority must be explicit. Content teams can discover that "whether on-premise deployment is supported" has no answer — but they must not invent the answer themselves. GEO brings facts into answers, which brings business commitments into public environments. High-impact claims require confirmation from someone who truly understands delivery conditions.

Review process: A joint question checklist can start a review, but final records should remain separate. SEO owners record page/query performance; GEO owners record answers and sources; business owners judge description accuracy.

10. Three Common Misconceptions

10.1 Treating GEO as Mass Q&A Writing

Creating a page for every long-tail question can produce duplicate and low-value content. Page count ≠ fact coverage. First confirm what decision information buyers need, then choose the best home (service page, documentation, case study, or article).

10.2 Treating Citation Counts as Final Business Results

Citations prove a page became a source in some answer — not that the answer was accurate, that users visited, or that inquiries occurred. Each layer needs its own evidence.

10.3 Combining Everything into One "GEO Score"

Rankings, citations, fact accuracy, visits, and inquiries have different meanings. Compressing them into one score hides where the problem occurred. Dashboards are acceptable, but raw fields and evidence should be preserved.

11. Four-Week Implementation Plan

WeekFocusActivities
Week 1Establish baselineSelect one important service and 10–20 real procurement questions; record search queries, primary landing pages, target platform answers, cited URLs, fact errors
Week 2Entry-point issuesFix crawling, indexing, canonical links, internal links, body readability. If no foundational faults found, do not create a separate technical project for GEO
Week 3Decision factsConfirm with fact owners: applicable audience, inputs, delivery, human review, data processing, limitations, validation methods. Publish only confirmed content; sync related languages and old pages
Week 4Retest against original questionsRecord search impressions & clicks, answer accuracy, source support, referred visits separately. If sample size is insufficient, keep raw records; do not write one change as a stable trend

Outcome after four weeks: A problem list, page list, fact gaps, and a re-checkable baseline — more useful for planning next work than an undefined "GEO score."

12. Applicability Boundaries (Explicitly Stated)

  • The article discusses visibility of public websites in search results and generative answers.
  • Different platforms use different indexes, crawl policies, retrieval methods, and answer interfaces.
  • Google's rules cannot substitute for Bing, OpenAI, or other platforms' actual documentation.
  • Completing SEO or GEO changes does not guarantee indexing, ranking, citations, traffic, or inquiries.
  • Platform reports only prove what their fields cover. Business value assessment requires combining website behavior, lead quality, and actual deal processes.

13. Validation Checklist (Provided by the Article)

  1. SEO tasks specify target queries, URLs, and search performance evidence.
  2. GEO tasks specify target questions, platforms, factual claims, and answer evidence.
  3. Shared technical issues get one backlog item; two validation records remain independent.
  4. Rankings, citations, accurate descriptions, visits, and inquiries are not combined into one vague score.
  5. High-impact claims have a fact owner; content staff do not expand service promises on their own.
  6. Chinese and English pages are checked separately; retesting preserves full answers and actual sources.
  7. Reports clearly distinguish observations, inferences, and unverified results.

14. Sources Cited (as listed on page)

  1. Google SEO Starter Guide
  2. Google AI Features & Websites
  3. Google Generative AI Search Optimization Guide
  4. Google Generative AI Performance Report
  5. Bing AI Performance documentation
  6. OpenAI Publisher & Developer documentation
  7. GEO original paper

Verification note: Materials checked September 21, 2026. Platform documentation and report fields may update; actual execution should follow current official pages.

15. Internal Links & Related Content

The page links to related articles on the same site:

  1. 网站已经做了 SEO，为什么还需要 GEO (September 8, 2026, 7 min read) — Why GEO is needed after SEO is done
  2. 官网被 AI 引用以后，怎么判断 GEO 改动有没有用 (September 18, 2026, 6 min read) — How to judge whether GEO changes worked after AI citations
  3. 从一个问题到带来源的回答：AI 搜索怎样使用网页 (September 16, 2026, 6 min read) — How AI search uses web pages, from question to sourced answer

Conversion paths: Open GEO Console, Open GEO project description, enterprise AI systems services, contact page.

16. Quality Assessment

Strengths
  • Clear operational framework: The SEO/GEO comparison table is practical and actionable.
  • Appropriate caveats: The article consistently warns against over-interpretation (e.g., citations ≠ business results, no universal AI ranking exists).
  • Platform-specific accuracy: Correctly distinguishes Google, Bing, and OpenAI data availability.
  • Governance emphasis: Strong on who approves facts and why that matters.
  • Honest about limitations: Explicitly states that the GEO paper is research, not an industry standard.
  • Structured for scanning: Tables, symptom guides, and checklists make it usable.
Limitations / Uncertainties
  • Dated information: All platform references are as of September 2026; the article itself acknowledges these may change.
  • Hypothetical case study: The invoice recognition example is explicitly not a real client project.
  • No original research: The article synthesizes existing public documentation rather than presenting new data.
  • Chinese-language focus: The brand consistency example (Chinese vs. English answers) may not apply to all markets.
  • No measurement of its own claims: The article does not provide evidence that its recommended framework produces results.
Potential Conflicts of Interest
  • The article promotes the author's own tools (Open GEO Console) and services (enterprise AI systems) at the end. This is disclosed through context but is a commercial motivation to consider.

17. Overall Assessment

This is a high-quality, practical reference article for teams trying to operationalize GEO alongside existing SEO work. Its primary value lies in:

  1. Providing a clear division of labor between SEO and GEO
  2. Establishing a four-layer measurement framework
  3. Offering a symptom-based prioritization guide
  4. Emphasizing governance and fact-approval processes

The article is not a research paper, does not present original experimental data, and its platform-specific claims are time-bound. It is best used as a working framework rather than an authoritative specification.

Recommended use: Teams with an existing SEO foundation who want to extend into GEO should use this article's checklist and four-week plan as a starting point, while verifying all platform-specific claims against current official documentation.

Freight Lead Agent — 页面分析报告

页面概述

该页面介绍了一个名为 Freight Lead Agent 的可部署系统，定位为“Google 地图获客与定制营销系统”。页面以中文撰写，面向的受众是销售人员或小团队，核心卖点是将“从 Google 地图找企业 → 读官网 → 找联系方式 → 写定制开发信 → 发送跟进”这一完整流程自动化，同时保留人工审核环节。

核心功能拆解

页面将系统能力分为四个层次：

  1. 系统接管的部分：按关键词和地区从 Google 地图采集目标企业，保留企业来源与官网；逐家访问官网，提取业务介绍、服务信息与公开联系方式；结合对方官网内容和发件方资料生成定制开发邮件，进入人工审核与发送计划。
  2. 人工保留的部分：逐条确认目标企业、官网内容、公开联系方式和定制邮件是否准确；人工决定是否修改、发送、安排节奏或停止联系，并处理后续回复。
  3. 最终交付物：包含企业来源、官网、公开联系方式和处理状态的目标客户库；依据每家企业官网内容生成、可逐条审核的定制开发邮件；带发送节奏、发件账号、投递状态和回复跟进的发送计划。
  4. 技术形态：项目已形成可独立部署的 Docker 系统，覆盖从企业发现到回复监控的完整链路。

使用范围与限制

页面明确列出两条边界：

  • 只处理公开企业信息，不抓取登录后页面或个人资料。
  • 外联内容必须人工审核，系统不提供无差别批量自动发送。

这两条限制值得注意：前者界定了数据来源的合法性边界，后者则明确该系统并非全自动群发工具，而是“半自动”的辅助系统。

页面末尾的特别声明

页面最后一段写道：“你的业务不需要复制这个项目；我们会从实际流程重新诊断。”并附有“讨论你的流程”的引导。这表明该页面不仅是产品介绍，还承担着销售线索转化的功能——它暗示读者无需自行部署这套系统，而是可以直接与卖方讨论定制化方案。

页面中未明确的信息

  • 定价：页面未提及任何价格信息。
  • 部署要求：虽然提到 Docker，但未说明服务器配置、运行环境或维护成本。
  • 数据合规细节：虽然声明“只处理公开企业信息”，但未涉及 GDPR、中国《个人信息保护法》或其他司法辖区的具体合规说明。
  • 效果数据：未提供任何案例数据、成功率或客户见证。
  • 技术细节：未说明 Google 地图数据采集的具体方式、频率限制或反爬应对策略。
  • 交付周期：未说明从购买到部署完成的时间预期。

页面语气与可信度评估

页面语气务实，没有夸大承诺。它明确承认“这套工作很难靠人工持续放大”，并强调人工审核环节不可省略，这在一定程度上增加了可信度。但页面也缺少可验证的第三方证据（如客户案例、技术文档链接或可运行的演示环境），因此其实际效果仍需通过进一步沟通验证。

总结

这是一个功能描述清晰、边界明确的 B2B 工具介绍页。它解决的是销售开发流程中“找企业、读官网、写定制信”这一重复性劳动密集环节，同时保留了人工审核的最终控制权。页面最大的未解问题是定价、实际效果和合规细节，这些都需要通过页面底部的“讨论你的流程”入口进一步获取。

19https://me.itheheda.online/articles/how-to-measure-geo-ai-citationshttps://me.itheheda.online/articles/how-to-measure-geo-ai-citations

How to Measure GEO AI Citations: A Practical Framework

Publisher: 实解智能 (Shijie Intelligence) | Date: September 18, 2026

Core Argument

A single AI citation is only a starting point for observation. To determine whether GEO (Generative Engine Optimization) changes to your website are working, you must separately track four layers of evidence: whether the answer is accurate, whether the citation supports the conclusion, whether visits occurred, and whether inquiries were valid. A citation link alone only shows that your website appeared in a particular answer or platform statistic; it cannot prove the answer described your business correctly, that anyone clicked through, or that a later inquiry resulted from that specific change.

What a Screenshot Can and Cannot Prove

The article uses a hypothetical example (explicitly labeled as fictional, not a project result) of a company that completes the applicable conditions on its service page. The next day, an employee asks a connected assistant a question and sees the new page cited. The screenshot proves what that account, at that time, with that phrasing, displayed. It cannot show whether the page was occasionally cited before the change, how other buyers might phrase their questions, or rule out changes from search indexing, user demand, or model updates.

A more easily overlooked issue is the answer text itself. If the link points to your service page but the answer still describes conditional capabilities as unconditional promises, the citation actually masks the problem. The article cites the ALCE citation evaluation research, which separates answer correctness from citation support, as the reason for this distinction.

Four Layers of Evidence

ObservationWhat it can answerWhat it cannot imply
Save the full answer and verify key factsWhether capabilities, limitations, and timing are stated correctlyThat other phrasings will get the same answer
Save the citation URL and verify the page textWhether the displayed link supports the adjacent claimThat citation equals endorsement, ranking, or clicks
Check source visits in your own analytics toolsWhether a recordable site visit occurredThat the visitor understood the service or is ready to buy
Cross-check inquiry records against real needsWhether an inquiry within the service scope appearedThat a single page edit alone caused the inquiry

Platform Data: Read According to Its Own Definitions

Bing Webmaster Tools: The AI Performance documentation lists visible citations, cited pages, and topic phrases used for retrieval as observation items. These phrases are not the user's original queries, and citation counts do not represent ranking, authority, or clicks. Coverage is limited to Microsoft Copilot, Bing's AI summaries, and some partner experiences—not a total count across all AI platforms. Bing's official release notes also position this data as aggregated citation visibility.

Google: Official documentation states that traffic from AI Overviews and AI Mode is included in the overall Search Console "Pages" search type data. Therefore, you cannot read the total table as showing how many visits each individual AI answer generated.

OpenAI: The publisher FAQ states that links from ChatGPT to websites carry utm_source=chatgpt.com, allowing sites to view recordable referral visits. Visit records still differ from answer impression counts and cannot replace demand assessment in sales conversations.

How to Run a Comparable Before/After Observation

  1. Select real buyer questions encountered in sales or delivery—not just phrasings most likely to surface your brand name. For each, write down the facts and conditions you want the answer to state clearly, and which page on your site provides the evidence. For example, "Can you handle scanned documents?" should also record "requires text recognition first" and "results are human-reviewed." Counting only brand mentions will miss these critical errors.

  2. Before changes: Fix the exact question wording, product entry point, whether search is enabled, language and region, and test date. Save the full answer and citation URL, and record the website page version.

  3. After changes: Re-ask using the same recording criteria. Keep records of non-citations and incorrect answers as well.

  4. Sample size: Different dates, phrasings, and products can yield different answers, so evaluate a set of questions over a period—do not cherry-pick the single best result. There is no universal "test ten times for significance" threshold; sample size should be determined by decision risk and question volatility.

  5. Connect visits and inquiries, but maintain evidence boundaries: Use your own analytics for traffic, and forms, email, or CRM records to verify whether inquiries match target needs. Without client consent or a reliable source record, write only "observed concurrent inquiries"—do not attribute them to a specific AI answer.

  6. Allow time for discovery and re-crawling: Google states that content changes may take time to be reflected in search systems.

The Website's Role in This Framework

The website is both a potential citation source and the place buyers verify promises after clicking. Service descriptions should state current capabilities and limitations; project records should show only publicly confirmed facts. Writing facts clearly, making target pages accessible, and ensuring the same question can find corresponding evidence are tasks within your control. Whether a platform chooses to cite you and how it displays you remains the platform's decision.

Open GEO Console: Where It Fits

The Open GEO Console is positioned as a website diagnosis and remediation entry point: it checks public pages against target buyer questions, organizes gaps in accessibility, content expression, question coverage, and citation evidence, and provides pages needing modification with priorities. It is not a real-time monitoring system for cross-platform citations or sales conversion, and cannot prove causal improvement from a single test. Product scope is described on the Open GEO project page.

Applicability Boundaries

This method suits judging "whether problems decreased, whether answers became more accurate, and whether follow-up business signals appeared"—it is not a randomized controlled experiment. Manual questioning is sampled observation; platform reports have their own coverage limits; website analytics can be affected by browser settings and collection methods. Bing's official documentation explicitly states that citation trend changes cannot be attributed to a single content modification. Without sufficiently stable before/after samples, write "observed changes," not "the modification caused growth."

Implementation Steps

  1. Select real buyer questions; first record the current website page and the original AI answer.
  2. Mark key facts, missing conditions, and cited text in each answer.
  3. After modifying the website, keep the page version and re-ask using the same recording criteria.
  4. Finally, cross-reference your own visit and inquiry records, and summarize "answer improvement," "citation appearance," "visit occurrence," and "valid demand" separately—do not merge them into one seemingly precise GEO score.

Acceptance Checklist

A reviewable record should include: the original question and questioning environment, date, full answer, citation URL, the website version checked, item-by-item fact judgments, and the source of visit or inquiry data. Negative samples must also be kept. If evidence reaches only "the website was cited," stop the conclusion at that layer; if subsequent visits and inquiries can be verified, continue downward, but do not skip attribution limitations.

Next Steps

If you already know what buyers will ask but are unsure which pages state the answers clearly, you can start with Open GEO Console for website detection. To discuss specific pages, business questions, and reviewable acceptance criteria, use the contact page. Test results and final public statements remain the responsibility of the website owner for verification.

  • Bing official blog: AI Performance public beta release notes
  • Google Search Central: AI features and websites
  • OpenAI: Publisher and developer FAQ
  • ALCE: Citation-based long-form answer evaluation research

2. Core Claims and Key Facts

The article makes several specific, verifiable claims about how AI search systems work:

ClaimSource cited by the article
ChatGPT may auto-search when current info is needed; users can also manually trigger searchOpenAI's ChatGPT search documentation
ChatGPT rewrites a question into one or more targeted queries when working with search providersOpenAI's search documentation
Google's AI Overviews and AI Mode may run related searches for multiple subtopicsGoogle's AI features documentation

The article is careful to state its limits: it does not claim to know internal ranking formulas, query scoring, or per-platform retrieval details. 3. Practical Guidance Offered

Implementation steps:

  1. Start with a real buyer question; record the original wording, query time, and whether the target AI product had search enabled.
  2. Save the full answer and cited URLs.
  3. Go sentence-by-sentence back to the original website and media sources; mark which sentence is supported by which material, and where dates, limitations, or human-confirmation conditions were dropped.
  4. Check whether the corresponding website page is publicly accessible and whether the body text puts capabilities, prerequisites, and evidence together.
  5. After making changes, re-test with the same question set and keep before/after records.

Acceptance checklist (four separate items):

  • Whether the page can be retrieved by the target system
  • Whether the answer mentions the company
  • Whether key facts are accurate
  • Whether displayed citations actually support those facts

The article stresses that a page returning HTTP 200 only proves accessibility, and a single citation in one answer does not prove long-term stable adoption.
