Page Analysis: "When Your Website Contradicts Itself, What Should GEO Fix First?"

Overview

This is a paid GEO (Generative Engine Optimization) report analyzing the page at https://me.itheheda.online/en/articles/geo-public-fact-governance-website-consistency, published by SolveReal Systems on September 21, 2026. The page addresses content governance for websites with contradictory public claims, positioning itself as a practical guide for establishing a single source of truth before pursuing retrieval and measurement strategies.

Key Facts and Claims

Core Thesis: When a homepage, service page, old article, and translated page state different conditions for the same capability, the first GEO task is to establish which claim is still true and who can approve it. The page argues that more articles, Schema markup, and backlinks cannot decide which business promise is valid.

Proposed Framework: The article recommends creating one governed record for every public fact that can change a buying decision. Each record should include:

  • Fact ID and approved claim
  • Fact owner (named role or person with decision authority)
  • Public evidence page
  • Scope (customer, region, version, or input qualifications)
  • Evidence status (live, planned, experimental, or third-party)
  • Time status (effective date and next review date)
  • Dependencies (pages and machine-readable surfaces)
  • Language status

Priority Matrix: The page provides a conflict-priority table identifying high-risk contradictions:

  • Eligibility and service scope
  • Price, region, and delivery time
  • Human review, safety, and privacy conditions
  • Product status and version requirements
  • Brand and legal identity

Stylistic variation is classified as low priority.

Technical References: The article cites Google Search Central guidance on publication dates, sitemaps, structured-data policies, localized versions, and canonical tags, plus IndexNow FAQ, OpenAI crawler documentation, and W3C PROV-O. It notes that canonical tags have no role in deciding which commercial claim is true, and that structured data must represent visible content.

Limitations and Boundaries

The page explicitly states several limitations:

  • Consistent facts do not guarantee indexing or citation by any platform
  • Allowing OAI-SearchBot makes a page eligible for consideration but does not promise placement or citation
  • The record does not replace legal, compliance, or professional review
  • External systems can still use old caches, third-party pages, or other sources
  • The hypothetical company example does not describe a SolveReal Systems customer or project

Practical Recommendations

The article suggests selecting ten to twenty public facts that materially affect buying decisions, assigning owners and evidence pages, auditing all language versions and structured data, repairing false commitments before stylistic variations, and treating fact changes as content releases with synchronized visible copy, structured data, and dates.

Verification Checklist

The page includes a seven-point verification checklist covering fact ownership, visible copy accuracy, cross-page consistency, language version alignment, date accuracy, historical page handling, and release records.

Next Steps Offered

The page promotes "Open GEO Console" as a tool that examines public pages against buyer questions, but clarifies it cannot decide which business claim is true, approve changes, or publish content. It directs readers to review the current service description, browse public projects, or use the contact page with a public URL and buyer questions.

Source Quality

The article cites official documentation from Google Search Central, IndexNow, OpenAI, and W3C. The page is directly readable with a source length of 12,677 characters. The content is structured with clear headings, tables, and a practical checklist format.

Overall Assessment

This page provides a structured, actionable framework for content governance in GEO contexts, with clear boundaries on what it does and does not address. It is written for organizations managing bilingual or multi-page websites with conflicting public claims. The recommendations are specific and verifiable, and the limitations are stated transparently.

页面分析报告 | 2026年9月30日

页面概述

本文由“实解智能”发布于2026年9月16日，标题为《GEO 里官网、新闻和公众号各占多少？先分清被引用与被采纳》。文章旨在澄清生成式引擎优化（GEO）中“来源权重”这一概念的常见误解，并基于2026年的两项预印本研究，说明官网、新闻媒体和公众号在不同AI产品中的可见引用占比及其局限性。

核心论点

文章的核心主张是：不存在适用于所有AI产品的通用来源权重比例表。作者区分了三个容易混淆的概念：

  1. 进入候选结果的机会（某类页面被检索系统选中的概率）
  2. 被显示为引用的频率（链接出现在最终回答中的次数）
  3. 事实被采纳的程度（页面内容是否真正支撑了回答中的具体判断）

文章强调，这三者的统计分母不同，不能混为一谈。

关键数据与研究发现

跨平台引用占比（2026年预印本研究）

文章引用了一项分析602个受控问题、21,143条有效搜索层引用的跨平台研究，给出了以下可见引用中的来源类型占比：

平台官方类新闻类垂直站点类
ChatGPT34.22%31.17%22.13%
Google AI Overview46.35%18.99%22%
Perplexity44.07%16.07%18.99%

重要限制条件（原文明确说明）：

  • 这些数字统计的是特定问题下已经显示出来的引用，并非产品设定的内部权重
  • 研究未取得整个网络的候选池
  • 来源以美国和英文网页为主
  • 分类存在未知与噪声
  • “官方类”涵盖多种机构页面，不能直接等同于企业官网
  • 被引用的页面未必支撑回答中的关键判断
中文场景研究

另一项2026年中文生成式搜索预印本研究，对豆包、DeepSeek、腾讯元宝和通义千问的网页及App入口，围绕614个问题各采样三次，发现：

  • 同一产品的网页端与App端，引用的来源集合存在系统性差别
  • 研究集中在几个消费领域，仅观察已出现在引用列表中的网页
  • 不能据此为所有行业的公众号或官网定价

方法论与证据评估

研究局限（原文承认）
  1. 两项研究均为预印本，未经同行评审
  2. 研究使用从答案和页面特征构造的代理分数，无法读取模型内部注意力分配
  3. 论文未证明把某种格式加进网页就能提高采纳率
  4. 相关性与代理分数不能直接证明因果关系
  5. 特定问题和时间窗口的样本，不能外推至所有场景
引用评估研究

文章引用ALCE引用评估研究指出：在其ELI5测试集上，即使表现最好的系统，也有约一半的回答未获得完整的引用支持。但作者明确说明，该结果属于当时的研究数据集，不能换算成今天某款产品的错误率。

实践建议

来源的证明任务区分

文章建议根据问题类型选择合适来源：

  • “这家公司现在提供什么、边界在哪里” → 官网服务说明是一手来源
  • “它是否得到独立报道” → 应回到新闻原文，官网自述不能代替第三方报道
  • “用户遇到了什么具体问题” → 有作者和时间的公开经验文章可能有价值，但需核实是否亲历、是否引用原始记录
实施步骤
  1. 从真实买家问题开始，保留原问法
  2. 记录各来源能证明的事实（原始网址、作者、发布日期、是否转载、矛盾之处）
  3. 在目标AI产品的具体入口复问，保存时间、回答全文和引用页面
  4. 逐句标出哪些主张由官网支持、哪些来自第三方、哪些无证据
  5. 隔一段时间重复同一组问题，观察答案是否采纳官网更新
验收清单
  • 官网被引用但未提供所需能力/限制/证据 → 补齐页面事实
  • 旧报道压过当前说明 → 核对发布日期和冲突原文
  • 多篇文章同稿转载 → 合并为一条证据链
  • 区分“出现链接”“事实被正确采用”“引用支持了具体句子”三个结果

商业推广内容

文章末尾推广了“Open GEO Console”工具，声称可对官网和目标买家问题做GEO检测，检查公开页面、问题覆盖与引用证据，输出问题清单、修改建议和整改优先级。明确声明：该工具不读取AI平台的内部权重，也不保证下一次回答一定引用官网。

总体评估

优点
  • 清晰区分了“被引用”与“被采纳”两个关键概念
  • 提供了具体的研究数据，同时明确标注了所有限制条件
  • 对研究方法的局限性有诚实披露
  • 实践建议具体可操作
局限
  • 所有数据来自2026年预印本研究，未经同行评审
  • 样本以美国英文网页为主，中文场景研究仅覆盖消费领域
  • 文章本身由GEO服务商发布，存在推广自家工具的潜在利益冲突
  • 未提供任何可复现的原始数据或完整研究方法细节
适用边界（原文明确）
  • 论文未公开各AI产品的内部选源规则
  • 公众号、封闭社区或登录后内容是否进入某次回答，需按具体产品与网址核对
  • 不能从一次截图推导平台长期的渠道占比

Hermes Notebook — 企业数据整理与 AI 应用引擎（页面分析）

页面概述

该页面介绍 Hermes Notebook，一个面向企业的数据整理与 AI 应用引擎。产品定位为“可部署系统”，核心价值是让企业资料可被 AI 检索和引用。页面以中文撰写，采用“原来的流程 / 系统接管什么 / 人工保留什么 / 最终交付什么”的结构化对比方式说明产品价值，并明确列出使用范围和限制。

核心功能

根据页面描述，Hermes Notebook 当前具备以下能力：

  • 多格式导入：支持文件、文件夹和 URL 导入，涵盖 PDF、Word、Excel、PPT、图片及业务网页
  • 文档结构恢复：按文件格式提取正文、标题、表格和图片文字，并保留每段内容与原始资料位置的关系
  • 可追溯检索：建立可检索的知识节点、来源记录和完整度状态
  • 带引用问答：基于证据生成带引用答案
  • 受权限限制的 API：受 Token 和知识库范围限制的检索与问答接口，供上层应用调用
  • 部署方式：支持 Docker Compose 本地部署

解决的问题

页面描述的目标场景是：企业有价值的数据散落在文件夹、Office 文档、PDF、图片和业务网页中，员工查找困难，且不同 AI 应用需要重复整理同一批资料。Hermes 的定位是让客服机器人、内部知识问答和业务助手复用同一份整理好的企业数据，避免为每个 AI 应用重新清洗和导入。

人工保留的职责

页面明确说明系统并非全自动，以下环节仍需人工介入：

  • 管理员决定哪些文件夹和资料进入哪个知识库，检查导入失败、重复文件和资料完整度
  • 业务负责人确认检索结果和引用是否足以支持回答，决定哪些知识库可提供给具体应用
  • 客服话术、对外回复和业务动作继续由对应应用和人员审核

使用范围与限制

页面明确列出以下边界：

  • Hermes 仅提供企业知识整理和检索内核；客服机器人、企业微信或飞书接入、界面和业务动作需由上层应用完成
  • 原始资料缺失、过期或扫描质量过低时，系统无法凭空补齐事实，需企业先修正资料来源
  • 企业群聊和部门身份不能只依赖模型判断，必须由接入层明确映射到允许访问的知识库

交付物

最终交付包括：

  1. 按业务主题整理的企业知识库（含来源、原文位置、完整度和处理记录）
  2. 供应用直接调用的证据检索结果，以及带来源引用的知识问答
  3. 面向客服机器人、内部知识问答和其他业务助手的检索与问答 API

页面其他信息

页面底部注明“你的业务不需要复制这个项目；我们会从实际流程重新诊断”，并附有“讨论你的流程”的行动号召，表明该项目可能由特定服务商提供定制化实施。页面顶部有“返回项目库”导航链接，说明该页面属于某个项目集合的一部分。

分析说明：本页面为产品介绍页，未提供定价、技术架构细节、性能指标或客户案例。页面中“项目目前支持”的表述暗示功能仍在迭代中。所有功能描述均以页面原文为准，未做超出页面信息的推断。

GEO vs SEO: A Practical Map of the Differences — Page Analysis

Executive Summary

This page, published by SolveReal Systems on September 21, 2026, provides an operational comparison between Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) and traditional Search Engine Optimization (SEO). It argues that while both share technical foundations, they differ in what they optimize, how success is measured, and who can approve completed work. The page is structured as a practical guide with comparison tables, a hypothetical case study, measurement frameworks, prioritization guidance, and a four-week implementation sequence.

Key Claims and Positions

The page makes several specific claims about the current state of GEO and SEO:

On Google's generative features: The article states that Google's AI Overviews and AI Mode are built on core ranking and quality systems, with no separate technical requirements for sites. It references Google's guide to generative AI search and the Generative AI performance report introduced in 2026.

On Bing: It notes that Bing Webmaster Tools introduced an AI Performance public preview reporting citation counts, cited pages, and grounding queries. The page includes Microsoft's warning that these aggregates do not represent rankings or authority.

On OpenAI: The page states that allowing OAI-SearchBot supports inclusion in ChatGPT search, and that referral links include utm_source=chatgpt.com.

On the GEO research paper: It describes the original GEO paper as "a research starting point, not an industry-wide ranking standard" and cautions against converting benchmark results into citation promises for commercial websites.

Content Structure and Quality

The page is well-organized with clear sections: a direct answer, operational differences table, unit-of-optimization discussion, a hypothetical enterprise software example, measurement layers, prioritization matrix, team responsibility division, common mistakes, a four-week sequence, boundaries, and an acceptance checklist.

The writing is clear and practical. The hypothetical example of an invoice-recognition software company effectively illustrates how SEO and GEO acceptance records differ for the same page. The four-layer measurement model (appearance, representation, support, downstream action) is a useful framework.

Notable Limitations and Uncertainties

The page acknowledges several important boundaries:

  • Platform differences: "Google's rules cannot stand in for Bing, OpenAI, or another provider's current documentation."
  • No guarantees: "SEO and GEO changes do not guarantee indexing, rankings, citations, traffic, or inquiries."
  • Report limitations: "Platform reports prove only the fields they cover."
  • Sample size caution: "When the sample is small, preserve the observations without presenting one movement as a stable trend."

The sources were checked on September 21, 2026, and the page notes that platform guidance can change.

Potential Concerns

Commercial context: The page is published by SolveReal Systems, which offers GEO-related services. It includes calls to action for an "Open GEO Console," enterprise AI system services, and a contact page. The content, while informative, serves as lead generation for these services.

Source verification: The page references several official sources (Google SEO Starter Guide, Google's AI features documentation, Bing AI Performance, OpenAI's publisher FAQ, the GEO paper) but does not provide direct URLs. Readers cannot verify these references without additional searching.

Date sensitivity: The page is dated September 21, 2026, and references platform features described as current for 2026. Given the rapid evolution of AI search products, some claims may become outdated quickly.

Hypothetical example: The enterprise software case is explicitly stated as not describing a SolveReal Systems customer, which is appropriate transparency.

Overall Assessment

This is a substantive, well-structured guide that offers practical distinctions between SEO and GEO work. It is notably measured in its claims, explicitly warning against over-interpreting citation counts and undefined "GEO scores." The emphasis on separate acceptance records and the need for business-owner approval of public claims is a responsible approach.

The page is best understood as both an educational resource and a marketing piece for SolveReal Systems' services. The educational content appears technically sound and appropriately cautious, but readers should verify platform-specific claims against current official documentation before acting on them.

Rating: 4 out of 5 — Useful practical guidance with appropriate caveats, though the commercial context and lack of direct source links warrant reader caution.

28https://me.itheheda.online/articles/llm-training-text-chunks-geo-retrievalhttps://me.itheheda.online/articles/llm-training-text-chunks-geo-retrieval

This page explains the difference between how large language models process text during training and how AI search engines retrieve web pages when answering questions. It clarifies that editing a webpage does not guarantee the model will "know" the new content tomorrow, because model training and retrieval are separate processes.

The article distinguishes three units that are often confused: tokens (the input unit from a tokenizer), training sequences (fixed-length segments used during model training), and retrieval passages (content selected by a search or retrieval system). It notes there is no fixed word-count conversion between them, and warns against treating unverified advice like "write in 300-character chunks" as an algorithmic rule.

Key points about retrieval and indexing: Google's public documentation states that pages must be indexed and eligible for normal search snippets to appear as supporting links in AI Overviews or AI Mode, but meeting those conditions does not guarantee display. After a page is edited, re-crawling can take days to months, so testing immediately after a change cannot be attributed to the model "not learning" the content. The article also advises checking what the crawler actually receives, since some page content only appears after JavaScript executes.

The page includes a practical workflow: pick an important service page, check the raw response for body text and key limitations, verify crawl and index status, then test with a real buyer question against a target AI product. It recommends writing capabilities clearly with conditions and evidence nearby, using titles and links to help readers, and notes that Google states AI search has no special file or Schema requirements.

The verification checklist suggests recording the question, time, answer, and cited URLs separately for three observations: whether the page was crawled, whether the answer used the page, and whether the answer showed a citation. If an answer overstates service scope, check the original sentence on the service page; for specific projects, look for public evidence on the project page. Without citations, record facts only and avoid inferring internal training materials from a single answer.

The article concludes that site owners can make public materials accurate and accessible and verify actual answers, but which source a platform ultimately selects and how it cites remains that platform's decision. It links to related articles on GEO vs. SEO, judging GEO changes after AI citations, and how AI search uses web pages.

Page Analysis: Codex Feishu Bridge — Enterprise AI Collaboration System

Overview

This page presents Codex Feishu Bridge, a deployable enterprise system that connects OpenAI's Codex to a Feishu (Lark) workspace. The core value proposition is enabling team members to submit AI tasks, files, and follow-up requests from Feishu on desktop or mobile, while Codex executes on a company workstation that remains online.

Key Claims and Capabilities

The system is described as providing:

  • Task submission from Feishu — Members can submit questions, attachments, and long-running tasks from computer or phone.
  • Asynchronous execution — Work is handed to Codex on an online company workstation; members can leave their desks and continue tasks remotely.
  • Trackable task states — The system tracks acceptance, queueing, execution, clarification, and delivery states, returning results to the original Feishu topic.
  • Reusable Skills — Repeatedly proven workflows can be packaged into "Skills" for other team members to invoke, reducing dependence on a few experienced Codex operators.
  • Authorization controls — Group and member authorization is validated before requests are processed.

Technical Requirements and Limitations

The page states several important constraints:

  • Deployment: Windows 10/11 x64 release; the customer workstation must have Codex installed and signed in.
  • Dependency on uptime: Tasks cannot continue when the workstation is powered off or the bridge service is offline.
  • Feishu permissions: The system depends on the customer's own Feishu application permissions and signed-in Codex environment.
  • Not open access: Unauthorized groups or members cannot use the system.

Human Oversight and Boundaries

The page emphasizes that certain functions remain human-controlled:

  • Codex asks clarifying questions in the original topic and waits for unambiguous answers from authorized members.
  • Members must verify final responses and attachments for completeness and usability.
  • Deployment, real external sending, and paid generation are separately authorized actions and are not triggered automatically by ordinary chat.
  • New Skills require team confirmation of conditions, execution steps, and acceptance criteria before use.
  • The system does not learn from employee behavior without confirmation.

Delivered Outputs

According to the page, outputs include:

  • Direct answers in the original Feishu topic, or trackable asynchronous tasks with identifiers.
  • Text, images, Office files, videos, and other artifacts generated or revised by Codex.
  • Queryable records for accepted, running, waiting-for-input, completed, failed, or uncertain task states.
  • Reusable Skills derived from approved, effective workflows.

Context and Positioning

The page frames the problem as: employees repeatedly move requests, files, and results between Feishu and separate AI tools; complex work is often delegated to a few Codex users; and tasks become difficult to continue once people leave the company workstation. The system positions itself as an "enterprise AI work entry point" deployed on the customer's own workstation.

Notable Caveats

  • The page does not provide pricing, deployment timeframes, or technical architecture details.
  • No customer testimonials, case studies, or performance metrics are presented.
  • The claim that "your business does not need to copy this project; diagnosis starts from the actual workflow" suggests a consulting-oriented approach rather than a pure product sale.
  • The page does not specify which Feishu plan or API tier is required, nor does it detail security certifications or data handling policies beyond the stated authorization controls.

Overall Assessment

This is a capability and positioning page rather than a detailed technical specification. It clearly communicates the system's purpose, operational boundaries, and human oversight requirements. The main uncertainties for a potential buyer would be: actual performance in production, setup complexity, Feishu API limitations, and the extent of customization needed for specific workflows. The page's emphasis on human confirmation and separate authorization for external actions suggests a cautious, compliance-aware design, but independent verification of these claims would be advisable before procurement.

30https://me.itheheda.online/en/articles/how-to-measure-geo-ai-citationshttps://me.itheheda.online/en/articles/how-to-measure-geo-ai-citations

Page Analysis: "When AI Cites Your Site, Did the GEO Change Work?"

URL: https://me.itheheda.online/en/articles/how-to-measure-geo-ai-citations
Publisher: SolveReal Systems
Date: September 18, 2026
Content type: Educational article on measuring Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) outcomes

Overview

This article provides a framework for measuring whether changes made to a website under a GEO program actually produced meaningful business results. The author argues that a single AI citation is insufficient evidence of success and proposes four separate outcome measurements: answer accuracy, citation support, site visits, and qualified inquiries.

Key Claims and Recommendations

Core Thesis

The central argument is that "a cited page is one observation, not a verdict." The article explicitly warns against merging multiple outcomes into a single "AI visibility" number, arguing that each outcome has a different owner and verification method.

Four Measurement Categories

  1. Answer accuracy — Whether the AI's response correctly describes the offer, including necessary conditions and qualifications. The article notes that "a brand mention without those qualifications can be commercially worse than no mention."

  2. Citation support — Whether the cited URL actually supports the adjacent claim. The article distinguishes between presence, support, and currency as separate fields, citing the ALCE research (Gao et al.) which evaluates correctness separately from citation support.

  3. Site visits — Observable analytics events with referral context. The article cautions against converting visits into "AI-generated revenue" without evidence.

  4. Qualified inquiries — Business-defined leads meeting an accepted qualification rule (e.g., named organization, relevant problem, reachable contact, plausible budget). The article states that "a web analytics tool cannot infer it reliably."

Practical Methodology

The article recommends:

  • Using a fixed buyer question (with recorded wording, language, product, search mode, date, answer, and citations) for comparability
  • Maintaining a claim ledger marking each material statement as accurate, inaccurate, incomplete, or not answered
  • Preserving baseline records before changes and retesting without overwriting
  • Comparing defined periods before/after changes while accounting for context (campaigns, seasonality, site changes)
Platform-Specific Notes
  • Google: AI-feature traffic appears in Search Console's overall Web reporting; there is no separate AI-features report. Web performance is a "useful supporting signal" but cannot isolate AI Overview or AI Mode.
  • OpenAI: OAI-SearchBot must be allowed for ChatGPT Search consideration; GPTBot serves a separate training purpose. ChatGPT Search appends utm_source=chatgpt.com to referral URLs, which is "useful referral context, not proof" of commercial causation.
  • Bing: AI Performance reports aggregated citation activity and grounding-query phrases across Microsoft AI surfaces. These are aggregated signals, not original prompts, and the product does not report referral traffic or organic ranking.

Limitations and Boundaries Acknowledged

The article is explicit about what its method does not do:

  • Does not reveal internal ranking or source weights of AI platforms
  • Does not guarantee citation, traffic, or commercial demand
  • Does not make live systems deterministic
  • Does not provide clean causal attribution (buyers may use AI answers and later return via other channels)
  • Ten citations to syndicated copies of one press release are not ten independent confirmations

Product Promotion

The article concludes by promoting GEO Console, described as a tool that "audits official pages against buyer questions and organizes access, content, answer, and citation gaps into prioritized website work." It explicitly states that GEO Console does not provide live citation tracking or conversion tracking and cannot promise platform citations.

Source Citations Used

  1. Google: AI features and your website
  2. OpenAI: Publishers and Developers FAQ
  3. Bing: AI Performance
  4. Bing Webmaster Blog: AI Performance public preview
  5. Gao et al., "Enabling Large Language Models to Generate Text with Citations"

Assessment Notes

Strengths: The article provides a disciplined, evidence-based approach that resists oversimplified metrics. The separation of outcomes into distinct measurement categories is methodologically sound. The explicit acknowledgment of platform limitations (especially Google's lack of separate AI reporting) is honest and useful.

Caveats: The article is published by a vendor (SolveReal Systems) that sells GEO services, so the framework serves partly as thought leadership for its product. The hypothetical example question about "scanned quotations" is clearly labeled as illustrative. The method requires significant manual effort (claim ledgers, saved answers, source-by-source review) that may be impractical for large-scale operations.

Uncertainty: The article does not provide empirical evidence that its framework produces better business outcomes than simpler approaches. It also does not address how frequently measurements should be taken beyond "an agreed interval."

This analysis is based solely on the supplied page content. External sources referenced within the article were not independently verified.

GEO Report: Page Analysis — "网站已经做了 SEO，为什么还需要 GEO？"

URL analyzed: https://me.itheheda.online/articles/why-geo-after-seo
Observed: September 30, 2026
Source length: ~3,540 characters (Chinese)

1. Executive Summary

This page is a well-structured Chinese-language explainer article published by 实解智能 (Shijie Intelligence) on September 8, 2026. It argues that websites which have already completed traditional SEO should still pursue GEO (Generative Engine Optimization), positioning SEO as the necessary foundation and GEO as the layer that extends visibility into AI-generated answers. The article is practical, cautious in its claims, and clearly written for enterprise website owners who have done SEO but are not yet appearing as sources in AI answers.

Overall assessment: The page is strong on clarity, structure, and practical guidance. It avoids overpromising, cites official sources appropriately, and provides a concrete starting methodology. Its main weaknesses are the absence of original research data, limited internal linking, and a lack of author credentials or company background information.

Page Analysis: "From Search Question to Cited Answer: How AI Uses Web Sources"

Overview

This page, published by SolveReal Systems on September 16, 2026, is an educational article explaining how web-enabled AI products move from a buyer's question through retrieval, synthesis, and citation. It is written for an audience interested in Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) and AI search behavior.

Key Content Summary

The article walks through a hypothetical scenario: a procurement manager asking whether a software provider can process scanned quotations and who reviews the result. It then explains the pipeline:

  1. Query fan-out – One question may become multiple searches. The article cites OpenAI's ChatGPT Search rewriting capabilities and Google's query fan-out across subtopics.

  2. Page eligibility – Pages must be discovered, crawled, and indexed before they can appear. OpenAI requires publishers to allow OAI-SearchBot for inclusion in summaries; Google requires indexed pages eligible for normal snippets. The article stresses that eligibility does not guarantee placement.

  3. Passage selection and synthesis – The article introduces Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) as an architectural model, citing the original Lewis et al. paper. It warns that if only one of several relevant passages is selected, the answer may overstate capabilities.

  4. Citation verification – The article distinguishes between visible citations and complete source logs, referencing Gao et al.'s ALCE framework, which separates citation correctness from citation completeness.

  5. GEO role of official sites – The official company website is described as the "accountable reference" for identity, scope, and conditions. The article notes that repetition does not make a repost independent evidence.

Practical Guidance Provided

The page includes a verification checklist with six questions, covering:

  • Whether web search was enabled for a recorded answer
  • Whether the target page is eligible for the candidate set
  • Whether selected material contains capability and conditions together
  • Whether each citation supports its adjacent claim
  • Whether first-party facts and independent evidence are recorded separately
  • Whether a person reviewed claims affecting public or commercial decisions

It also offers practical steps: preserve the buyer question's wording, time, product mode, answer, and cited URLs; read passages against claims; and retest after reviewed changes.

Scope and Limitations Acknowledged

The article explicitly states it cannot reveal internal weights, predict citation rates, or describe exact queries or ranking scores. It notes that products differ in search, indexes, passage selection, and citations. It also cautions that fluent prose is not proof that a condition remains current.

Sources Cited

The article references six sources:

  • OpenAI: Searching the web with ChatGPT
  • OpenAI: Publishers and Developers FAQ
  • Google: AI features and your website
  • Google: How Google Search works
  • Lewis et al., Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
  • Gao et al., Enabling Large Language Models to Generate Text with Citations

Related Articles

Three related articles are listed, all dated September 2026:

  • "When AI Cites Your Site, Did the GEO Change Work?" (Sep 18)
  • "In GEO, How Much Do Websites, News, and Social Posts Count?" (Sep 16)
  • "GEO vs SEO: A Practical Map of the Differences" (Sep 21)

Assessment Notes

Strengths:

  • Clear, structured explanation of a complex pipeline
  • Explicit separation of distinct concepts (eligibility, selection, citation, claim)
  • Honest acknowledgment of uncertainty and undocumented internal mechanisms
  • Practical, actionable checklist for verification
  • Well-sourced with primary references

Limitations:

  • The article is educational rather than empirical; it does not present original research or data
  • It relies on public documentation from OpenAI and Google, which may change
  • The hypothetical scenario is illustrative, not a real observed case
  • No information about the author's credentials or the publication's editorial standards is provided on this page

Potential concerns:

  • The page promotes SolveReal Systems' Open GEO Console product, which may introduce commercial bias
  • The "Sources" section lists titles but does not include full URLs or access dates on this page
  • The article's date (September 16, 2026) is in the future relative to typical knowledge, so the cited OpenAI and Google documentation may have evolved

Recommendation for Use

This page is useful as a conceptual framework for understanding AI search and GEO verification. It is not a substitute for checking current official documentation from OpenAI or Google, nor does it provide empirical evidence about citation behavior. For material decisions, readers should follow the article's own advice: inspect original records, dates, and authorities directly.

How Language Models Read Web Pages: What It Means for GEO Optimization

Publisher: 实解智能 (Shijie Intelligence) | Date: September 4, 2026

This article explains, with accessible examples, how large language models process web page text—from tokenization and context understanding to semantic retrieval—and what these principles mean in practice for GEO (Generative Engine Optimization) content work.

Direct Answer

A company website may describe its products thoroughly, yet AI answers still fail to mention it. The cause could be that the page was never retrieved, or that the content retrieved was insufficient to support an answer. To decide what to fix, it helps to first understand how a language model processes text.

The article draws on Transformer and retrieval-augmented generation papers, as well as public documentation from Google and OpenAI. It discusses only what is relevant to website content, does not expand formulas, and does not treat model principles as search ranking rules.

GEO stands for Generative Engine Optimization. For a company website, the goal can be understood as making public information easier for AI search systems to discover and use accurately in relevant answers. Two connected processes are involved: how the model understands input, and how the search system decides which content to hand to the model. A website must address both.

What Happens When Text Enters a Model

When a model processes text, it typically first passes through a tokenizer, which converts text into small units called tokens and maps them to numeric IDs. A token may correspond to a word or only part of one; the exact segmentation depends on the tokenizer. It is not correct to assume a Chinese character or an English word always equals one token. Hugging Face tokenizer documentation

The model then converts these IDs into numerical representations and processes context through multiple layers. The Transformer's attention mechanism combines information from different positions according to computed weights, allowing one position's representation to incorporate content from other positions. This is a technical foundation for understanding word relationships. Transformer original paper

A teaching example illustrates this relationship:

The document assistant supports uploading PDFs, but scanned files require OCR first.

To understand this sentence accurately, the relationship between "scanned files" and "OCR first" must be preserved. If only "supports uploading PDFs" remains, the applicable condition is lost.

For website editors, the practical task is to place limitations next to the relevant feature descriptions. Product names should be explicit, and pronouns should make clear what they refer to. These are editorial suggestions for reducing ambiguity; they cannot be used to claim that a particular sentence structure will receive higher model attention or reliably increase citations.

Tokens are also not the same as web page paragraphs. The former is a model input unit; paragraphs are how authors organize content; and the retrieval snippets used by search systems are yet another level. There is no fixed one-to-one correspondence among them.

What an AI Search Engine Actually Receives May Be Only Part of a Page

Beyond input processing, one step further matters: what does the answering model actually receive?

Retrieval-augmented generation, usually abbreviated as RAG, combines information retrieved from external sources with a generative model, allowing answers to use material from current inputs. Early RAG papers studied this combination and used retrieved text passages to assist generation. RAG original paper

The following simplified flow is for understanding; it describes a common approach and does not mean all commercial platforms run the same architecture:

Web page → acquisition and processing → retrievable material User question + retrievable material → retrieve relevant content → hand to model → generate answer

Google publicly states that AI Overviews and AI Mode may expand a question into multiple related queries and then look for web pages that support an answer. Material for a single question may come from multiple pages. Google AI search feature documentation

This means writing should consider partial reading. If a feature description is extracted on its own, does the reader still know which product it refers to? Does a result only hold under specific test conditions? Is there nearby evidence to verify it?

A simple editorial check: copy a key paragraph into a blank document, ignore the preceding brand introduction, and read whether it can still be accurately restated. If you must search back and forth for what "it," "this solution," or "the above capability" refers to, add the necessary names and conditions back in.

There is no need to chop the entire article into many short blocks. Google's generative search guidance explicitly states there is no fixed ideal length and no requirement to fragment content for AI. Similarly, llms.txt and dedicated Schema are not required conditions for Google AI search. These conclusions apply to Google and cannot be generalized to every system. Google generative search optimization guide

Similar Meaning Matters More Than Repeating the Same Word

Retrieval systems can compare texts using semantic vectors. This sounds complex but can be understood as converting a passage into a set of numbers used to calculate similarity with other texts. Sentence-BERT demonstrates sentence-vector-based semantic similarity comparison. Sentence-BERT paper

This is a technical capability; it does not mean we know the retrieval implementation of every AI search platform. Commercial systems may combine other search and ranking methods.

For website writing, a more useful check follows from this: when users ask in their own words, does your page contain information that can answer the question?

The following two passages are fictional product copy written for illustration; they do not correspond to 实解智能 or any real client project.

This tool has powerful document processing capabilities, suitable for many business scenarios.

A more specific version could be written as:

The example document assistant is for procurement staff who need to organize supplier quotes. After users upload a PDF with a text layer, it can extract product names, quantities, and prices, and export them to a table. Scanned files require OCR first; exported results still need procurement staff to verify, and the tool will not send purchase orders on the user's behalf.

The second passage helps readers judge whether the tool suits quote processing, how to prepare scanned files, and which work remains human. It adds information usable for decisions. Whether the rewrite is more easily retrieved and cited by a particular platform requires actual observation; it cannot be inferred from semantic vector principles alone.

Longer Content Does Not Replace Clearer Evidence

Models have an upper limit on input length per processing run, usually called the context window. Allowing more text does not mean every piece of information will be used equally reliably.

The 2023 paper Lost in the Middle found, in the models and tasks tested at the time, that the position of relevant information in the input affected performance, with information in the middle of long contexts being particularly poorly utilized. It provides a specific research result; it cannot be used to assert that all models today behave identically, nor to conclude that "putting the brand at the beginning will get it recommended." Long-context research paper

For editorial work, the safer approach is to place conclusions and applicable conditions together. When presenting test results, state the sample and test time nearby, and provide sources that support the result. If a limitation would change a buyer's decision, do not leave it in a distant footnote.

Citations also need verification. A link's presence only shows a source was provided; the reader must still be able to find, in that source, content supporting the statement. Describing a model's general capability cannot prove a specific product achieves the same result.

This step can be done manually. Read the most important factual sentences one by one, open the nearby source, and judge how much the source actually supports. If the scope is overstated, pull it back; if evidence is missing, add it or delete the claim.

Scope and Limitations

This article is aimed at content editing and technical checks for public websites. The following steps are for identifying problems; they cannot guarantee indexing, citation, or business conversion.

Implementation Steps

First make the text obtainable, then observe how answers use it.

The editorial work above has a precondition: the target system can access the body text. Google's JavaScript documentation notes that some pages only show actual content after scripts execute, and not all crawlers can run JavaScript. Having key explanations readable in the initial HTML helps reduce this access dependency. Google JavaScript documentation

In practice, compare the page response with what appears in a browser. Beyond titles and navigation, check whether key limitations in the body text and tables are preserved. A browser displaying the full page alone does not prove a given target crawler obtained the same information.

Access settings should also be distinguished by purpose. OpenAI separates OAI-SearchBot, used for search, from GPTBot, which may be used for training data collection. Allowing search access does not require allowing training collection; and allowing access does not guarantee citation. OpenAI crawler documentation

Acceptance Checklist

Use a set of real buyer questions to observe the effect of changes. Before testing, fix the question list; record the platform, language, and whether web search is enabled; and save the test time, the original answer text, and the URLs actually cited. Check Chinese and English separately; do not substitute Chinese answers for English acceptance testing.

Record three outcomes separately: whether the website appears in sources, whether the answer describes it accurately, and whether users continue to visit the website. A first mention after changes counts as one observation; repeated checks under similar conditions are needed before discussing whether the change is stable.

References

Technical papers and official documentation are linked inline at the relevant sections. Materials were verified on September 4, 2026. Platform rules may change; follow the current instructions at the linked URLs.

Next Steps

If you are starting from an existing website, you can use Open GEO Console to organize issues related to access, public content, and citation evidence, then let the website owner determine the order of fixes. Starting with one key service page and filling in the facts it lacks to answer buyer questions will make results easier to see than changing the entire site at once.

You can also review the Open GEO project description, learn about enterprise AI system services, or use the contact page to describe the website and buyer questions you need checked.

Usage Scope and Limitations

Problem Statement

This suggests the page is not merely a product pitch but positions the project as a reference example, with the actual service being workflow diagnosis rather than replication of this specific system.

  • The human-in-the-loop emphasis is a meaningful differentiator, particularly given the stated limitation against automated bulk sending
  • The scope limitation to public business information is clearly stated
  • The final disclaimer is unusual and worth noting — it reframes the project as illustrative rather than prescriptive
  • No pricing, timeline, or technical requirements beyond Docker are mentioned
  • No customer testimonials, case studies, or performance metrics are provided

This page functions as a project overview rather than a detailed technical specification. For a paid GEO report, the key facts are the system's capabilities, its human-review requirement, its public-data-only scope, and the explicit statement that the project need not be copied — diagnosis starts from the actual workflow.

In GEO, How Much Do Websites, News, and Social Posts Count?

SolveReal Systems | September 16, 2026

This page addresses a common question in Generative Engine Optimization (GEO): how much "weight" different source types—company websites, news outlets, and social posts—carry in AI-generated answers. The article argues that there is no fixed media mix and that source influence depends on the specific claim, the question asked, and the AI product used.

Key Points

The Short Answer
  • Public research does not establish fixed percentages for how much AI answers weigh different source types.
  • A source can occupy at least three positions: retrieved as candidate material, used while forming an answer, or shown as a citation. These events overlap but are not interchangeable.
  • The original retrieval-augmented generation paper (Lewis et al.) distinguishes generating text while conditioning on retrieved documents versus relying only on training parameters—but this is a conceptual model, not a blueprint for every consumer AI product.
Three Layers That Are Easy to Confuse

The article uses a buyer's question as an example: "Which parts of an AI workflow can this provider handle, and who approves external sends?"

  • Company website: Normally the right source for claims about what a company currently offers and stands behind. A dated, named service page with a clear owner is more useful than a broad promise.
  • Independent report: Can corroborate that a product launch happened or describe an external event, but cannot replace the provider's current service terms. A four-year-old press story may be excellent evidence about history and poor evidence about today's service boundary.
  • Practitioner or creator posts: Can add operational texture but are weak evidence for formal commitments unless the author has direct authority and the statement is attributable. Some posts may be inaccessible to certain products or regions.

The article stresses that channel labels ("news," "social," "official site") describe where a page lives, not whether the claim is current, primary, attributable, independent, or entailed by the words on the page.

Retrieval, Use, and Citation Are Different Observations
  • Availability only tells you a page could be considered; a retrieved passage may never affect the wording.
  • A citation tells you which link was displayed, not the source's internal weight.
  • The strongest check: open the cited page and see whether it supports the particular sentence beside the link.
  • The ALCE benchmark separates correctness from completeness—a response can cite something accurately while leaving other important statements unsupported.
What Recent Studies Do and Do Not Show

The article cites three studies:

  1. The original GEO paper (Aggarwal et al.): Made answer visibility an empirical research problem but did not disclose platform-internal channel percentages.

  2. A 2026 preprint (Zhang et al.): Analyzed 602 controlled prompts and 21,143 valid search-layer citations. Displayed citation compositions were:

    • ChatGPT: Official 34.22%, news 31.17%, vertical 22.13%
    • Google AI Overview: Official 46.35%, news 18.99%, vertical 22.00%
    • Perplexity: Official 44.07%, news 16.07%, vertical 18.99%

    The article emphasizes these are sample compositions, not internal source weights. "Official" includes several kinds of institutional pages, not only company websites. The study's "absorption score" is a proxy, not a causal trace of model attention. The sample is largely US and English oriented.

  3. Another 2026 preprint (Zhen et al.): Asked 614 Chinese-language questions three times across web and app interfaces of Doubao, DeepSeek, Tencent Yuanbao, and Qwen. Source sets differed even between interfaces of the same product. The observed outputs cannot set a rule for every enterprise query or disclose a system's ranking function.

Conclusion from studies: Source mix varies with question, language, interface, and product. The research does not support putting a permanent "40% official site" label on GEO.

The Official Site's Role: Accountability
  • The company website can hold the organization accountable for a current statement, even though no AI system is obliged to prefer it.
  • A good official page can name the service, define what it will and will not do, identify human decision points, and link to governing evidence.
  • The site serves as the anchor for first-party facts, giving outside coverage something precise to confirm, dispute, or contextualize.
  • However, a vague page can be less helpful than a careful independent explanation, and an official site cannot establish independent praise, market adoption, or customer outcomes by assertion alone.
Repetition Is Not Corroboration

One press release can be republished by ten outlets; creators and public accounts may quote it further. A citation sampler could show many domains while the underlying evidence comes from one organization. For each important claim, trace back to origin:

  • Who first made it?
  • Who has authority to update or correct it?
  • Does the later page add independently reported facts, or only repeat earlier text?
  • Is the cited passage actually sufficient for the sentence it is attached to?
A Useful GEO Review Starts with One Answer

The article recommends a practical method:

  1. Choose one buyer question with a real decision behind it.
  2. Write down what a careful answer would need before asking an AI product.
  3. Ask the target AI system the exact question; preserve the date, answer, citations, and product interface.
  4. Read each cited passage; mark which claims were answered, supported, merely asserted, and which sources were repeated.
  5. Repeat the same questions after a website update to see whether the answer reflects the current statement.

The article notes OpenAI's search help warns that cited material can be incomplete, outdated, or incorrect.

Where Open GEO Fits

Open GEO Console is described as a tool that helps turn a GEO review into website decisions. It checks a site's technical foundation, public content, question coverage, and citation evidence, organizing findings into an issue list, page recommendations, and remediation priorities.

Limitations acknowledged: It does not measure hidden source percentages, prove that an uncited page was used, or promise that an AI product will cite the site.

Sources Cited

  • Lewis et al., Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
  • Aggarwal et al., GEO: Generative Engine Optimization
  • Zhang et al., From Citation Selection to Citation Absorption
  • Zhen et al., What Do Chinese-Language Generative Search Engines Cite and Surface?
  • Gao et al., Enabling Large Language Models to Generate Text with Citations
  • OpenAI, Searching the web with ChatGPT
  • Google, AI features and your website

Related Articles

  • "When AI Cites Your Site, Did the GEO Change Work?" (Sep 18, 2026)
  • "From Search Question to Cited Answer: How AI Uses Web Sources" (Sep 16, 2026)
  • "GEO vs SEO: A Practical Map of the Differences" (Sep 21, 2026)

Assessment: This is a well-structured, evidence-based article that directly addresses a common GEO misconception. It provides specific study data while carefully noting limitations. The practical methodology for conducting a GEO review is actionable. The article is transparent about what public research can and cannot establish, and it does not overstate the capabilities of the author's own tool (Open GEO Console). The main limitation is that the cited studies' data points are presented as sample compositions, and the article itself emphasizes they should not be generalized into universal rules.

Page Analysis: "Google 已收录，AI 搜索为什么仍认不出英文品牌名？双语官网检查与修复清单"

Page Overview

This is a Chinese-language article published by 实解智能 (SolveReal Systems) on September 1, 2026, addressing a specific GEO (Generative Engine Optimization) problem: a bilingual corporate website whose English brand name has been indexed by Google but is still not reliably recognized as a brand entity by AI-powered search engines. The article uses the company's own public case as a worked example.

Core Subject Matter

The page documents a real diagnostic situation:

  • The company: 实解智能, with English brand name SolveReal Systems, providing enterprise AI system design and delivery services.
  • The problem: Both the Chinese homepage (/) and English homepage (/en) show "URL is indexed on Google" in Search Console as of September 1, 2026. However, when searching the English brand name, AI-generated answers (Google AI Overview, ChatGPT Search, Perplexity) may interpret "SolveReal Systems" as ordinary words related to mathematical problem-solving rather than as a brand entity.
  • The stated cause: Indexing alone does not mean the search system has connected the English name, Chinese name, official domain, and enterprise services into one public entity. AI systems, lacking clear relational signals, default to literal word-level interpretation.

Key Technical Claims and Recommendations

The article makes several specific, verifiable claims about how the three AI search products operate:

Google
  • AI Overview and AI Mode operate within Google's existing search infrastructure.
  • Pages must first be indexed and qualify for ordinary search snippets before appearing in generative features.
  • No special AI markup is needed; mechanically repeating long-tail keyword variants does not increase relevance.
  • Google's official documentation is cited for: search workings, Organization structured data, site name guidelines, multilingual site guidelines, generative AI search explanations, and re-crawl request procedures.
ChatGPT Search (OpenAI)
  • OpenAI advises publishers not to block OAI-SearchBot if they want content to appear in ChatGPT Search summaries, citations, and links.
  • Website hosts or CDNs must allow OAI-SearchBot's public IP ranges.
  • OAI-SearchBot (search discovery) and GPTBot (potential training use) are distinct and should be controlled separately.
  • ChatGPT Search referral links carry utm_source=chatgpt.com, which can be isolated in analytics.
Perplexity
  • Official documentation distinguishes PerplexityBot (discovery and linking of public pages; manageable via robots.txt) from Perplexity-User (visits pages during user queries; generally not subject to robots.txt restrictions).
  • When using a WAF, Perplexity recommends verifying both User-Agent and official IP ranges; matching only a User-Agent string can admit disguised requests, and IP-only configurations become stale after official range updates.

Recommended Fixes (as presented)

  1. Write both names in the same visible paragraph on each homepage — e.g., Chinese page states "实解智能，英文品牌名 SolveReal Systems"; English page states "SolveReal Systems, also known as 实解智能 in Chinese." Both pages should use identical official domain, service scope, and contact paths.
  2. Unify public identity configuration — article authors, page creators, Organization structured data, and site name should not each use different name variants. Google's Organization structured data documentation lists name, alternateName, and url as relevant properties; Google also advises site name consistency with homepage visible usage. Structured data expresses existing facts; it cannot resolve contradictions in body text.
  3. Use separate stable URLs per language — Chinese at /, English at /en, with hreflang annotations and visible language signals. English article detail pages should only contain reviewed full English text; wrapping Chinese content in an English summary on an English URL reintroduces ambiguity.
  4. Request re-crawl via Search Console — only for live, checked URLs; Google's official waiting range is days to weeks; repeated submissions do not speed crawling. The article notes its own requests returned "Requested indexing" receipts, which prove acceptance but not that brand relationships have updated or AI answers have changed.

Evidence Status and Honest Limitations

The article is notably disciplined about what it does and does not claim:

  • No Before/After success screenshot is published. Re-crawl requests were accepted; same-condition AI answer re-testing had not been completed at publication time.
  • A status table separates: (a) initial check (indexed, brand query interpreted literally), (b) page modifications live, (c) re-crawl requests accepted, (d) follow-up re-test pending — with explicit statements of what each stage does not prove.
  • The article explicitly states the method cannot control model answers or guarantee knowledge panels, AI citations, recommendations, rankings, traffic, or inquiries.
  • Legal entity names, if different from brand names, should be separately identified and not stuffed into alternateName for keyword purposes.

Measurement Guidance

The article distinguishes five separate events that should not be conflated:

  1. Indexing — Search Console.
  2. Brand recognition — whether brand queries point to the official site.
  3. AI citation — whether answers reference the site.
  4. Visits — Search Console for Google; utm_source=chatgpt.com referrals for ChatGPT Search; separately saved Perplexity referrals.
  5. Inquiries — forms or CRM.

A citation without a visit may mean the answer satisfied the user; a visit without an inquiry does not retroactively invalidate the article's value. Teams must decide which step a given article is meant to serve, then examine the corresponding data.

Verification Checklist (as given)

  • Chinese and English homepages both directly accessible from official URLs.
  • Both homepages' visible text states the relationship between Chinese and English names.
  • Page titles, authors, site name, and Organization data use reviewed names.
  • Chinese and English pages have separate canonicals and mutual language annotations.
  • Search Console records indexing status and re-crawl receipts for both URLs.
  • Re-test preserves original query, product, date, language, region, answer, and cited URLs.
  • Crawler access for Google AI Overview, ChatGPT Search, and Perplexity checked separately.
  • Indexing, brand recognition, AI citation, visits, and inquiries are not merged into one metric.
  • Legal entity, brand, product, and project names are not substituted for one another as keywords.
  • The report promises no knowledge panel, recommendation, ranking, traffic, or inquiry outcomes.

Applicability Boundaries

The method is stated to suit: corporate websites with Chinese and English names, brand renames, abbreviation launches, and coexisting regional names. Public names must be confirmed by the enterprise. Visible text, structured data, and multilingual URLs can reduce ambiguity and improve the chance of consistent facts reaching search systems — but cannot control model responses.

Sources Referenced

The article cites official documentation from: Google (search workings, Organization structured data, site name, multilingual sites, generative AI search, re-crawl requests), OpenAI (publisher/developer guidance), and Perplexity (crawler documentation). Specific URLs are not listed inline; the page presents them as named references.

Promotional Elements

The page promotes Open GEO Console, described as a free check covering public identity, robots.txt, sitemap.xml, visible body text, and buyer-question coverage. It explicitly states the free check gives verifiable gaps and does not promise platform adoption of site content. Links are also provided to the company's Open GEO Console project description, enterprise AI services, and a contact/submission path.

Related Articles (internal links)

Three related Chinese-language articles are listed, all under the "AI 搜索与 GEO" category:

  1. "官网自己说法不一时，GEO 应该先改哪一页？" (September 21, 2026, 9 min) — about establishing traceable public fact records when homepages, service pages, old articles, and English versions state different conditions for the same capability.
  2. "GEO 和 SEO 到底有什么区别？一张可执行的工作地图" (September 21, 2026, 12 min) — a task/indicator/case comparison of SEO and GEO.
  3. "官网被 AI 引用以后，怎么判断 GEO 改动有没有用？" (September 18, 2026, 6 min) — about separating answer accuracy, citation support, visits, and inquiries when evaluating GEO changes.

Overall Assessment

This page functions as a transparent, methodical case study rather than a promotional success story. Its principal value lies in:

  • Clearly separating indexing from entity recognition and from AI answer behavior.
  • Providing product-specific crawler guidance (OAI-SearchBot vs. GPTBot; PerplexityBot vs. Perplexity-User) with appropriate WAF caveats.
  • Insisting on visible-text name relationships rather than relying on structured data alone.
  • Explicitly refusing to claim results before same-condition re-testing is complete.

The article's main limitation is that it presents a diagnosis and a remediation plan without completed outcome data — a limitation the page itself acknowledges and frames as methodologically necessary. For a reader evaluating whether to follow this approach, the page offers a concrete, auditable procedure with clearly stated boundaries on what can and cannot be guaranteed.

Analysis: "When Does an AI Model Read an Updated Web Page? Training, Retrieval, and GEO"

Publisher: SolveReal Systems
Date: September 16, 2026
URL: https://me.itheheda.online/en/articles/llm-training-text-chunks-geo-retrieval

Summary

This article explains the difference between how AI models encounter web content during training versus how AI search systems retrieve pages when answering questions. It clarifies that updating a page today does not guarantee an AI assistant will know about it tomorrow, and distinguishes between three separate concepts often conflated as "chunks": tokens, training sequences, and retrieved passages.

Key Points

Training vs. Retrieval Distinction
  • A model may learn patterns from training data; an answer system may also retrieve a page while answering a question. These are separate events.
  • Page updates are generally outside the site owner's control regarding training runs. GEO work is more concrete when following the public page through access, retrieval, and answer use.
Tokenization and Training
  • Tokenizers turn text into token identifiers; a token may be a word or part of one. Chinese characters do not reliably equal one token.
  • The GPT-3 paper describes autoregressive next-token prediction and notes short documents were packed into training sequences for efficiency. The paper describes one model and one setup; its sequence length is not a rule for every model today.
  • Even if a page appeared in training data, it would not become a live, individually editable record. Outsiders generally cannot verify page-by-page what a commercial model's training set contained.
Three Different "Chunks"
  • Token: input unit for the model
  • Training sequence: span of tokens processed under a particular training setup
  • Retrieved passage: material selected from an external source to help with a question
  • There is no universal word count converting one into another. The original RAG paper combines a pretrained model with retrieved external passages without retraining on the page first.
How a Page Reaches an Answer
  • Google says AI Overviews and AI Mode may issue several related searches and find supporting pages. Eligibility requires the page to be indexed and eligible for snippet display in ordinary Search—eligibility does not promise display.
  • After an edit, the relevant system must fetch the page again and update searchable material. Google says recrawling can take days to months.
  • Some pages need JavaScript execution before main text appears; other bots may not have the same rendering ability.
Boundaries
  • The article covers text models and public web pages. GPT-3 and RAG papers are documented technical examples; Google's guidance describes its own features. None reveals another platform's passage splitting or citation rules, or promises indexing, citations, or inquiries.
Practical Steps
  1. Pick one important service page; inspect its initial response for main explanation, audience, and important limits.
  2. Check crawl and index status.
  3. Ask a real buyer question in the AI product you care about.
  4. State one capability with its conditions and supporting evidence nearby; use headings and source links.
  5. Google says its AI Search features require no special AI file or dedicated schema markup.
Checking Results
  • Save the question, time, answer, and cited URLs. Record access, answer use, and visible citation separately.
  • If an answer overstates the service, check the service page's wording. For project-specific claims, look for public evidence on project pages. If no URL appears, record that observation without inferring what was in training data.

Sources Cited

  • GPT-3 paper
  • Hugging Face tokenizer documentation
  • Original retrieval-augmented generation paper
  • Google AI Search guidance
  • Google JavaScript Search guide
  • Google recrawling guidance
  • Google site-owner guidance

Related Articles (from same publisher)

  • "GEO vs SEO: A Practical Map of the Differences" (Sep 21, 2026)
  • "When AI Cites Your Site, Did the GEO Change Work?" (Sep 18, 2026)
  • "From Search Question to Cited Answer: How AI Uses Web Sources" (Sep 16, 2026)

Assessment Notes

Strengths: The article provides a clear, well-sourced explanation of the distinction between training and retrieval. It appropriately hedges claims, cites specific papers and Google documentation, and avoids overpromising. The practical steps are concrete and actionable.

Limitations: The article does not provide platform-specific passage-splitting or citation rules beyond Google. It explicitly acknowledges this limitation. The "short answer" section is somewhat indirect; a more direct statement of the core finding would improve scannability.

Uncertainty: The article appropriately notes that recrawling timelines vary (days to months), that eligibility does not guarantee display, and that commercial training data cannot be verified externally. These uncertainties are preserved accurately.

Overall: This is a technically sound, well-referenced guide suitable for website owners seeking to understand GEO mechanics. It avoids hype and clearly separates editorial judgment from citation-ranking claims.

GEO 页面分析报告：官网已被 Google 收录，为什么 AI 还是不推荐你？

分析对象：https://me.itheheda.online/articles/google-indexed-ai-does-not-recommend-website
页面标题：官网已经被 Google 收录，为什么 AI 还是不推荐你？
发布者：实解智能 | 2026年8月30日
页面类型：长文指南（约 3,900 字符，中文）
分析时间：2026年9月30日

一、页面定位与核心论点

本文是一篇面向企业负责人和网站运营者的 GEO（生成式引擎优化）科普与诊断指南。核心论点可概括为：

Search Console 显示“已编入索引”只说明 Google 已处理并保存页面，并不等于 AI 会在采购类问题中推荐该企业。 企业能否出现在 AI 的供应商回答中，取决于问题匹配、主体清晰度、服务边界完整度，以及关键说法能否被公开证据支撑。

文章明确区分了“收录”与“推荐”两个概念，并指出排查重点应从“页面有没有进 Google”转向“官网能否支持一项具体的推荐判断”。

二、内容结构与关键信息

1. 直接答案（开篇结论）
  • 收录 ≠ 推荐资格。Google 收录不要求 ChatGPT、Perplexity 或其他 AI 在回答采购问题时采用该页面。
  • 企业负责人向 AI 提问通常是带条件的（如“能把 AI 接进现有业务流程、保留人工审核并交付验收记录的服务商”），AI 需要辨认公司身份、服务匹配度，并找到公开材料支撑回答。
  • 仅凭官网一句“提供领先的 AI 解决方案”无法回答采购者的追问。
  • 收录仍是 Google 生成式搜索功能的技术前提之一，但推荐、引用和点击需分别观察，不能从索引状态直接推导。
2. AI 回答的是买家问题
  • 文章建议企业不要用“你知道某某公司吗”测试 AI 可见性——这类问题只检查品牌识别。
  • 真实买家更可能问：“哪家公司能帮制造企业整理知识库”“谁能把重复审批改成可审核的 AI 工作流”等供应商型问题。
  • 品牌查询可被公司介绍页满足；供应商查询要求官网同时说明服务对象、要解决的工作问题、交付过程和限制。
  • 建议选取三个真实买家问题（来自销售沟通、站内搜索、咨询表单或业务负责人确认的采购场景），为每个问题找到最合适的公开页面；找不到页面即说明缺口。
3. 被收录的页面也可能说不清公司是谁
  • 索引保存的是页面，企业身份需从多张页面的共同事实中辨认。
  • 首页、项目页、英文页使用不同品牌名或省略产品与公司关系，会造成读者困惑，机器也只能在冲突描述中做选择。
  • 正式域名、品牌名称、产品名称、服务范围和联系方式应保持一致；结构化数据不能替代正文缺失的事实。
  • 企业服务需写明适用边界：谁适合购买、客户需提供哪些数据和权限、哪一步由人审核、交付物如何验收、失败后如何恢复。
  • 内部审核过的名称和边界最好有权威来源，页面和结构化数据都从那里读取。
4. 推荐要经得起下一句追问
  • 当 AI 找到两家候选公司，买家会追问：哪家有明确流程、怎样验收、有无公开证据。
  • “专业”“领先”“一站式”等形容词无法提供核验动作；流程说明、输入与输出、验收条件、公开演示边界和原始来源更有用。
  • 引用 Google 官方指南：强调独特、可靠、面向人的内容，提醒不要追逐特殊文件、机械拆段和虚假外部提及。
  • 明确说明 llms.txt 不会帮助或损害网站在 Google 搜索中的表现。
  • 外部引用必须真实：独立评测、合作方公开文档或行业目录可帮助交叉核对；批量制造账号、软文和无关链接只会增加不可信痕迹。
  • 没有公开客户结果时，可展示验收方法和产品边界，不要补一个好看的增长数字。
5. 公开抓取仍然是门槛
  • OpenAI：发布者说明要求网站不要阻止 OAI-SearchBot，内容才有机会进入 ChatGPT 搜索摘要和引用。可量化信号：ChatGPT 搜索引荐链接带 utm_source=chatgpt.com，可在分析工具中单独统计。
  • Perplexity：官方文档区分两种访问——PerplexityBot 负责发现并链接公开网页，Perplexity-User 在用户提问时访问页面以帮助回答。使用 WAF 时需结合官方 IP 范围和 User-Agent 检查真实响应，不能只看普通浏览器里的 200 状态码。
  • 抓取权限只解决“进入候选材料”的机会；页面是否被引用、品牌是否被提及、用户是否点击、是否产生咨询，需各自独立取证。
  • 一次回答未出现品牌，应记录问题、时间、产品和引用来源，不能直接写成“AI 永远不会推荐我们”。
6. 适用边界（重要限制声明）
  • 本方法适用于公开的企业官网、服务页、产品页、文章和经审核的案例材料。
  • 登录后页面、客户私有资料、访问令牌和内部报告不应为 AI 可见性而公开。
  • 不同 AI 产品使用不同数据、检索和回答方法；同一产品回答可能随时间、地点、账号状态和问题写法变化。
  • 文章只说明网站可核验的条件，不推测模型内部权重。
  • 明确声明：Open GEO 诊断不能控制搜索平台，不保证收录、引用、推荐、排名、流量或咨询转化。
7. 实施步骤（五步）
  1. 固定一个采购问题：选一个对应收入或咨询的买家问题，写下使用者、业务场景和必要条件；不用公司名测试，不同时覆盖十个行业。
  2. 找到能回答它的页面：从首页进入服务页、产品页和证据页，检查公司身份、服务匹配与限制；缺答案时标出应修改页面和有权审核事实的人。
  3. 给关键说法配依据：把交付流程、输入输出、验收方法和失败边界放到读者可见位置；外部事实连接原始来源；无证据的结果数字暂时删除。
  4. 核对真实抓取响应：检查重要网址的 robots、状态码、canonical、初始 HTML 和 WAF 响应；Google、OAI-SearchBot 与 PerplexityBot 的准入分别核对。
  5. 保留同一组复查输入：记录问题原文、测试产品、日期、回答中的品牌和引用网址；整改后用同一组输入复查；收录、AI 提及、引荐访问和咨询分别记账。
8. 验收清单（九项）
  • 目标问题来自真实采购场景，查询中不依赖品牌名
  • 至少一张公开页面直接回答服务对象、工作问题和适用边界
  • 品牌、产品、正式域名与联系方式在中英文页面保持一致
  • 流程、交付物和验收方法能从正文中找到
  • 重要说法旁有公开事实、原始来源或明确的证据边界
  • 目标页面允许对应搜索机器人访问，并能通过真实响应复核
  • 测试记录保留问题、时间、AI 产品、回答和引用来源
  • 收录、推荐或引用、曝光、点击和咨询使用不同指标
  • 整改任务写清页面、负责人、完成证据和复查日期
  • 报告没有承诺 AI 推荐或业务结果
9. 参考来源（六项）
  • Google 搜索技术要求
  • Google 生成式 AI 搜索优化指南
  • Google 搜索排名系统说明
  • OpenAI 面向发布者与开发者的说明
  • Perplexity 爬虫官方说明
  • Open GEO Console 中文页面
10. 行动号召与相关文章
  • 引导读者带真实买家问题进入 Open GEO Console 免费检查（核对首页、robots.txt、sitemap.xml 和公开内容）。
  • 提供本站 Open GEO Console 项目说明、企业 AI 服务与公开项目链接。
  • 相关文章三篇（均为本站内容）：
    • 《为什么 AI 总在推荐竞争对手，却不推荐我的企业？》（2026/8/31，9 分钟）
    • 《为什么企业官网在 AI 时代越来越重要》（2026/9/2，12 分钟）
    • 《为什么 AI 搜索看不到你的官网？从可抓取性、买家问题到引用缺口做一次 GEO 诊断》（2026/8/29，8 分钟）

三、页面质量评估

优点
  1. 论点清晰：开篇即给出直接答案，避免读者在长文中迷失。
  2. 实操性强：提供五步实施流程和九项验收清单，可直接交给执行人员。
  3. 限制声明充分：明确说明不保证结果、不推测模型权重、不公开私有资料，体现专业克制。
  4. 引用权威来源：引用 Google、OpenAI、Perplexity 官方文档，增强可信度。
  5. 区分概念：清晰区分收录、推荐、引用、点击、咨询等不同指标，避免混淆。
局限与不确定性
  1. 时效性风险：文中引用的是 2026 年 8 月的官方指南状态，AI 产品和搜索引擎政策变化较快，部分细节（如 OAI-SearchBot 的 utm 参数、Perplexity 的 IP 范围）可能已更新，读者需以最新官方文档为准。
  2. 未提供具体数据：文章没有给出任何案例数据或量化证据（如某企业通过整改后获得推荐的实例），属于方法论指南而非实证报告。
  3. 品牌自荐性质：页面末尾引导至本站 Open GEO Console 产品，属于软性推广，读者需注意其商业立场。
  4. 未覆盖所有 AI 产品：仅涉及 Google、ChatGPT/OpenAI、Perplexity，未讨论 Claude、Gemini（作为独立产品）、百度文心、豆包等国内 AI 产品的抓取与引用机制。
  5. “公开证据”标准未量化：文章强调“公开证据托住”，但未说明多少证据算足够、何种来源算权威，留给执行者较大判断空间。

四、对目标读者的实用价值

适用对象：已拥有被 Google 收录的官网、但担心 AI 不推荐自己的企业负责人、SEO/GEO 从业者、内容运营人员。

可直接执行的动作：

  1. 停止用品牌名测试 AI，改用真实采购问题。
  2. 选取 3 个买家问题，逐一检查是否有公开页面能完整回答。
  3. 核对官网品牌名、域名、联系方式在中英文页面的一致性。
  4. 为关键说法补充可核验的流程、验收方法和原始来源。
  5. 检查 robots.txt 和 WAF 是否放行 OAI-SearchBot、PerplexityBot。
  6. 建立测试记录表，用同一组输入定期复查。

不适用场景：登录后内容、私有客户资料、内部报告不应为 AI 可见性而公开；本方法不适用于非公开页面的优化。

五、总结

本文是一篇结构完整、实操导向的 GEO 诊断指南，核心价值在于纠正“收录 = 推荐”的常见误解，并提供了一套可复用的排查框架。文章在技术细节（抓取机器人、utm 参数、WAF 检查）和方法论（买家问题、证据链、验收清单）之间取得了较好平衡，同时明确划定了能力边界，未做过度承诺。

主要不足在于缺乏实证案例支撑、未覆盖更多 AI 产品、以及带有本站产品推广意图。建议读者将其作为初始检查清单使用，并结合最新官方文档和自身业务场景做调整。

综合评分：8/10（方法论扎实，实操性强；扣分项为缺少案例数据、覆盖范围有限、存在品牌自荐）
