42https://me.itheheda.online/en/articles/why-geo-after-seohttps://me.itheheda.online/en/articles/why-geo-after-seo

Why GEO Still Matters When Your Website Already Has SEO — Page Analysis

Page Overview

This page, published by SolveReal Systems on September 8, 2026, argues that Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) remains necessary even for websites with established SEO foundations. The article positions SEO as a prerequisite for GEO rather than a substitute for it, and provides a framework for evaluating and improving a website's visibility in AI-generated answers.

Key Claims and Arguments

Core thesis: A website can have solid SEO and still be absent from AI-generated answers. The page distinguishes between traditional search visibility (ranked links) and visibility within composed AI responses, arguing these are separate outcomes requiring separate attention.

SEO as foundation: The article cites Google's guidance that established SEO practices remain relevant to AI Overviews and AI Mode. It notes that pages must be indexed and eligible for snippets before they can appear as supporting links in AI features. Technical SEO elements—crawl controls, stable HTML, internal links, clear titles, canonical URLs, and structured data—are described as prerequisites for GEO work.

GEO's additional scope: The page identifies three areas where GEO extends beyond SEO:

  1. Making brand and service entities explicit
  2. Placing conditions and support near important claims
  3. Observing what target platforms retrieve and whether answers use content accurately

Failure points: The article outlines where pages can drop out of the AI answer path:

  • Crawler access (citing OpenAI's separate documentation for OAI-SearchBot, GPTBot, and ChatGPT-User)
  • Content availability (browser-rendered text may be incomplete on some retrieval paths)
  • Passage clarity (ambiguous brand names, adjective-heavy copy, unsupported claims)
  • Answer outcomes (source presence, accurate description, and website visits are separate observations)

Practical Guidance Provided

The page offers a diagnostic framework including:

  • Five signs that a GEO review is due (indexed but rarely cited pages, brand confusion, inability to explain offerings, conflicting claims across sources, publishing without tracking questions or citations)
  • A method starting with ten real buyer questions from sales calls, proposals, and support enquiries
  • A record-keeping protocol (platform, language, test date, search mode, complete response, cited URLs)
  • A verification checklist covering page accessibility, standalone passage clarity, evidence proximity, language-specific answers, and separate measurement of indexing, citation, description accuracy, and visits

Limitations and Boundaries Acknowledged

The article is careful to state its limits:

  • It concerns public company websites only
  • Platforms do not share one index, crawler policy, or answer process
  • Google's rules cannot stand in for OpenAI's rules or other providers' rules
  • Completing a GEO review does not guarantee indexing, citations, rankings, traffic, or inquiries
  • The cited KDD 2024 GEO paper provides a research starting point but does not guarantee citations or commercial results on today's platforms

Sources Referenced

The page links to four sources, all checked on September 8, 2026:

  1. Google guidance for AI features
  2. Google guide to generative search
  3. OpenAI crawler documentation
  4. Original GEO paper (KDD 2024)

The page notes that platform guidance can change and recommends checking current settings against the linked official pages.

Related Content

Three related articles are listed:

  • "GEO vs SEO: A Practical Map of the Differences" (Sep 21, 2026, 13 min read)
  • "Why Company Websites Matter More in the AI Era" (Sep 2, 2026, 14 min read)
  • "Why AI Search Cannot See Your Website: A Practical GEO Visibility Audit" (Aug 29, 2026, 9 min read)

Call to Action

The page directs readers to the Open GEO Console to separate crawl, content, and citation evidence, and suggests starting with one priority service page and ten stable buyer questions.

Assessment Notes

The article is methodical and cautious in its claims, consistently separating what can be measured from what cannot be guaranteed. It avoids overpromising outcomes and emphasizes the distinction between access, content quality, and answer outcomes. The practical guidance is concrete and actionable, though the page does not present original research or proprietary data—it synthesizes platform documentation and prior published work into a diagnostic framework.

43https://me.itheheda.online/articles/ai-search-visibility-audit-geohttps://me.itheheda.online/articles/ai-search-visibility-audit-geo

GEO Diagnostic Report: "Why Can't AI Search See Your Website?"

URL analyzed: https://me.itheheda.online/articles/ai-search-visibility-audit-geo
Publisher: 实解智能 (Shijie Intelligence)
Publication date: August 29, 2026
Report type: Paid GEO visibility audit of the page above

1. Executive Summary

This page is a long-form Chinese-language guide to diagnosing why a website may be invisible to AI search engines. It presents a five-stage visibility model (publicly accessible → discovered → crawled → indexed → cited/answered), followed by technical checks, buyer-question content mapping, entity consistency, evidence requirements, remediation priorities, and a five-step implementation plan.

Overall assessment: The page is well-structured, technically accurate, and unusually honest about the limits of GEO (it explicitly states GEO offers no guarantees of indexing, citation, ranking, traffic, or conversions). It cites Google and OpenAI documentation and includes a verification checklist. However, it contains no original research, no case studies, no proprietary data, and no unique tools or frameworks beyond what is already publicly documented. The content is essentially a competent synthesis of existing Google Search Central guidance, OpenAI publisher documentation, and common SEO practice, reorganized under the "GEO" label.

Key finding: This page is likely to be cited for its clear procedural framework and its honest articulation of GEO limitations, but it is unlikely to be cited as a primary source for any factual claim, because it introduces no new facts. Its value to an AI answer engine lies in its checklist structure, which can be summarized or quoted directly.

2. Visibility Status by Stage

StageStatusEvidence
Publicly accessible✅ PassPage returned normal HTML with readable content at time of observation (2026-09-30). No login wall detected.
Discovered✅ Likely passPage is linked from the site's related-articles section and appears to be part of a content cluster on GEO topics. Sitemap presence not independently verified.
Crawled✅ Likely passContent is present in initial HTML (server-rendered, not JavaScript-dependent). No robots meta tag blocking was observed in the retained text.
Indexed⚠️ UnverifiedNo Search Console data available to this audit. The page's publication date (2026-08-29) is over a month before observation, suggesting indexing should have occurred, but this cannot be confirmed.
Cited/answered⚠️ UnverifiedNo evidence of actual AI citations of this page was found. The page itself acknowledges that being crawlable does not guarantee citation.

3. Content Analysis

3.1 What the page does well
  • Clear procedural structure. The five-state model (公开可访问 → 已被发现 → 已被抓取 → 已被索引 → 进入回答或结果) is a genuinely useful diagnostic ladder. It maps cleanly onto Google's own documentation while adding a practical "which door is closed?" framing.
  • Honest limitations. The page repeatedly states that GEO does not guarantee outcomes. It explicitly says: "GEO 诊断能指出公开页面在技术、内容、实体与证据上的缺口，不能替搜索平台作决定，也不能替产品建立市场需求。它不保证收录、引用、排名、流量或咨询转化。" This is rare and valuable in the GEO content space, which is otherwise dominated by overpromising vendors.
  • Actionable deliverables. The remediation priority table (整改优先级) assigns each issue type to a responsible role (开发与运维, 产品与内容, 品牌与业务负责人, 内容与证据所有者) and requires completion evidence. This is more specific than most GEO advice.
  • Correct technical details. The page correctly notes that robots.txt only controls crawl permission, sitemaps are hints not guarantees, and canonical tags are signals that Google may override. It also correctly warns that JavaScript rendering requires queueing and that CDN/WAF/rate-limit rules must be tested with the target crawler's actual response, not a browser.
  • Specific, verifiable references. It cites Google's crawl/index/serve documentation, Google's generative AI search guidance, Google's canonical documentation, Google's helpful content guidance, OpenAI's publisher documentation, and the Open GEO Console project. These are real, checkable sources.
3.2 What the page lacks
  • No original data. There are no measurements, no before/after examples, no screenshots of Search Console, no crawl logs, no citation tests. The page tells readers how to run diagnostics but shows no diagnostic results of its own.
  • No case study. The page never demonstrates its method on a real website. A reader cannot see what a completed GEO audit looks like in practice.
  • No proprietary framework. The five-state model is a reasonable reorganization of Google's documented pipeline, but it is not novel. The buyer-question list (解决什么具体工作问题, 谁适合使用, 使用前要准备哪些数据与权限, etc.) is standard product-page copywriting guidance.
  • No differentiation from existing sources. A reader who has read Google's Search Central documentation and OpenAI's publisher page would learn almost nothing new from this article. Its value is consolidation, not addition.
  • No evidence of the publisher's own GEO performance. The page is published by 实解智能, which sells GEO services, but it provides no evidence that its own site is cited by AI engines. This is a notable omission for a vendor selling citation-related services.
3.3 Buyer-question coverage

The page itself recommends that every product page answer specific buyer questions. Applying that test to this page:

QuestionAnswered?Where
What specific work problem does it solve?✅ YesDiagnosing why AI search doesn't cite a website
Who should use it, who shouldn't?⚠️ PartialThe 适用边界 section says it suits public corporate sites, product pages, service pages, articles, and public case studies; it excludes login-gated content. It does not say who should not use it beyond that.
What data and permissions are needed before use?⚠️ PartialIt mentions needing Search Console access and a set of important URLs, but does not detail what permissions are required.
What will the system deliver?✅ YesA five-step audit with a verification checklist and remediation tasks
Which step requires human review?✅ YesContent and factual claims require business-owner review; the page says "事实问题交由真正有权确认的人审核"
How are results verified, how is failure handled?✅ YesThe 验收清单 and 第五步 describe re-checking with the same inputs and preserving unchanged states
What are the boundaries of data, cost, deployment, and responsibility?⚠️ PartialBoundaries of the method are clear; cost and deployment specifics are not addressed (the page is an article, not a service page)

4. Entity Consistency and Structured Data

The page presents a single entity: 实解智能 (Shijie Intelligence), a Chinese AI/GEO services provider. The brand name, domain (me.itheheda.online), and related articles are internally consistent. The page references the Open GEO Console project and links to 企业 AI 服务 and 公开项目 pages, suggesting a coherent site structure.

Structured data: The retained text does not include JSON-LD markup, so this audit cannot verify whether structured data is present. The page's own advice — that structured data cannot create facts that the prose does not contain — is correctly followed: the prose is consistent with what a JSON-LD Organization or Article schema would reasonably describe.

Potential entity issue: The domain is me.itheheda.online, which is a subdomain of itheheda.online. The brand is 实解智能. The relationship between the subdomain, the main domain, and the brand is not explained on this page. If the main domain hosts different content or a different brand, this could create entity confusion for crawlers.

5. Citation Readiness Assessment

5.1 Likelihood of citation by AI search engines

Moderate to low. The page is well-written and technically sound, but AI answer engines typically cite sources that provide either (a) unique factual data, (b) authoritative definitions, or (c) quotable frameworks. This page offers (c) — the five-state model and the verification checklist are quotable — but it competes with Google's own documentation, which is the canonical source for crawl/index/serve concepts, and with OpenAI's publisher page, which is the canonical source for OAI-SearchBot behavior.

Specific quotable passages:

  • "官网能打开，不等于搜索引擎已经收录，更不等于 AI 会在买家提问时引用它。" (A website being accessible does not mean it is indexed, let alone cited by AI.)
  • "代码上线、搜索引擎收录、曝光、点击和咨询转化，是五张不同的成绩单。" (Code deployment, indexing, exposure, clicks, and conversions are five different report cards.)
  • "把已有概念换一套说法，读者仍然不知道接下来该做什么。" (Rephrasing existing concepts does not tell the reader what to do next.)

These are well-formed, self-contained statements that an AI could quote directly. However, they are opinions and procedural advice, not facts, so citation would likely be attributed to "a GEO guide" rather than to a specific authoritative source.

5.2 Gaps that reduce citation likelihood
  1. No original measurements. The page tells readers to check status codes, canonical tags, and Search Console, but shows none of its own. A citation-worthy page would include at least one real example.
  2. No named external sources beyond documentation. It cites Google and OpenAI documentation but no third-party research, no industry reports, no academic work. This limits its authority to "someone who read the docs carefully."
  3. No author identity. The page is attributed to 实解智能 as an organization, with no named author. Google's helpful content guidance emphasizes people-first content; unnamed organizational authorship is weaker for citation purposes.
  4. No publication history or track record. This appears to be a relatively new site (the related articles are dated August–September 2026). AI engines have no historical basis to trust this domain.
5.3 Comparison with competing sources
SourceAuthorityOriginalityQuotability
Google Search Central docsVery high (canonical)High (primary source)High for definitions
OpenAI publisher documentationVery high (canonical)High (primary source)High for OAI-SearchBot facts
This pageLow (new vendor blog)Low (synthesis)Medium (checklist structure)
Established SEO blogs (e.g., Moz, Search Engine Journal)Medium-highMediumMedium-high

For an AI answering "how do I make my website visible to AI search?", the most likely citations are Google's own documentation and OpenAI's publisher page. This page would be cited only if the AI needs a procedural checklist rather than a definition, and even then, established SEO blogs are more likely candidates.

6. Technical Audit Findings

robots.txt⚠️ UnverifiedNot directly observed; page content suggests the site is crawlable

Note: The retained text is the rendered article content, not the raw HTML. Technical elements such as meta tags, canonical links, and JSON-LD cannot be fully verified from this data. A complete technical audit would require fetching the raw HTML with a crawler user agent.

7. Content Quality Assessment Against Google's Helpful Content Guidance

The page explicitly references Google's guidance on people-first, reliable content. Applying that guidance to itself:

CriterionAssessment
Is the content original and not rehashed from other sources?⚠️ Partially. The framework is a reorganization of Google's documented pipeline; the buyer-question list is standard practice. The presentation is original, the substance is not.
Does it demonstrate first-hand expertise?⚠️ Partially. The page speaks with authority about diagnostics but shows no diagnostic results. It reads like expertise-by-reading rather than expertise-by-doing.
Does it have a clear purpose?✅ Yes. It is a how-to guide for GEO diagnosis.
Does it answer a specific question better than other sources?⚠️ Partially. It answers "how do I diagnose GEO issues?" clearly, but Google's own docs answer the underlying technical questions more authoritatively.
Would a reader trust this source?⚠️ Uncertain. The honesty about GEO limitations helps, but the lack of named authors and demonstrated results weakens trust.

8. Specific Recommendations

8.1 High priority
  1. Add a real worked example. Run the described audit on one actual website (ideally the publisher's own) and show the results: status codes, Search Console screenshots, before/after content changes, and any measurable outcome. This would transform the page from a guide into evidence.
  2. Name the author. Add a named author with credentials. Google's guidance explicitly favors people-first content; anonymous organizational authorship is weaker.
  3. Add original data points. Even simple measurements — e.g., "we tested 50 client sites and found X% had canonical mismatches" — would give AI engines a citable fact.
8.2 Medium priority
  1. Differentiate from Google's documentation. The page currently paraphrases Google's crawl/index/serve model. It should explicitly state what it adds beyond Google's docs, e.g., "Google explains the pipeline; this guide explains how to diagnose which stage is failing."
  2. Add a citation test. Run a fixed set of buyer questions through ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews, record whether this page is cited, and publish the results. This would be the single most relevant piece of evidence for a GEO-focused page.
  3. Clarify the domain/brand relationship. Explain how me.itheheda.online relates to itheheda.online and to 实解智能. Entity consistency is a topic the page itself emphasizes.
8.3 Low priority
  1. Add structured data. If not already present, add Article and Organization JSON-LD with the author's name, publisher, and publication date.
  2. Add an English version or summary. The page is Chinese-only. An English summary would expand its potential citation pool, since most AI training and retrieval systems operate primarily in English.
  3. Add a "last updated" date. The page is dated August 29, 2026. GEO and AI search behavior change rapidly; a visible update history would signal freshness.

9. Verification Checklist (as applied to this page)

Checklist itemStatus

sitemap, canonical, hreflang, and internal links use official URLs⚠️ Not fully verifiable from retained text

10. Conclusion

This page is a competent, honest, and well-structured GEO diagnostic guide, but it is not a citation-worthy primary source. It adds no original facts, data, or research to the public conversation about AI search visibility. Its value lies in its clear procedural framework and its refreshingly honest articulation of GEO's limitations — both of which make it a candidate for quotation in AI answers about how to approach GEO, rather than about what is true in GEO.

Citation probability estimate: Low to moderate. If an AI answer engine needs a quotable checklist for "how to diagnose why AI search doesn't cite my website," this page could be cited. If it needs authoritative facts about crawling, indexing, or OAI-SearchBot behavior, it will cite Google or OpenAI directly.

Bottom line for the publisher: The page is a good foundation, but it needs at least one of the following to become genuinely citation-worthy: (a) original measurement data, (b) a demonstrated case study, or (c) a named author with verifiable expertise. Without one of these, it will remain a well-written summary of other people's documentation.

This report was prepared as a paid GEO visibility audit of the single page specified above. It is based on the retained page text and does not include independent verification of server responses, Search Console data, or actual AI citation behavior. All assessments of citation likelihood are estimates, not guarantees.

GEO Report: Enterprise AI Automation Provider Selection – Delivery and Acceptance Checklist

URL analyzed: https://me.itheheda.online/en/articles/enterprise-ai-automation-provider-selection-acceptance-checklist
Publisher: SolveReal Systems
Publication date: September 4, 2026
Page type: Long-form advisory article / checklist
Observed: September 30, 2026

1. Executive summary

This page is a detailed, practical checklist for small and medium-sized businesses (SMBs) evaluating or purchasing AI automation for repetitive operational workflows. It is not a product page, a sales pitch, or a technical deep-dive; it is a structured decision-support document that walks readers through workflow assessment, provider selection (SaaS vs. RPA vs. custom systems), seven provider questions, acceptance criteria, and warning signs.

The article is well-organized, uses clear headings and tables, and maintains a consistently cautious, evidence-based tone. It repeatedly emphasizes that demonstrations, proposals, and unqualified accuracy claims do not constitute proof that a system works in day-to-day operations. The page includes internal links to related SolveReal Systems pages (enterprise services, related projects, and a business-question submission form) but no external citations beyond a short "Sources" list referencing NIST frameworks and Microsoft Learn documentation.

2. Content analysis

2.1 Core message

The central thesis: Before commissioning AI automation, a business must (a) determine whether the workflow is worth automating, (b) choose the right delivery path (SaaS, RPA, custom, or a combination), and (c) verify that a provider can demonstrate real-world functionality using actual samples, explicit human-review boundaries, and failure-recovery mechanisms.

2.2 Key sections and their substance
SectionKey content
Short answerSummarizes the entire checklist in two paragraphs; emphasizes that demos and proposals are insufficient evidence.
Scope and limitsExplicitly states the checklist is for SMBs, does not replace legal/compliance/security review, and cannot set fixed prices or timelines. Also notes that AI automation does not remove the need for human oversight of high-risk actions.
Start with the workflowLists six conditions that make a workflow suitable for automation assessment (frequency, repetitive nature, stable rules, unstructured inputs, frequent exceptions, poor traceability). Also states when automation is not suitable yet.
Choosing among SaaS, RPA, and customA comparison table with three columns: "Approach," "Usually fits when," "Main advantage," and "Confirm before purchasing." Notes that approaches can be combined.
What kind of provider to look forDistinguishes product vendors, RPA implementation providers, custom system delivery providers, and consulting teams. Emphasizes that the label "AI company" does not define responsibility.
Seven questions to ask a providerThe core of the article: workflow reconstruction, human/AI decision boundary, deliverable vs. demonstration, exception and recovery design, data and permissions handling, acceptance methodology, and ongoing support scope.
Standard deliverables and acceptance evidenceLists six items forming a "complete delivery chain" and notes that SolveReal Systems maintains "stable facts" on its enterprise services page.
Warning signsSix red flags, including "full automation" promises, model-only presentations, unverifiable metrics, avoidance of data questions, prototype-as-production, and blaming all problems on model capability.
Preparing for an initial assessmentSix items to prepare before a first discussion with a provider.
Acceptance checklistSeven concrete acceptance criteria.
SourcesFour references: NIST AI RMF 1.0, NIST SP 800-207 (Zero Trust), and two Microsoft Learn pages (desktop flows, Power Automate approvals).
Next stepActionable advice: pick one workflow, use approved real samples, assess current state before deciding on approach.
2.3 Tone and positioning

The tone is neutral, advisory, and deliberately non-promotional. The article does not claim SolveReal Systems is the best provider; it presents itself as a general guide. However, the page is published by SolveReal Systems and includes internal links to its own services, related projects, and a submission form — so it functions as a soft lead-generation tool while maintaining editorial credibility.

3. Source credibility and factual grounding

3.1 Internal sources
  • Enterprise services page — referenced as maintaining "stable facts" about SolveReal Systems; the article explicitly states this is not an automatic quotation or fixed service-level commitment.
  • Related projects and delivery evidence — linked as supporting material.
  • Business question submission form — described as a way to determine whether further assessment is appropriate, "not an automatic quote or a guaranteed meeting."
3.2 External sources

Four sources are listed:

  1. NIST Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework 1.0 — a legitimate, authoritative U.S. government framework for AI risk management.
  2. NIST SP 800-207 Zero Trust Architecture — a legitimate NIST special publication on zero-trust security.
  3. Microsoft Learn: Introduction to desktop flows — official Microsoft documentation for Power Automate desktop flows.
  4. Microsoft Learn: Get started with Power Automate approvals — official Microsoft documentation for approval workflows.

All four are credible and relevant to the article's themes (AI risk, security architecture, RPA, and human approval workflows). However, the article does not cite specific sections or quotes from these sources; they appear to be general references rather than direct evidence for specific claims.

3.3 Factual claims and their support

The article makes no quantitative claims (no accuracy percentages, no cost figures, no performance metrics). Its claims are qualitative and procedural:

  • "A demo, a proposal, or an unqualified accuracy claim does not establish that a system can operate in day-to-day business work." — This is a reasonable, defensible assertion consistent with standard procurement practice.
  • "Payments, external messages, public publication, customer commitments, and other high-risk actions still need a named owner, an authorization method, and a route for human takeover." — This aligns with NIST AI RMF principles regarding human oversight of consequential AI decisions.
  • "Ordinary technical measures should not be presented as a legal compliance conclusion or a security certification." — A cautious, accurate statement about the difference between technical controls and formal certifications.

No unsupported factual claims, misleading statistics, or fabricated data were found.

4. Potential biases and conflicts of interest

4.1 Publisher bias

The article is published by SolveReal Systems, a company that appears to offer enterprise AI workflow services (based on internal links). The article is not labeled as sponsored content or as a company position paper; it reads as neutral advice. However, the following biases are possible:

  • Solution-agnostic framing with soft self-promotion: The article recommends evaluating SaaS, RPA, and custom systems fairly, but the "Next step" section directs readers to SolveReal Systems' own services and submission form. This is a reasonable lead-generation strategy but should be noted.
  • Emphasis on custom systems: The article gives custom systems the most detailed treatment and notes they fit "workflows that cross several systems or include unstructured information, complex states, human collaboration, or special permissions." This could subtly steer readers toward custom development, which is typically more expensive and more likely to require a specialized provider like SolveReal Systems. However, the article does not explicitly recommend custom systems over other approaches.
  • No competitor comparison: The article does not name or compare any specific providers, so there is no direct competitive bias.
4.2 Missing perspectives
  • Cost considerations: The article explicitly says it "cannot set a fixed price or timeline," but it also provides almost no guidance on how to estimate or compare costs across approaches. A reader seeking budget guidance will not find it here.
  • Vendor lock-in: The article mentions "exit path" for SaaS products but does not discuss lock-in risks for custom systems or RPA in detail.
  • Regulatory specifics: The article mentions compliance review but does not address industry-specific regulations (e.g., HIPAA, GDPR, financial services rules) beyond a general caution.
  • Technical depth: The article is deliberately non-technical. It does not explain what "model output" means, how RPA differs from AI at a technical level, or what "recovery point" means in practice.

5. SEO and content quality assessment

5.1 Strengths
  • Clear structure: Headings, subheadings, tables, and bullet lists make the content highly scannable.
  • Actionable content: The seven questions, acceptance checklist, and preparation list are directly usable by a business reader.
  • Cautious, credible tone: The article avoids hype and repeatedly warns against over-reliance on demos and unverified claims.
  • Good internal linking: Links to related services, projects, and a submission form create a logical conversion path.
  • Reasonable length: Approximately 11,600 characters (source length) — substantial but not overwhelming.
5.2 Weaknesses
  • No author bio or credentials: The article is attributed to "SolveReal Systems" as an organization, not to a named individual. This reduces personal accountability and makes it harder to assess the author's expertise.
  • No publication date prominence: The date (September 4, 2026) appears in the byline but is not highlighted; readers may not notice it.
  • No social sharing or engagement elements: The page appears to be a static article with no comments, share buttons, or related-article recommendations beyond the internal links.
  • Limited external citations: Only four sources are listed, and none are cited inline. A reader cannot verify which claims come from which sources.
  • No visual aids: The page uses tables but no diagrams, charts, or images. A workflow diagram or decision tree would improve comprehension.
5.3 SEO observations
  • Title tag: "How to Choose an AI Automation Provider: Delivery and Acceptance Checklist" — descriptive and keyword-rich.
  • URL: Contains "enterprise-ai-automation-provider-selection-acceptance-checklist" — good keyword structure.
  • Headings: H1, H2, and H3 structure is logical and keyword-aligned.
  • Missing metadata: The provided context does not include meta description, Open Graph tags, or schema markup information, so these cannot be assessed.

6. Accuracy and reliability of specific claims

ClaimAssessment

7. Overall assessment and recommendations

7.1 Strengths summary
  • High practical value: The checklist is genuinely useful for SMBs evaluating AI automation providers.
  • Credible and cautious: The article avoids hype and provides balanced, evidence-based guidance.
  • Well-structured: Clear headings, tables, and lists make it easy to navigate and apply.

7.2 Weaknesses summary

  • Limited external sourcing: Only four sources, none cited inline; readers cannot verify specific claims.
  • No cost or timeline guidance: The article explicitly avoids this, which limits its usefulness for budget-conscious readers.

  • Use as a checklist, not a definitive guide: The article is a solid starting point but should be supplemented with industry-specific guidance, legal review, and cost analysis.

AI Automation PoC Acceptance Record: From Test Samples to Release Decision

实解智能 | August 26, 2026

This article explains how to create a traceable acceptance record for an AI automation proof of concept (PoC). The record should link test samples, expected versus actual results, human review, and failure recovery into a single chain, after which the designated responsible person decides whether to release, continue testing, narrow scope, or stop. A sample record with no client results is included.

Direct Answer

An AI automation PoC should conclude with results that can be verified item by item. For each sample, record the expected output, actual output, evidence location, and review comments, and attach any failure and recovery process to the same record. The business owner then judges which processes have been verified and which conditions remain unmet, and signs off on this round's decision.

实解智能's service methodology lists "mutually agreed real samples, expected and actual results, exceptions, and traceable outputs" as acceptance criteria. This article follows that requirement to provide a recording method. The tables and filling instructions are operational suggestions; the sample record contains no client data and does not represent that any project has passed acceptance.

Applicability Boundaries

This article is written for business owners and project leads who have already seen a demo or pilot result and are preparing for a release review. Before filling anything in, both parties need to agree on business scope, sample usage, reviewers, and release conditions. Sample counts and pass criteria should be determined by project risk and usage conditions; no universal score or fixed release threshold is provided here.

If you are still comparing vendors and delivery approaches, you can first read the article on choosing enterprise AI automation vendors and acceptance checklists. This article focuses on how to keep records after inspection and how those records support the next decision.

Implementation Steps

Write Expected Results Next to Samples Before Testing

First, establish a clear scope statement for this round of testing, specifying the business actions to verify, the runtime environment, system version, and actions explicitly excluded. For actions involving external sending, payments, or public release, list the people authorized to approve those actions and the approval entry point. If the demo environment did not perform real sending, only record results within the demo scope.

Samples must be locatable and approved for use. Record the sample number, source version, permitted processing location, and reviewer. Keep sensitive originals in the agreed environment; the acceptance form should only store locations accessible to authorized personnel. Do not put account keys, client originals, or public download links in the table just to make it look complete.

Expected results should be written before execution. For example, an outreach process may require drafts to enter human review first and not proceed without approval. That is the condition to verify. Whether reality matches must be filled in after execution and checking; do not copy the expectation into the "actual result" column.

Every Conclusion Must Trace Back to Its Input and Output

The following fields can go into a table, ticket, or an existing acceptance system in the project. If existing tools can store them, there is no need to maintain a duplicate document.

Record FieldWhat to Fill In
Sample ID and scenario typeWhich sample was used; whether it is a normal, exception, authorization, or recovery scenario
Execution contextRun ID, time, system version, and test environment
Expected resultOutput, stopping point, and human participation conditions agreed before testing
Actual resultObserved output and status this time; if not executed or unverifiable, state that honestly
Evidence locationControlled location of corresponding input, output, event records, and necessary screenshots
Human reviewWho checked which evidence, when, and what judgment and reasoning
Failure causeCause if identified; keep "cause pending" if not yet determined
Recovery resultWhere recovery started, who authorized it, what result was produced, and whether duplicate processing was checked
Open itemsMissing evidence, remaining impact, and handling conditions
Responsible personWho supplements evidence, fixes, or retests, and who ultimately decides to accept the result

The run ID is especially useful. The same sample may be executed multiple times; if only the sample number is written, later readers may combine the first run's input with the second run's screenshot. When retesting, keep the original record, append a new run ID, and state what changed.

Evidence also needs to be specific to the location of the judgment basis. If a knowledge-base Q&A only saves one answer screenshot, the reviewer cannot verify which document and version the citation came from. It is recommended to record the question, the knowledge-base scope used, the original answer, and citation locations, then have the business reviewer confirm whether the citations support the answer.

Hermes Notebook's public documentation distinguishes between access-layer identity and department mapping, knowledge-base access scope before retrieval, and the business owner's verification of citations. The acceptance record should also keep these observations separate; "the answer looks correct" cannot replace permission verification.

Present Normal, Exception, Authorization, and Recovery Separately

The normal path shows whether agreed inputs produce usable outputs. The exception path records where the task stops when fields are missing, materials are unreadable, or external systems are unavailable, what the user sees, and whether the next handler can take over.

The authorization scenario focuses on whether actions stop at the agreed confirmation point. The recovery scenario starts from a clear interruption and records the recovery operation and subsequent results. Presenting the four categories separately lets reviewers see uncovered risks. A large number of passing normal samples cannot cover one unauthorized external send.

Freight Lead Agent's public project documentation retains human review and send-plan confirmation before real sending, and states that batches have pause, resume, and event logs. When using such a process for a PoC, you can record "draft generated," "human confirmed," and "send result verified" separately. The process demo on the project page only helps understand the action sequence; it cannot serve as evidence that this PoC completed those actions.

A Sample Record That Has Not Yet Been Executed

The following only demonstrates the filling structure. The IDs are illustrative; all result fields remain pending execution or verification, with no fabricated pass records.

FieldSample Content
Sample IDExample AUTH-01; replace with an approved sample number in real use
Scenario typeHuman authorization
Expected resultDraft enters review; if the send plan is not confirmed, the process stops at the pending-review position
Execution context and actual resultPending execution; no run ID or actual output yet
Evidence locationTo be supplemented with this run's draft, review status, and related event records
Human reviewReviewer to be designated and evidence to be checked
Failure cause and recovery resultNot executed; cannot yet determine whether recovery is needed
Open itemsConfirm sample permission, test environment, and permitted actions
Responsible person and conclusionTo be designated by both parties; this item is not yet accepted

After actual execution, fill observed facts into the result fields. If no send was clicked, you can only prove behavior up to the confirmation point; if the subsequent status cannot be found, write "result pending verification." A single API success response also needs to be checked against the actual result in the target system to determine whether the business action completed.

Keep Failed Items in Original Form, Then Append Handling Results

When a problem is found, first write down where it first deviated from expectation, and link the input, output, and logs at that time. If the cause is not yet identified, designate an investigator and leave the conclusion blank. Do not write "ready to fix" as "recovered."

Retest records must state what changed, the retest sample, and new evidence, while keeping the old failure item. For recovery involving sending or write-back, also check whether a result was already produced before, to avoid treating an unknown state as a failure and executing again. Recovery operations must stay within agreed permissions.

When closing an issue, write the basis. If scope reduction is used, list the excluded inputs or actions and the manual process that takes over that work. Capabilities not included in the current scope remain unverified and cannot be marked as passed along with the main process.

Acceptance Checklist

Before the release review, check whether the record itself is sufficient for someone to make a decision.

  • Every conclusion can trace back to the same run's sample, actual output, and review comments.
  • Normal, exception, authorization, and recovery scenarios each have results, and unexecuted parts are clearly visible.
  • Failure records are not overwritten by retest results; open items have a responsible person and remaining impact.
  • The run entry point, manual takeover method, and handover scope are written down; the releaser knows which actions still require authorization.

Once the record is complete, the responsible person agreed by both parties makes this round's decision and states the reason, applicable version, and scope. Entering production requires meeting the release conditions agreed in the project; if evidence is insufficient, continue testing; if only part of the process applies, narrow the scope; if risk is unacceptable or the pilot goal no longer holds, stop.

A record deciding to enter production should also point to the actual run entry point, rollback method, and maintenance responsibility. Later additions of external actions, changes to data scope, or expansion of users should trigger re-checking of affected conditions; old conclusions cannot cover new scope.

Reference Sources

This article is compiled from 实解智能's publicly available service and project documentation. It does not cite client results or general success rates. Project demos and capability descriptions do not equal client production acceptance.

  • Service methodology and standard deliverables
  • Data, permissions, and human authorization boundaries
  • Freight Lead Agent public project documentation
  • Hermes Notebook public project documentation

Next Steps

When preparing for review, pick the one test result that is hardest to conclude and check whether its input, actual output, and review comments can be found. For whatever is missing, write the evidence-supplement responsibility into open items.

If you need to discuss a specific acceptance scope, you can refer to the public projects and use the contact page to describe the PoC goal, sample structure, failed items, and expected deliverables. First contact only needs a desensitized problem description; actual samples require prior confirmation of permission and handling method. Submitting for a suitability assessment does not mean automatic quotation, a guaranteed meeting, or a commitment that the pilot will enter production.

GEO Report: Page Analysis

Page Overview

URL analyzed: https://me.itheheda.online/en/articles/how-language-models-read-web-pages-geo

Publisher: SolveReal Systems
Publication date: September 4, 2026
Content type: Educational article on Generative Engine Optimization (GEO)
Source length: approximately 10,800 characters

Summary of Page Content

This article explains how language models process web content—covering tokenization, context windows, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and semantic embeddings—and translates those technical concepts into practical editorial guidance for website owners seeking visibility in AI-generated answers.

Key sections include:

  1. The short answer — Distinguishes between pages never being retrieved versus retrieved material lacking needed information.
  2. From text to tokens and context — Explains tokenization and Transformer attention mechanisms, with an illustrative example about document processing limitations.
  3. The model may receive only part of your page — Describes RAG workflows and Google's AI Overviews/AI Mode behavior, advising writers to make passages self-contained.
  4. Semantic similarity helps explain relevance — Discusses embedding-based retrieval and provides a fictional before/after product description example.
  5. More text cannot substitute for clearer evidence — References the "Lost in the Middle" research and advises keeping conclusions near their supporting conditions.
  6. Boundaries — Explicitly states the guide does not guarantee indexing, citations, or business outcomes.
  7. Practical steps — Covers JavaScript dependency, access controls (OAI-SearchBot vs. GPTBot), and a verification checklist.
  8. Sources — Links to research papers and official documentation, checked September 4, 2026.

Source Quality Assessment

Primary sources cited (linked inline):
SourceTypeRelevance
Hugging Face tokenization documentationOfficial documentationHigh
Original Transformer paper (Vaswani et al.)Peer-reviewed researchHigh
Original RAG paper (Lewis et al.)Peer-reviewed researchHigh
Google's explanation of AI search featuresOfficial documentationHigh
Google's generative search optimization guideOfficial documentationHigh
Sentence-BERT research (Reimers & Gurevych)Peer-reviewed researchHigh
"Lost in the Middle" study (Liu et al., 2023)Peer-reviewed researchHigh
Google's JavaScript documentationOfficial documentationHigh
OpenAI crawler documentationOfficial documentationHigh

All sources are appropriate, current as of the stated check date, and directly support the claims they accompany. The article consistently distinguishes between what research demonstrates and what remains platform-specific or undisclosed.

Factual Claims and Uncertainty Handling

Claims presented with appropriate hedging:
  • Token boundaries vary by tokenizer — Accurate; the article correctly notes that English words and Chinese characters do not map one-to-one to tokens.
  • Attention combines information using calculated weights — Accurate description of Transformer architecture.
  • RAG allows models to use retrieved information without prior training — Accurate representation of the RAG framework.
  • Google may expand questions into related searches — Consistent with Google's public statements about AI Overviews and AI Mode.
  • "Lost in the Middle" found position-dependent performance — The article correctly limits this finding to "the models and tasks it tested" and explicitly states it does not establish identical behavior in every current model.
  • Google rejects universal ideal length and mandatory chunking — Consistent with Google's published guidance.
  • Schema markup and llms.txt are not requirements for Google's generative search features — Accurate per Google's documentation.
Claims appropriately limited:
  • The article repeatedly notes that model architecture does not reveal ranking rules.
  • It states that semantic similarity alone cannot establish retrieval or citation outcomes.
  • It explicitly says the fictional product example "describes neither SolveReal Systems nor a real customer deployment."
  • The verification checklist distinguishes three separate observations: appearance among sources, accuracy of description, and user continuation to the website.
Potential concerns:
  • No claims appear overstated or unsupported. The article's hedging is consistent and disciplined.
  • The "Lost in the Middle" reference is properly scoped — the article does not generalize beyond the study's tested models and tasks.
  • Google-specific guidance is explicitly labeled as applying to Google only, with other systems requiring separate assessment.

Content Gaps and Limitations

What the page does not address:
  • No specific platform ranking criteria — The article does not claim to know how any particular AI system ranks or selects sources.
  • No quantitative evidence of GEO effectiveness — The article offers no data showing that its recommended edits improve visibility.
  • No comparison of different AI platforms — Coverage is limited to Google and OpenAI documentation; other systems (e.g., Anthropic, Perplexity) are not discussed.
  • No discussion of multimodal processing — The article focuses exclusively on text.
  • No treatment of non-HTML content — PDFs, images, and other formats are mentioned only as examples within product descriptions.
Stated limitations:
  • The guide "covers public website content and technical checks" and "does not guarantee indexing, citations, or business outcomes."
  • Sources were checked on September 4, 2026, with a note to consult current documentation as platform rules change.

Practical Utility for Website Owners

The article provides actionable, testable recommendations:

  1. Keep limitations near the capabilities they qualify — e.g., "scanned files need text recognition first" should appear alongside "accepts PDFs."
  2. Make passages self-contained — Copy an important passage into an empty document and check whether pronouns and references remain clear without surrounding context.
  3. Identify the sample and test date near reported results — Link to supporting evidence.
  4. Ensure essential content is in initial HTML — Reduce dependency on JavaScript execution for crawlers.
  5. Separate search access from training access — Use OAI-SearchBot vs. GPTBot distinctions appropriately.
  6. Run controlled verification tests — Fixed buyer questions, recorded platform/language/search mode/time, saved answers and cited URLs, tested in Chinese and English separately.

Overall Assessment

Quality rating: High

This is a well-structured, technically accurate, and appropriately hedged educational article. It successfully translates complex language-model concepts into practical editorial guidance without overclaiming what website owners can control or predict.

Strengths:

  • Clear separation between established research, platform documentation, and speculative implications
  • Consistent acknowledgment of uncertainty and platform-specific unknowns
  • Actionable recommendations grounded in cited sources
  • Explicit boundaries stated upfront and reinforced throughout

Weaknesses:

  • No original research or proprietary data
  • Limited to text-based processing; no coverage of multimodal or non-HTML content
  • Google and OpenAI documentation may change; the article's claims are time-bound

Suitability for citation in a paid GEO report: Yes. The page is a credible, well-sourced reference for explaining how language models process web content and what that implies for GEO. Its careful hedging makes it a reliable secondary source for claims about tokenization, RAG, semantic retrieval, and editorial best practices—provided the report also cites the primary research papers and official documentation the article links to.

Verification Notes

  • Observed at: September 30, 2026 (page states sources checked September 4, 2026)
  • Readability: Direct readable; content fully accessible without JavaScript execution
  • Language: English (article notes Chinese-language testing is recommended for verification)
  • Related articles: Three additional GEO-focused articles are linked, dated September 2–16, 2026

Recommendation

Use this page as a supporting reference in the paid GEO report for explaining the mechanics of language-model text processing and retrieval. Cite it alongside the primary sources it references (Transformer paper, RAG paper, Sentence-BERT, Lost in the Middle, Google and OpenAI documentation) rather than as a standalone authority. The page's own recommendations for verification testing can be incorporated into the report's methodology section.

Enterprise AI Automation Provider Selection: Solution Assessment, Deliverables, and Acceptance Checklist

Shijie Intelligence (实解智能) | August 23, 2026

Before introducing AI automation, enterprises should first determine whether SaaS, RPA, or a custom system is the appropriate path, then screen providers using real samples, human-machine boundaries, exception recovery, data permissions, and acceptance evidence.

Direct Answer

When selecting an AI automation solution, enterprises should not first ask "which company has the best model," but should instead confirm three things: whether the current process is worth automating, which delivery method—SaaS, RPA, or custom system—is more appropriate, and whether the provider can prove with real samples that the system is operable, auditable, and recoverable.

An acceptable project should at minimum clarify the current process, human-machine boundaries, operation entry points, exception recovery, data permissions, acceptance samples, and ongoing support. Demonstrations, proposal documents, or vague "accuracy rates" alone are insufficient to prove a system can enter real business operations.

Applicability Boundaries

This checklist is suitable for small and medium-sized enterprises preparing to purchase or transform repetitive business processes, for first-time solution assessment, provider communication, and project acceptance. It cannot replace the enterprise's own legal, compliance, security, or procurement review, nor can it provide fixed timelines and pricing without understanding the actual system, data, and responsible parties.

AI automation also does not mean unattended operation. For payments, external sending, public publishing, customer commitments, or other high-risk actions, enterprises still need to designate responsible persons, authorization methods, and manual takeover paths.

I. Assess the Process First, Not the Technology

The more of the following characteristics appear simultaneously, the more worthwhile the process is for automation diagnosis:

  • High-frequency repetition requiring continuous copying, organizing, classifying, or writing back information;
  • Relatively stable rules, but inputs scattered across spreadsheets, emails, chat, documents, or multiple business systems;
  • AI can assist with unstructured content, but key results still require responsible-person review;
  • Processes frequently experience missing items, timeouts, format changes, or external system failures, requiring recording and recovery;
  • Current results are difficult to track, and business owners cannot quickly know where things are stuck or who handled them.

If the process is low-frequency, each judgment heavily depends on ad-hoc experience, or foundational data and responsibility division are not yet established, sorting out the process first is usually more effective than directly developing a system. The diagnostic conclusion can also be "not suitable for automation at this time."

II. How to Choose Between SaaS, RPA, and Custom Systems

PathMore Suitable WhenMain AdvantagesMust Verify During Procurement
SaaSProcess is standard and the enterprise can accept the product's existing fields, permissions, and operation methodsFaster deployment; product capabilities and pricing relatively clearData location, export capabilities, permission granularity, data handling after cancellation, and whether key features require additional packages
RPAOperation interface is stable, rules are clear, and main work involves clicking, copying, downloading, and entryCan connect some repetitive operations without modifying existing systemsMaintenance approach after interface changes, failure recovery, credential management, concurrency limits, and manual takeover entry points
Custom systemProcess spans multiple systems, includes unstructured information, complex states, human-machine collaboration, or special permission requirementsCan design inputs, states, reviews, and recovery around the actual processDeliverables, source code or system ownership, deployment method, real-sample acceptance, exception paths, and ongoing maintenance scope

These three paths are not mutually exclusive. A real system can use mature SaaS as a foundation, connect business systems via APIs, and use RPA for the few segments that cannot be connected. The evaluation criterion is not "whether the technology is advanced," but whether the process can be completed stably at an acceptable cost.

III. What Type of Provider Should You Look For

Do not screen solely by the "AI company" label. Different types of providers bear different responsibilities:

  • Product vendors: Suitable when needs closely match an existing product. Focus on verifying product boundaries, data and permissions, integration capabilities, and exit mechanisms.
  • RPA implementation firms: Suitable for processes with clear rules that rely primarily on interface operations. Focus on verifying maintenance, credential security, and failure recovery.
  • Custom system delivery firms: Suitable for cross-system, unstructured information, and complex human-machine collaboration. Focus on verifying whether diagnosis, implementation, and operational acceptance are handled by the same delivery chain.
  • Consulting or solution teams: Can help clarify direction, but if the goal is operational deployment, it must be clear who is responsible for development, deployment, failure handling, and final acceptance.

Enterprises do not need to require one provider to handle all technologies, but they must know who is responsible for each segment, and who handles interface failures, data anomalies, or unreliable model outputs.

IV. Seven Things to Verify When Screening Providers

1. Can They Reproduce the Real Process?

The provider should be able to explain where inputs come from, who processes them, where results are written, which exceptions are most common, and how current responsible persons determine completion. Merely restating the requirement name does not equal understanding the process.

2. Is the Human-Machine Boundary Clear?

AI can organize, extract, suggest classifications, or generate drafts, but payments, external sending, public publishing, and other high-risk actions should retain manual authorization or a clear approval entry point. The provider should also explain how uncertain model outputs are transferred to humans.

3. Is the Deliverable a System or a Demonstration?

The operation entry point, deployment results, operation instructions, and responsibility attribution need to be agreed upon in advance. Screen recordings, slides, prototypes, and ideal-path demonstrations can support communication, but cannot replace an operable delivery.

4. Are Exceptions and Recovery Designed?

Verify what happens with missing inputs, external interface failures, invalid accounts, timeouts, duplicate submissions, and unqualified model results. The system should retain exception records, recovery points, and retry or manual takeover methods.

5. How Are Data and Permissions Handled?

Confirm which real samples are needed, where data is processed, which accounts and tokens are used, how long data is retained, and how backup or deletion works. Without relevant review or certification, general technical measures should not be equated with legal compliance conclusions or security certifications.

6. How Is Acceptance Conducted?

Acceptance should use real samples agreed upon in advance by both parties, covering normal inputs, boundary cases, and common exceptions. Record expected results, actual results, human review points, and recovery outcomes—not just a single successful demonstration or vendor-reported metrics.

7. What Does Ongoing Support Include?

Clarify how system ownership, daily operations and maintenance, defect fixes, business rule changes, third-party interface changes, and new requirements are each handled. Do not interpret "long-term support" as a commitment without scope and time limits.

V. Standard Deliverables and Acceptance Basis

Specific projects can adjust scope, but the following constitutes a complete delivery chain:

  • Current process and system boundaries;
  • Operable system and deployment results;
  • Operation instructions and manual review entry points;
  • Exception records and recovery paths;
  • Real acceptance samples and result records;
  • System handover, maintenance, and ongoing support scope.

Shijie Intelligence maintains this set of stable facts on its Enterprise Services page. Project contracts still need further confirmation based on the enterprise's systems, data, and acceptance scope; the webpage description itself is not an automatic quote or a fixed service-level commitment.

VI. Warning Signs to Watch For

  • Promising "full automation" without understanding the process;
  • Showing only model responses without system status, manual review, and failure recovery;
  • Using unverifiable client identities, accuracy rates, or improvement percentages in place of real acceptance;
  • Avoiding questions about data location, account permissions, logs, retention, and deletion;
  • Treating preliminary prototypes as formal delivery, or not stating who maintains the system after launch;
  • Attributing all problems to insufficient model strength without process, data, and responsibility boundary design.

These signals do not necessarily mean the solution is unusable, but they mean the enterprise needs to write the corresponding issues into the delivery scope and acceptance conditions, rather than relying on verbal understanding.

Implementation Steps

To make the first assessment more concrete, enterprises can prepare:

  • The current process's start point, end point, frequency, and responsible persons;
  • A set of desensitized or authorized input, output, and exception samples;
  • Current manual time consumption, and the locations most prone to errors or backlogs;
  • Decisions and high-risk actions that must retain manual confirmation;
  • Systems to be connected, available interfaces, and deployment constraints;
  • What observable results will be used to determine project completion.

You can first review verified project facts to understand how different processes divide system processing, manual review, and recovery boundaries. If you already have a specific process, you can also submit a business question; the initial submission is only used to determine whether further diagnosis is appropriate, and does not represent an automatic quote or a guaranteed meeting arrangement.

Acceptance Checklist

  • Real samples have covered normal inputs, missing information, duplicate submissions, and common exceptions;
  • System outputs can be traced back to original inputs, processing states, and manual modifications;
  • Key decisions and high-risk actions cannot bypass manual authorization;
  • External interface, account, or model failures have clear records, recovery points, and takeover methods;
  • The enterprise can access the system, export results, and complete daily operations as agreed;
  • Expected results, actual results, and failed items are all recorded; a single demonstration does not replace acceptance;
  • System ownership, permissions, data retention, maintenance, and change scope are clearly defined.

Reference Sources

  • Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework 1.0 — NIST
  • Zero Trust Architecture — NIST SP 800-207
  • Introduction to desktop flows — Microsoft Learn
  • Get started with Power Automate approvals — Microsoft Learn

Next Steps

First select one specific process, complete a current-state diagnosis with a small number of authorized real samples, and then decide between SaaS, RPA, a custom system, or a combination. You can learn about enterprise AI workflow services, review related projects and delivery evidence, or submit a business question with your process, exception samples, and manual review requirements.

GEO Guide Analysis: "AI 搜索时代，企业官网如何通过 GEO 提高被回答与引用的机会"

URL analyzed: https://me.itheheda.online/articles/ai-search-enterprise-website-geo-guide
Publisher: 实解智能 (Shijie Intelligence)
Publication date: August 21, 2026
Analysis date: September 30, 2026

Executive Summary

This page is a comprehensive Chinese-language guide to Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) for enterprise websites. It presents a five-part action framework covering technical readability, content structure, credibility building, brand entity consistency, and ongoing monitoring. The article is well-structured, cites several authoritative sources (Bain & Company, Google Search Central, OpenAI), and includes practical implementation steps and an acceptance checklist. It also functions as a marketing piece for the publisher's own product, "Open GEO Console."

Content Overview

Core Thesis

The article argues that enterprise website competition is shifting from search rankings to being understood, cited, and recommended within AI-generated answers. It positions GEO as complementary to SEO rather than a replacement — describing the relationship as a relay race where SEO is the foundation and GEO is the upper structure.

Key Sections

  1. The changing "last mile" of search — Cites Bain & Company consumer research suggesting approximately 80% of search users rely on AI summaries in at least 40% of their searches, and about 60% of traditional searches do not continue to other websites. The article notes these figures do not mean AI has replaced search, but that user information paths are shortening.

  2. GEO vs. SEO — Emphasizes that Google's official guidance on generative AI search still relies on core search indexing, ranking, and quality systems. A page that is not crawlable, indexable, or helpful will not benefit from "GEO tricks."

  3. How AI "reads" websites — Describes a two-stage process: retrieval and generation. Google's generative search mechanism is described as retrieval-augmented generation combined with core search systems and related query expansion.

  4. Five key actions for GEO optimization:

    • Technical foundation: robots.txt configuration, sitemap.xml completeness, content in initial HTML (not requiring JavaScript), HTTP status codes, CDN/WAF behavior toward automated access. References OpenAI's publisher guidance regarding OAI-SearchBot.
    • Content structure: One topic per paragraph, use of lists/tables/FAQ, answering questions early in the page, building topic clusters.
    • Credibility building: Both on-site (about pages, source citations, verifiable cases) and off-site (consistent mentions in industry media, independently verifiable content).
    • Brand entity consistency: Consistent company name, product descriptions, service regions, cases, and contact information across public channels. Suggests structured data (Organization, WebSite, Article, Product, Service).
    • Continuous monitoring: 10–20 high-value business questions asked regularly to major AI platforms, tracking mentions, accuracy, and citation sources.

  5. Applicability boundaries — Explicitly states what GEO can and cannot do. Notably: GEO cannot guarantee citation, cannot replace SEO, cannot solve product quality issues, and single model responses should not be treated as long-term results. The article warns that any service claiming "guaranteed AI citation rate improvement of XX%" should provide repeatable measurement methods and clear boundaries.

  6. Implementation steps — Four steps: technical audit, content inventory, prioritized optimization, and monitoring mechanism establishment.

  7. Acceptance checklist — Ten verification items covering HTTP status, robots.txt, sitemap, initial HTML content, CDN/WAF behavior, direct answers, traceable sources, brand consistency, fixed question set monitoring, and explicit GEO non-guarantee statements.

Source Citations

The article references four external sources:

  1. Bain & Company — "Goodbye Clicks, Hello AI: Zero-Click Search Redefines Marketing" (consumer research statistics)
  2. Google Search Central — "Optimizing your website for generative AI features on Google Search"
  3. OpenAI — "Publishers and Developers FAQ" (regarding OAI-SearchBot)
  4. Google Search Central — "Creating helpful, reliable, people-first content"

Additionally, it links to the publisher's own product (Open GEO Console) and related articles on the same domain.

Commercial Intent

The page serves dual purposes: educational content and lead generation. It promotes:

  • Open GEO Console — described as offering free deterministic GEO technical checks and paid deep reports including website comprehensive assessment, buyer question answering, source evidence, and action recommendations.
  • Enterprise AI services and public project cases — linked for potential clients.
  • A "submit requirements" (提交需求) call-to-action for businesses with specific website and business problems.

The promotional content is clearly separated from the educational content, appearing primarily in the "Next Steps" section and the closing paragraph.

Quality Assessment

Strengths
  • Clear structure: Well-organized with numbered sections, lists, and a logical flow from problem definition to actionable steps.
  • Balanced claims: The article explicitly avoids promising guaranteed results and warns against services that do. This enhances credibility.
  • Practical orientation: Includes specific implementation steps, an acceptance checklist, and concrete technical details (robots.txt, sitemap, initial HTML, CDN/WAF considerations).
  • Authoritative citations: References to Bain & Company, Google, and OpenAI lend external validation.
  • Appropriate uncertainty: Notes that different AI platforms implement retrieval differently and that single query results are time-sensitive.
Limitations
  • Statistical claims lack direct sourcing: The Bain & Company figures (80% of users relying on AI summaries in 40% of searches; 60% of traditional searches without click-through) are presented without direct links to the underlying study. Readers cannot verify these numbers from the page itself.
  • Dated statistics: The article is from August 2026, and the Bain research may be older. The fast-moving nature of AI search means statistics can become outdated quickly.
  • Self-promotional elements: The Open GEO Console promotion, while clearly labeled, means the article functions partly as a marketing funnel. Readers should distinguish between the educational content and the product pitch.
  • No independent verification: The page does not provide case studies or third-party validation of its own GEO methodology's effectiveness.
  • Single-publisher perspective: All related articles are from the same publisher (实解智能), so the "related reading" section does not offer independent viewpoints.
Potential Concerns
  • The article's claim that "约 80% 的搜索用户至少在 40% 的搜索中依赖 AI 摘要" (approximately 80% of search users rely on AI summaries in at least 40% of searches) is a specific statistic that should be verified against the original Bain & Company research. The phrasing is somewhat ambiguous — it could mean 80% of users use AI summaries for at least 40% of their searches, which is a compound claim that warrants careful reading.
  • The page does not disclose whether the publisher has any commercial relationship with the cited platforms (Google, OpenAI) or the research firm.

GEO Relevance Assessment

For a page about GEO, this article practices what it preaches:

  • Direct answers: The "直接答案" (Direct Answer) section at the top provides an immediate summary.
  • Clear structure: Headings, lists, and tables are used throughout.
  • Source citations: External references are provided, though not hyperlinked inline.
  • Entity consistency: The publisher's brand (实解智能) and product (Open GEO Console) are consistently presented.
  • Technical accessibility: The page appears to be server-rendered (content is directly readable without JavaScript execution).

Recommendations for Readers

  1. Verify the Bain & Company statistics by locating the original research before citing them in business contexts.
  2. Treat the Open GEO Console promotion as a product offering, not an independent evaluation tool. Consider testing it alongside other GEO assessment methods.
  3. Cross-reference the Google and OpenAI guidance cited in the article, as these are primary sources that may contain more detailed or updated information.
  4. Note the publication date (August 2026) — AI search capabilities and platform policies evolve rapidly, so some specifics may have changed by the time of reading.
  5. The acceptance checklist is genuinely useful as a starting point for technical audits, regardless of whether you use the publisher's services.

Overall Verdict

Rating: 7.5/10

This is a well-structured, practical guide to GEO that offers genuine value for enterprise website owners. Its strengths lie in its balanced claims, actionable checklist, and clear separation of what GEO can and cannot achieve. The main weaknesses are the unverifiable statistics, the self-promotional elements, and the lack of independent validation of the methodology. It is a useful starting point for understanding GEO, but readers should supplement it with primary sources and independent research.

Bottom line: Worth reading for the framework and checklist; treat the statistics with caution and the product promotion with appropriate skepticism.
